turns.text: Socrates, before I even met you I used to hear that you are always in a state of perplexity and that you bring others to the same state, and now I think you are bewitching and beguiling me, simply putting me under a spell, so that I am quite perplexed.
turns.speaker: MENO

turns.text: Indeed, if a joke is in order, you seem, in appearance and in every other way, to be like the broad torpedo fish, for it too makes anyone who comes close and touches it feel numb, and you now seem to have had that kind of effect on me, for both my mind and my tongue are numb, and I have no answer to give you.
turns.speaker: MENO

turns.text: Yet I have made many speeches about virtue before large audiences on a thousand occasions, very good speeches as I thought, but now I cannot even say what it is.
turns.speaker: MENO

turns.text: You are a rascal, Meno, and you nearly deceived me.
turns.speaker: SOCRATES

turns.text: Why so particularly, Socrates?
turns.speaker: MENO

turns.text: Because I know why you likened me to the torpedo fish.
turns.speaker: SOCRATES

turns.text: If I do numb you, it is because I myself am numb, and I cause others to be so; for I do not know what virtue is either.
turns.speaker: SOCRATES

turns.text: I am even more at a loss than you are, and so I share with you only my own perplexity.
turns.speaker: SOCRATES

turns.text: And how will you look for something, Socrates, when you do not know at all what it is?
turns.speaker: MENO

turns.text: How will you aim to search for something you do not know? If you find it, how will you know that this is what you did not know?
turns.speaker: MENO

turns.text: You understand what an eristic argument you are bringing up—that a man cannot search either for what he knows or for what he does not know.
turns.speaker: SOCRATES

turns.text: For he cannot search for what he knows—since he knows it—and he cannot search for what he does not know—since he does not know what to look for.
turns.speaker: SOCRATES

turns.text: As it is, we must not believe that this argument is sound.
turns.speaker: SOCRATES

turns.text: I have heard wise men and women speak of divine matters—they include priests and priestesses.
turns.speaker: SOCRATES

turns.text: They say that the soul of man is immortal, and that when one dies, it departs and is born again, and nothing is ever destroyed.
turns.speaker: SOCRATES

turns.text: Thus, because the soul has been born many times and has seen all things, there is nothing it has not learned; it is no wonder that it can recollect what it once knew.
turns.speaker: SOCRATES

turns.text: Therefore one ought to be courageous and try to discover what one does not presently know, or recollect it.
turns.speaker: SOCRATES

turns.text: Can you teach me that this is so, Socrates?
turns.speaker: MENO

turns.text: I can, if you are willing to follow me closely.
turns.speaker: SOCRATES

turns.text: Call one of your attendants, whichever you like, so that I may show you by example.
turns.speaker: SOCRATES

turns.text: Certainly.
turns.speaker: MENO

turns.text: Pay close attention, and watch whether he learns or recollects.
turns.speaker: SOCRATES

turns.text: Can you tell me, Socrates, can virtue be taught? Or is it not teachable but the result of practice, or is it neither of these, but men possess it by nature or in some other way?
turns.speaker: MENO

turns.text: Before now, Meno, Thessalians had a high high reputation among the Greeks ... If I do not know what something is, how could I know what qualities it possesses?
turns.speaker: SOCRATES

turns.text: Do you really not know what virtue is? Are we to report this to the folk back home about you?
turns.speaker: MENO

turns.text: Not only that, my friend, but also that, as I believe, I have never yet met anyone else who did know.
turns.speaker: SOCRATES

turns.text: It is not hard to tell you, Socrates. First, if you want the virtue of a man ... and very many others.
turns.speaker: MENO

turns.text: I seem to be in great luck, Meno; while I am looking for one virtue, I have found you to have a whole swarm of them.
turns.speaker: SOCRATES

turns.text: If I were asking you what is the nature of bees ... Tell me, what would you answer?
turns.speaker: SOCRATES

turns.text: I would say that they do not differ from one another in being bees.
turns.speaker: MENO

turns.text: The same is true of virtues. They all share one form. That is what we must seek.
turns.speaker: SOCRATES

turns.text: I am asking whether you think it is only in the case of virtue that there is one for man, another for woman ... does it have the same form everywhere?
turns.speaker: SOCRATES

turns.text: The health of a man seems to me the same as that of a woman.
turns.speaker: MENO

turns.text: And so with size and strength? If a woman is strong ... strength is the same?
turns.speaker: SOCRATES

turns.text: I do not think so.
turns.speaker: MENO

turns.text: So all human beings are good in the same way. They acquire the same qualities.
turns.speaker: SOCRATES

turns.text: What else but to be able to rule over people, if you are seeking one description to fit them all.
turns.speaker: MENO

turns.text: But is this true of children and slaves as well? Should they rule too?
turns.speaker: SOCRATES

turns.text: And should we not add: rule justly and not unjustly?
turns.speaker: SOCRATES

turns.text: Certainly—for justice is virtue.
turns.speaker: MENO

turns.text: Is it virtue, Meno, or a virtue? As roundness is a shape, but not shape itself?
turns.speaker: SOCRATES

turns.text: Suppose someone asked you: What is shape? And you replied: roundness. Would he not ask: is roundness a shape, or a shape among many?
turns.speaker: SOCRATES

turns.text: I would say it is a shape among many.
turns.speaker: MENO

turns.text: Then you would be asked: what is that in which all shapes share? Speak in terms known to your questioner, not in clever disputations.
turns.speaker: SOCRATES

turns.text: I think I understand what you mean.
turns.speaker: MENO

turns.text: Shape is the boundary of a solid. That is a definition in common terms.
turns.speaker: SOCRATES

turns.text: Tell me, boy, do you know that a square figure is like this?
turns.speaker: SOCRATES

turns.text: Yes.
turns.speaker: SLAVE

turns.text: And that a square has all these four equal sides?
turns.speaker: SOCRATES

turns.text: Yes.
turns.speaker: SLAVE

turns.text: And has it not also equal lines drawn across it through the middle?
turns.speaker: SOCRATES

turns.text: Yes.
turns.speaker: SLAVE

turns.text: Now if this side is two feet, and this other side is also two, how many feet will the whole be?
turns.speaker: SOCRATES

turns.text: Four.
turns.speaker: SLAVE

turns.text: And if one wished to make another square double its size, how long would each of its sides be?
turns.speaker: SOCRATES

turns.text: Plainly, Socrates, twice the length.
turns.speaker: SLAVE

turns.text: You say that a square double in area must have sides twice as long?
turns.speaker: SOCRATES

turns.text: Yes.
turns.speaker: SLAVE

turns.text: Let us see. If the side becomes twice as long, it will be four feet, will it not?
turns.speaker: SOCRATES

turns.text: Yes.
turns.speaker: SLAVE

turns.text: Then the area will be sixteen feet, will it not? For four times four is sixteen.
turns.speaker: SOCRATES

turns.text: It seems so.
turns.speaker: SLAVE

turns.text: But you were saying that double the area would be eight?
turns.speaker: SOCRATES

turns.text: Yes.
turns.speaker: SLAVE

turns.text: So it is not by doubling the side that one gets a double area.
turns.speaker: SOCRATES

turns.text: That is true.
turns.speaker: SLAVE

turns.text: Now tell me: if the double area is not produced by doubling the side, what length should the side be?
turns.speaker: SOCRATES

turns.text: I do not know.
turns.speaker: SLAVE

turns.text: You see, Meno, he is now in the state of not knowing.
turns.speaker: SOCRATES

turns.text: And yet, formerly he thought he knew and answered confidently.
turns.speaker: SOCRATES

turns.text: Now he is perplexed and numbed like he was before, yet he is better off about the matter he did not know.
turns.speaker: SOCRATES

turns.text: Observe then whether the side of the double square might not be this diagonal.
turns.speaker: SOCRATES

turns.text: What is a diagonal?
turns.speaker: SLAVE

turns.text: It is the line drawn from one corner to the opposite corner of the square.
turns.speaker: SOCRATES

turns.text: Yes, I know that.
turns.speaker: SLAVE

turns.text: Then consider whether four such equal lines will not enclose the double area.
turns.speaker: SOCRATES

turns.text: So it seems, Socrates.
turns.speaker: SLAVE

turns.text: Do you see, Meno, how he is now answering? And does he not now say what he thinks is true?
turns.speaker: SOCRATES

turns.text: Yes.
turns.speaker: MENO

turns.text: And yet he did not know this before he was questioned.
turns.speaker: SOCRATES

turns.text: True.
turns.speaker: MENO

turns.text: He was led into confusing and contradicting himself. But now he has recovered himself and found the right answer.
turns.speaker: SOCRATES

turns.text: Does this not seem to you like recollection?
turns.speaker: SOCRATES

turns.text: Indeed.
turns.speaker: MENO

turns.text: Well then, Socrates, what do you think? Is virtue teachable?
turns.speaker: MENO

turns.text: I would be surprised if we were able to say, since we do not yet know what virtue is.
turns.speaker: SOCRATES

turns.text: Do you not think we have made some progress?
turns.speaker: MENO

turns.text: Perhaps. But not enough to answer whether it is teachable.
turns.speaker: SOCRATES

turns.text: Here is Anytus, Meno. Let us ask him whether virtue can be taught.
turns.speaker: SOCRATES

turns.text: By the gods, Socrates, I think it would be better if you would talk about someone else. I am quite prepared to speak on virtue, but I do not enjoy hearing people slander our politicians.
turns.speaker: ANYTUS

turns.text: Do you think, Anytus, that the good men of the city made their sons good by instruction?
turns.speaker: SOCRATES

turns.text: Any Athenian gentleman could teach them better than the sophists could.
turns.speaker: ANYTUS

turns.text: Have the sophists done you any harm, Anytus?
turns.speaker: SOCRATES

turns.text: By Heracles, I would be glad if no citizen of Athens were ever corrupted by them.
turns.speaker: ANYTUS

turns.text: Yet you have never met any of them nor spoken to any of them?
turns.speaker: SOCRATES

turns.text: No, and I do not need to know them to know what they are.
turns.speaker: ANYTUS

turns.text: You speak harshly, Anytus, without having tested them. But tell me: do the good men of the city make others good?
turns.speaker: SOCRATES

turns.text: You will come to harm, Socrates, if you go on speaking in this way.
turns.speaker: ANYTUS

turns.text: I am saying nothing but the truth, Anytus. If they could teach virtue, they would teach their own sons.
turns.speaker: SOCRATES

turns.text: I advise you to be careful.
turns.speaker: ANYTUS

turns.text: With that, Anytus moved away, angry.
turns.speaker: NARRATION

turns.text: You see, Meno, there are no teachers of virtue.
turns.speaker: SOCRATES

turns.text: For if good men had been able to teach it, they would have handed it on to their own sons.
turns.speaker: SOCRATES

turns.text: It seems they do not.
turns.speaker: MENO

turns.text: Nor do the sophists teach it, as Anytus claimed, for none of them make their pupils virtuous.
turns.speaker: SOCRATES

turns.text: Which do you think is worse, Polus—to do what’s unjust or to suffer it?
turns.speaker: Socrates

turns.text: To suffer it. No one would choose the other.
turns.speaker: Polus

turns.text: So you agree that doing injustice is shameful?
turns.speaker: Socrates

turns.text: Of course—everyone admits that.
turns.speaker: Polus

turns.text: And what is shameful is bad, isn’t it?
turns.speaker: Socrates

turns.text: Yes, that seems to follow.
turns.speaker: Polus

turns.text: Then doing injustice is worse than suffering it.
turns.speaker: Socrates

turns.text: Being punished is the way the soul is relieved of its injustice.
turns.speaker: Socrates

turns.text: How can punishment benefit the one who suffers it?
turns.speaker: Polus

turns.text: Because punishment is a kind of cure, Polus. No one wants to keep the soul diseased.
turns.speaker: Socrates

turns.text: You’re saying the criminal is made better by suffering?
turns.speaker: Polus

turns.text: Exactly—just as the sick body is better for painful treatment.
turns.speaker: Socrates

turns.text: The man who does what’s unjust is miserable, Polus.
turns.speaker: Socrates

turns.text: How can that be? He gets whatever he wants.
turns.speaker: Polus

turns.text: No—the one who does injustice and escapes punishment is the most miserable of all.
turns.speaker: Socrates

turns.text: You’re saying the tyrant—the freest man—is actually the worst off?
turns.speaker: Polus

turns.text: Yes. For he corrupts the soul most deeply and has no one to heal him.
turns.speaker: Socrates

turns.text: The man devoted to unchecked pleasure is like a jar full of holes—no matter how much he pours in, it leaks out again.
turns.speaker: Socrates

turns.text: That’s a ridiculous image, Socrates.
turns.speaker: Callicles

turns.text: Yet it’s your way of life I’m describing, Callicles—endless craving, never satisfaction.
turns.speaker: Socrates

turns.text: I deny that such a life is miserable.
turns.speaker: Callicles

turns.text: But you agree the one who can be satisfied is better off than one who constantly needs refilling?
turns.speaker: Socrates

turns.text: Do you say that the pleasant and the good are the same, Callicles?
turns.speaker: Socrates

turns.text: Yes. I stand by that.
turns.speaker: Callicles

turns.text: Is it pleasant to scratch an itch endlessly?
turns.speaker: Socrates

turns.text: It can be.
turns.speaker: Callicles

turns.text: Then the man covered in itching sores is living the best life, if he scratches constantly?
turns.speaker: Socrates

turns.text: No—that’s absurd.
turns.speaker: Callicles

turns.text: Then the pleasant and the good are not the same.
turns.speaker: Socrates

turns.text: Tell me, Gorgias, does the orator know what is just and what is unjust?
turns.speaker: Socrates

turns.text: Yes, he does—if he is to be an orator at all.
turns.speaker: Gorgias

turns.text: And does he teach these things to others?
turns.speaker: Socrates

turns.text: Certainly. That is part of his craft.
turns.speaker: Gorgias

turns.text: Then an unjust orator would not exist, for he knows justice and teaches it?
turns.speaker: Socrates

turns.text: Please answer the question I put to you, Gorgias—shortly.
turns.speaker: Socrates

turns.text: I am trying, Socrates, but you keep shifting the topic.
turns.speaker: Gorgias

turns.text: Not at all. You’re giving long speeches instead of the simple answer required.
turns.speaker: Socrates

turns.text: Very well, ask again.
turns.speaker: Gorgias

turns.text: I already did. You owe me the answer—not another speech.
turns.speaker: Socrates

turns.text: You claim the orator has great power, Polus?
turns.speaker: Socrates

turns.text: Yes—the greatest of human powers.
turns.speaker: Polus

turns.text: Does he know what is truly good and what is bad?
turns.speaker: Socrates

turns.text: Not necessarily. But that doesn't lessen his power!
turns.speaker: Polus

turns.text: Then you’ve admitted he acts without knowledge—and the man without knowledge harms himself the most.
turns.speaker: Socrates

turns.text: By nature, Socrates, the stronger and better should rule the weaker.
turns.speaker: Callicles

turns.text: And you call ‘stronger’ the majority or the one?
turns.speaker: Socrates

turns.text: The one, of course—the superior man.
turns.speaker: Callicles

turns.text: Then if the many restrain this one by law, the many are stronger?
turns.speaker: Socrates

turns.text: That’s not what I meant.
turns.speaker: Callicles

turns.text: But it’s what you said—and your principle collapses under its own definition.
turns.speaker: Socrates

turns.text: Tell me plainly, Callicles—what life are you defending as best?
turns.speaker: Socrates

turns.text: The life of the man who indulges his desires freely.
turns.speaker: Callicles

turns.text: And is this life admirable because it is pleasant, or for some other reason?
turns.speaker: Socrates

turns.text: Because pleasure is the good.
turns.speaker: Callicles

turns.text: Then you must defend that principle to its end. Are you prepared to?
turns.speaker: Socrates

turns.text: Tell me, Callicles—do you yourself indulge your desires without restraint?
turns.speaker: Socrates

turns.text: Of course not. I exercise discipline like any man of sense.
turns.speaker: Callicles

turns.text: Yet you said the best life is the unrestrained one.
turns.speaker: Socrates

turns.text: Yes, but that doesn’t mean one should practice it constantly.
turns.speaker: Callicles

turns.text: Then you admit your doctrine contradicts your own way of living.
turns.speaker: Socrates

turns.text: A pilot does not merely steer whichever way he wishes. He knows what is best for the ship and those aboard.
turns.speaker: Socrates

turns.text: Yes, because his craft demands it.
turns.speaker: Callicles

turns.text: Then a man who rules must know what is best—not merely act on desire.
turns.speaker: Socrates

turns.text: You’re smuggling your assumptions into my view.
turns.speaker: Callicles

turns.text: No—I’m showing that true power requires knowledge, just as navigation requires skill.
turns.speaker: Socrates

turns.text: I won’t answer your childish questions anymore.
turns.speaker: Callicles

turns.text: If you refuse to answer, there’s no way for us to examine the truth together.
turns.speaker: Socrates

turns.text: I’m tired of your traps.
turns.speaker: Callicles

turns.text: They are not traps, Callicles. They are conditions for any rational inquiry.
turns.speaker: Socrates

turns.text: Fine—ask again.
turns.speaker: Callicles

turns.text: Picture the soul, Callicles, stripped naked before the judge—every deed visible.
turns.speaker: Socrates

turns.text: That’s just myth-making.
turns.speaker: Callicles

turns.text: Myths teach truths the arrogant cannot hear plainly.
turns.speaker: Socrates

turns.text: And what truth is that supposed to reveal?
turns.speaker: Callicles

turns.text: That injustice deforms the soul—and punishment restores it.
turns.speaker: Socrates

turns.text: I am the only one of the Athenians, Callicles, who tries to practice the true political art.
turns.speaker: Socrates

turns.text: You boast that, yet the city ignores you.
turns.speaker: Callicles

turns.text: Better ignored while doing right than praised while corrupting my soul.
turns.speaker: Socrates

turns.text: And what is it you want from me, then?
turns.speaker: Callicles

turns.text: Only this: choose which life you will live—the life of discipline or the life of ruin.
turns.speaker: Socrates

turns.text: Polus agreed with you that doing what’s unjust is more shameful than suffering it. As a result of this admission he was bound and gagged by you in the discussion, too ashamed to say what he thought.
turns.speaker: Callicles

turns.text: So you admit that shame compelled him—not understanding?
turns.speaker: Socrates

turns.text: Yes. He was forced to contradict himself because he dared not say what he truly believed.
turns.speaker: Callicles

turns.text: Then Polus conceded not conviction, but fear of appearing base before the many.
turns.speaker: Socrates

turns.text: Either refute philosophy, or else, by the Dog, Callicles will not agree with Callicles, but will be out of harmony with himself all his life long.
turns.speaker: Socrates

turns.text: Socrates, you’re grandstanding in these speeches, acting like a crowd pleaser.
turns.speaker: Callicles

turns.text: It is better for the many to contradict me than for me to contradict myself, though I am only one person.
turns.speaker: Socrates

turns.text: You twist everything—first forcing Gorgias to contradict himself, and now Polus.
turns.speaker: Callicles

turns.text: I believe I practice the true political craft, because my speeches do not aim at gratification but at what is best.
turns.speaker: Socrates

turns.text: Yet here you are persuading—using rhetoric to deny rhetoric.
turns.speaker: Callicles

turns.text: If I persuade, it is not as a pastry chef persuades children, but as a doctor speaking bitter truths.
turns.speaker: Socrates

turns.text: Still, you must use the very craft you condemn to defend your view.
turns.speaker: Callicles

turns.text: Which do you think is more shameful, doing what’s unjust or suffering it?
turns.speaker: Socrates

turns.text: Doing it.
turns.speaker: Polus

turns.text: And which is worse?
turns.speaker: Socrates

turns.text: Suffering it is worse.
turns.speaker: Polus

turns.text: Then shame does not track evil—your claim collapses.
turns.speaker: Socrates

turns.text: Isn’t disciplining the soul better for it than indulgence?
turns.speaker: Socrates

turns.text: I don’t know what you mean. Ask somebody else.
turns.speaker: Callicles

turns.text: This fellow won’t put up with being benefited and disciplined.
turns.speaker: Socrates

turns.text: And I couldn’t care less about anything you say.
turns.speaker: Callicles

turns.text: If an orator and a doctor competed before a city, the doctor would make no showing at all, but the orator would be appointed.
turns.speaker: Gorgias

turns.text: So persuasion defeats knowledge among the ignorant.
turns.speaker: Socrates

turns.text: Such is the accomplishment of this craft.
turns.speaker: Gorgias

turns.text: And such is why it must be used justly, lest it mislead those who lack expertise.
turns.speaker: Socrates

turns.text: Socrates, you asked what piety is. I still say it is what I am doing now. Is this not sufficient?
turns.speaker: Euthyphro

turns.text: But by Zeus, Euthyphro, do you think you have such accurate knowledge about piety and impiety that you are not afraid of committing another impiety by prosecuting your father?
turns.speaker: Socrates

turns.text: I would be of no use, Socrates, if I did not have accurate knowledge of all such matters.
turns.speaker: Euthyphro

turns.text: Then teach me. Isn’t the pious always the same as itself, and the impious the opposite of the pious?
turns.speaker: Socrates

turns.text: It certainly is.
turns.speaker: Euthyphro

turns.text: So tell me what the pious itself is.
turns.speaker: Socrates

turns.text: The pious is what I am doing now: prosecuting a wrongdoer.
turns.speaker: Euthyphro

turns.text: I asked for the form itself, not an example of one of the many pious things.
turns.speaker: Socrates

turns.text: Very well, Socrates, I will try again: what is beloved by the gods is pious, and what is not beloved by them is impious.
turns.speaker: Euthyphro

turns.text: Weren’t we just saying that the gods disagree with one another?
turns.speaker: Socrates

turns.text: Yes, we were.
turns.speaker: Euthyphro

turns.text: Then the same things will be loved by some gods and hated by others.
turns.speaker: Socrates

turns.text: It seems so.
turns.speaker: Euthyphro

turns.text: So the same act would be both pious and impious?
turns.speaker: Socrates

turns.text: I'm afraid so.
turns.speaker: Euthyphro

turns.text: Explain again, Socrates — how must we examine this definition?
turns.speaker: Euthyphro

turns.text: Consider: is the pious loved by the gods because it is pious, or is it pious because it is loved?
turns.speaker: Socrates

turns.text: I don’t know what you mean.
turns.speaker: Euthyphro

turns.text: We say something is carried because it is being carried, not the reverse. Likewise something is loved because it is being loved.
turns.speaker: Socrates

turns.text: Necessarily.
turns.speaker: Euthyphro

turns.text: Then the pious is loved because it is pious — not pious because it is loved.
turns.speaker: Socrates

turns.text: Socrates, whatever I put forward keeps wandering off and will not stay where we put it.
turns.speaker: Euthyphro

turns.text: These things seem to belong to my ancestor Dedalos — your definitions do not stay put.
turns.speaker: Socrates

turns.text: They would stay put for me, at least; you are the one who makes them move.
turns.speaker: Euthyphro

turns.text: Then I must be more skilled than Dedalos, moving not only my arguments but others’. Yet I want them fixed more than wealth.
turns.speaker: Socrates

turns.text: Piety is the part of justice that is attending to the gods.
turns.speaker: Euthyphro

turns.text: Does attending mean benefiting them, as horse-training benefits horses?
turns.speaker: Socrates

turns.text: By Zeus, no.
turns.speaker: Euthyphro

turns.text: Then what kind of attending is it?
turns.speaker: Socrates

turns.text: The kind slaves provide to masters.
turns.speaker: Euthyphro

turns.text: And what is the great work the gods accomplish using us as servants?
turns.speaker: Socrates

turns.text: Saying and doing what is pleasing to the gods in prayers and sacrifices.
turns.speaker: Euthyphro

turns.text: So the pious is what is pleasing to the gods — again?
turns.speaker: Socrates

turns.text: We must begin again from the beginning to examine what the pious is — I will not give up until I understand it.
turns.speaker: Socrates

turns.text: Unless you knew clearly, you would never have tried to prosecute your father.
turns.speaker: Socrates

turns.text: Some other time, Socrates. I am in a hurry and must go.
turns.speaker: Euthyphro

turns.text: You cast me down from a great hope — that I would learn from you what is pious and free myself from Meletos' charge.
turns.speaker: Socrates

turns.text: Master Gotama, does the Tathāgata exist after death?
turns.speaker: Vacchagotta

turns.text: Vaccha, that does not apply.
turns.speaker: The Buddha

turns.text: Then, Master Gotama, does the Tathāgata not exist after death?
turns.speaker: Vacchagotta

turns.text: Vaccha, that does not apply.
turns.speaker: The Buddha

turns.text: Then is it that the Tathāgata both exists and does not exist after death?
turns.speaker: Vacchagotta

turns.text: Vaccha, that does not apply.
turns.speaker: The Buddha

turns.text: But Master Gotama, when a fire goes out, is it correct to say that the fire has gone east, west, north, or south?
turns.speaker: Vacchagotta

turns.text: Vaccha, the question does not apply. The fire depended on fuel. When that fuel is used up, it is said to be 'out' through lack of fuel.
turns.speaker: The Buddha

turns.text: Then how should I understand the disappearance of the fire, Master Gotama?
turns.speaker: Vacchagotta

turns.text: In the same way, Vaccha, all terms for the Tathāgata after death do not apply. Freed from reckoning by form, feeling, perception, fabrications, or consciousness, he is deep, immeasurable, unfathomable — like the ocean.
turns.speaker: The Buddha

turns.text: Then, Master Gotama, is there a self?
turns.speaker: Vacchagotta

turns.text: Vaccha, if I were to say 'there is a self,' you would be aligned with the eternalists.
turns.speaker: The Buddha

turns.text: Then, Master Gotama, is there no self?
turns.speaker: Vacchagotta

turns.text: If I were to say 'there is no self,' you would fall into confusion: 'Formerly I had a self; now I have no self at all.'
turns.speaker: The Buddha

turns.text: Vaccha, this question is not answered because you are not yet ready for the grasping to be stilled.
turns.speaker: The Buddha

turns.text: Then why, Master Gotama, do you not declare these things plainly?
turns.speaker: Vacchagotta

turns.text: Vaccha, if I were to answer in your terms, it would not lead to dispassion, to peace, to cessation, to direct knowledge, to awakening.
turns.speaker: The Buddha

turns.text: So Master Gotama leaves me uncertain and without ground.
turns.speaker: Vacchagotta

turns.text: Vaccha, it is precisely your ground that must be seen as groundless.
turns.speaker: The Buddha

turns.text: Then I will consider this further, Master Gotama.
turns.speaker: Vacchagotta

turns.text: I will question the ascetic Gotama. If he answers me well, so much the better. If he does not, I will shake him, agitate him, pull him about, as a strong man might shake a feeble goat!
turns.speaker: Saccaka

turns.text: But what is your doctrine, Aggivessana? What is it that you hold?
turns.speaker: The Buddha

turns.text: Form, Master Gotama, is the self. Feeling is the self. Perception is the self. Fabrications are the self. Consciousness is the self.
turns.speaker: Saccaka

turns.text: Do you say, Aggivessana, that all five aggregates are the self?
turns.speaker: The Buddha

turns.text: Exactly so, Master Gotama.
turns.speaker: Saccaka

turns.text: Aggivessana, is form permanent or impermanent?
turns.speaker: The Buddha

turns.text: Impermanent, Master Gotama.
turns.speaker: Saccaka

turns.text: Is what is impermanent easeful or stressful?
turns.speaker: The Buddha

turns.text: Stressful, Master Gotama.
turns.speaker: Saccaka

turns.text: Is it fitting to regard what is impermanent, stressful, subject to change, as ‘This is mine; this is my self; this is what I am’?
turns.speaker: The Buddha

turns.text: No indeed, Master Gotama.
turns.speaker: Saccaka

turns.text: Aggivessana, did you not say that form is the self?
turns.speaker: The Buddha

turns.text: I did, Master Gotama.
turns.speaker: Saccaka

turns.text: But now, Aggivessana, you admit it is impermanent, stressful, subject to change, and cannot rightly be regarded as self. How can both of your claims stand?
turns.speaker: The Buddha

turns.text: And at that moment, Saccaka, the debater, broke into a sweat, as if water were streaming from his body.
turns.speaker: Narrator

turns.text: Aggivessana, your doctrine is being pressed. Take care.
turns.speaker: The Buddha

turns.text: Master Gotama, let us set aside form. Let us discuss feeling...
turns.speaker: Saccaka

turns.text: Aggivessana, we will not move on until we settle what has already been said.
turns.speaker: The Buddha

turns.text: But Master Gotama, I wish to proceed.
turns.speaker: Saccaka

turns.text: Aggivessana, when you made your claim, you stood upon it. Now that it falters, you try to flee. But the matter must be resolved here.
turns.speaker: The Buddha

turns.text: Then proceed, Master Gotama.
turns.speaker: Saccaka

turns.text: Aggivessana, is feeling permanent or impermanent?
turns.speaker: The Buddha

turns.text: Impermanent, Master Gotama.
turns.speaker: Saccaka

turns.text: Is perception permanent or impermanent?
turns.speaker: The Buddha

turns.text: Impermanent, Master Gotama.
turns.speaker: Saccaka

turns.text: And fabrications, consciousness — are they permanent or impermanent?
turns.speaker: The Buddha

turns.text: Impermanent, Master Gotama.
turns.speaker: Saccaka

turns.text: Then, Aggivessana, is it fitting to regard any of these as ‘This is mine; this is my self; this is what I am’?
turns.speaker: The Buddha

turns.text: No indeed, Master Gotama.
turns.speaker: Saccaka

turns.text: Form is not-self. For if form were self, it would not lead to affliction, and one could say: 'Let my form be thus.' But you cannot.
turns.speaker: THE BUDDHA

turns.text: Feeling is not-self. If feeling were self, it would not oppress, and one could command it. But it does not obey.
turns.speaker: THE BUDDHA

turns.text: Perception is not-self. If it were self, it would not shift and change against your will.
turns.speaker: THE BUDDHA

turns.text: Fabrications are not-self. They arise and pass without regard for your wishes.
turns.speaker: THE BUDDHA

turns.text: Consciousness is not-self. If it were self, it would not alter. But it flickers and fades.
turns.speaker: THE BUDDHA

turns.text: Seeing this with wisdom, the instructed disciple becomes disenchanted. Disenchantment leads to fading. Fading leads to release.
turns.speaker: THE BUDDHA

turns.text: Monks, the eye is burning. Forms are burning. Eye-consciousness is burning. Eye-contact is burning.
turns.speaker: THE BUDDHA

turns.text: Burning with what? Burning with the fire of greed, the fire of hatred, the fire of delusion.
turns.speaker: THE BUDDHA

turns.text: The ear is burning. Sounds are burning. The nose is burning. Smells are burning. The mind is burning. Thoughts are burning.
turns.speaker: THE BUDDHA

turns.text: Seeing this, the instructed disciple becomes disenchanted with the sense fields. Through disenchantment comes fading. Through fading comes release.
turns.speaker: THE BUDDHA

turns.text: While this discourse was being spoken, the hearts of a thousand monks were liberated.
turns.speaker: NARRATION

turns.text: Lady, what is feeling?
turns.speaker: Visakha

turns.text: There are three feelings, friend Visakha: pleasant feeling, painful feeling, and neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling.
turns.speaker: Dhammadinna

turns.text: But Lady, what is the cause and condition for feeling?
turns.speaker: Visakha

turns.text: Contact, friend Visakha, is the cause and condition for feeling.
turns.speaker: Dhammadinna

turns.text: But Lady, what is the cause and condition for contact?
turns.speaker: Visakha

turns.text: Name-and-form is the condition for contact.
turns.speaker: Dhammadinna

turns.text: Lady, what is the cause and condition for craving?
turns.speaker: Visakha

turns.text: Feeling, friend Visakha, is the cause and condition for craving.
turns.speaker: Dhammadinna

turns.text: And what is the cause and condition for feeling?
turns.speaker: Visakha

turns.text: Contact is the condition for feeling.
turns.speaker: Dhammadinna

turns.text: And for contact?
turns.speaker: Visakha

turns.text: Name-and-form is the condition for contact.
turns.speaker: Dhammadinna

turns.text: Lady, what is the cessation of craving?
turns.speaker: Visakha

turns.text: The ending of craving, the abandonment of craving, the relinquishing of craving—this, friend Visakha, is the cessation of craving.
turns.speaker: Dhammadinna

turns.text: And what is the path leading to the cessation of craving?
turns.speaker: Visakha

turns.text: The Noble Eightfold Path leads to the cessation of craving.
turns.speaker: Dhammadinna

turns.text: And what is the Noble Eightfold Path?
turns.speaker: Visakha

turns.text: Lady, what is the self? And what is not-self?
turns.speaker: Visakha

turns.text: Form, friend Visakha, is not self. Feeling is not self. Perception is not self. Fabrications are not self. Consciousness is not self.
turns.speaker: Dhammadinna

turns.text: Lady, why are these not self?
turns.speaker: Visakha

turns.text: Because, friend Visakha, they are impermanent, changing, subject to decay.
turns.speaker: Dhammadinna

turns.text: Is there, then, any self?
turns.speaker: Visakha

turns.text: Visakha, that is a matter for the Tathāgata.
turns.speaker: Dhammadinna

turns.text: But tell me now, friend Visakha—what is feeling?
turns.speaker: Dhammadinna

turns.text: Lady, feeling is pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant.
turns.speaker: Visakha

turns.text: And what is the cause of feeling?
turns.speaker: Dhammadinna

turns.text: Contact is the cause of feeling.
turns.speaker: Visakha

turns.text: Good, Visakha. You have understood well.
turns.speaker: Dhammadinna

turns.text: There are thoughts of sensuality, ill will, and cruelty. And there are thoughts of renunciation, goodwill, and harmlessness.
turns.speaker: THE BUDDHA

turns.text: When I directed my mind to thoughts of sensuality, I understood: 'This thought leads to my own harm, to the harm of others, and to the harm of both.'
turns.speaker: THE BUDDHA

turns.text: Knowing this, such a thought is to be abandoned.
turns.speaker: THE BUDDHA

turns.text: When I directed my mind to thoughts of renunciation, I understood: 'This leads to my welfare, the welfare of others, and the welfare of both.'
turns.speaker: THE BUDDHA

turns.text: Knowing this, such a thought is to be cultivated.
turns.speaker: THE BUDDHA

turns.text: Thus I sorted thoughts into two classes: those to be abandoned and those to be developed.
turns.speaker: THE BUDDHA

turns.text: He systematically divided and trained his mind in this way.
turns.speaker: NARRATION

turns.text: When unskillful thoughts arise, one should replace them with a skillful counterpart.
turns.speaker: THE BUDDHA

turns.text: If that does not calm the mind, one should attend to the danger in the unskillful thought.
turns.speaker: THE BUDDHA

turns.text: If that does not calm it, one should ignore and forget the thought.
turns.speaker: THE BUDDHA

turns.text: If that does not calm it, one should relax the formation of the thought itself.
turns.speaker: THE BUDDHA

turns.text: If that does not calm it, one should crush the mind with the mind, restraining it.
turns.speaker: THE BUDDHA

turns.text: A mind so trained becomes steady and settled.
turns.speaker: NARRATION

turns.text: Rahula, any action you wish to do with body, speech, or mind should be examined again and again, just as one looks into a mirror.
turns.speaker: THE BUDDHA

turns.text: If, on reflection, you know: 'This action would lead to harm for myself or others,' then such an action should not be done.
turns.speaker: THE BUDDHA

turns.text: But if, upon reflection, you know: 'This action would lead to no harm,' then it is fitting to do it.
turns.speaker: THE BUDDHA

turns.text: And having done an action, you should reflect: 'Did this action lead to harm?'
turns.speaker: THE BUDDHA

turns.text: If it did, confess it, reveal it, make amends, and train yourself not to repeat it.
turns.speaker: THE BUDDHA

turns.text: If it did not lead to harm, you may rest easy, and continue training in wholesome qualities.
turns.speaker: THE BUDDHA

turns.text: Yes, sir.
turns.speaker: RAHULA

turns.text: Kesi, you are a trainer of horses. How do you train them?
turns.speaker: THE BUDDHA

turns.text: Lord, I train them first with gentleness. If that fails, with firmness. If that fails, with both. And if a horse cannot be tamed by any method, I end its life.
turns.speaker: KESI

turns.text: So too, Kesi, I train by gentleness, by firmness, and by a blend of both.
turns.speaker: THE BUDDHA

turns.text: But if a person cannot be tamed by any method, I do not end their life. I simply do not instruct them further.
turns.speaker: THE BUDDHA

turns.text: It is better to let such a person go than to waste training on one who refuses to learn.
turns.speaker: THE BUDDHA

turns.text: It is wonderful, lord, how you train people without causing harm.
turns.speaker: KESI

turns.text: Master Gotama, this is my view: ‘I take no view. Nothing is acceptable to me.’
turns.speaker: Dighanakha

turns.text: Aggivessana, do you hold that view as true?
turns.speaker: The Buddha

turns.text: Yes, Master Gotama, this is truly my view.
turns.speaker: Dighanakha

turns.text: But if you take that as true, then at least this one view is acceptable to you.
turns.speaker: The Buddha

turns.text: Master Gotama, it seems this view does not stand as I thought.
turns.speaker: Dighanakha

turns.text: When one says ‘Nothing is acceptable to me,’ that itself is something accepted.
turns.speaker: The Buddha

turns.text: And Dighanakha’s view was thereby shaken.
turns.speaker: Narrator

turns.text: Aggivessana, there are three kinds of views: ‘Everything is pleasing to me,’ ‘Nothing is pleasing to me,’ and ‘Some things are pleasing to me and some are not.’
turns.speaker: The Buddha

turns.text: Master Gotama, how does this apply to one who claims that nothing is acceptable?
turns.speaker: Dighanakha

turns.text: One who says that nothing is acceptable is bound by that view, and thus is not free from clinging.
turns.speaker: The Buddha

turns.text: So even rejecting all things creates a bond?
turns.speaker: Dighanakha

turns.text: Indeed. To grasp the idea ‘nothing is acceptable’ is itself a form of clinging.
turns.speaker: The Buddha

turns.text: Aggivessana, when you experience a pleasant feeling, is it permanent or impermanent?
turns.speaker: The Buddha

turns.text: Impermanent, Master Gotama.
turns.speaker: Dighanakha

turns.text: And unpleasant feelings—permanent or impermanent?
turns.speaker: The Buddha

turns.text: Impermanent, Master Gotama.
turns.speaker: Dighanakha

turns.text: Neutral feelings—permanent or impermanent?
turns.speaker: The Buddha

turns.text: Impermanent as well.
turns.speaker: Dighanakha

turns.text: Aggivessana, when one sees the arising of feeling, its passing away, and its change while it persists—then one is not bound by feeling.
turns.speaker: The Buddha

turns.text: Master Gotama, how should one attend to such seeing?
turns.speaker: Dighanakha

turns.text: Attend simply as ‘feeling arises, feeling remains, feeling passes away.’ When one sees this, there is no ‘I’ in feeling.
turns.speaker: The Buddha

turns.text: So one stands apart from it?
turns.speaker: Dighanakha

turns.text: Just so. One stands as the watcher, not the owned.
turns.speaker: The Buddha

turns.text: And as the Blessed One spoke this teaching, Dighanakha’s mind was liberated from the fetter of views.
turns.speaker: Narrator

turns.text: Master Gotama, marvelous indeed are these teachings.
turns.speaker: Dighanakha

turns.text: When views are abandoned, Aggivessana, one knows directly what arises and ceases.
turns.speaker: The Buddha

turns.text: Venerable sir, what is right view?
turns.speaker: Kaccanagotta

turns.text: Kaccana, by and large, this world is supported by a duality: by existence and by non-existence.
turns.speaker: The Buddha

turns.text: How does this duality bind the world?
turns.speaker: Kaccanagotta

turns.text: One who sees the arising of the world as it really is does not hold the view of non-existence. One who sees the cessation of the world as it really is does not hold the view of existence.
turns.speaker: The Buddha

turns.text: Then right view avoids both?
turns.speaker: Kaccanagotta

turns.text: Indeed. Right view is free from these two extremes.
turns.speaker: The Buddha

turns.text: Kaccana, this world is mostly bound by clinging, taking hold of something or other.
turns.speaker: The Buddha

turns.text: What is the view that abandons clinging?
turns.speaker: Kaccanagotta

turns.text: When one sees dependent origination as it is—‘When this exists, that comes to be; with the arising of this, that arises’—one does not cling to any view of existence or non-existence.
turns.speaker: The Buddha

turns.text: So right view is seeing conditions?
turns.speaker: Kaccanagotta

turns.text: Just so. Seeing conditional arising and conditional cessation.
turns.speaker: The Buddha

turns.text: This seems a middle way beyond views.
turns.speaker: Kaccanagotta

turns.text: It is the middle by which the Tathāgata teaches the Dhamma.
turns.speaker: The Buddha

turns.text: Venerable sir, how does one see rightly?
turns.speaker: Kaccanagotta

turns.text: By seeing that all is merely arising and ceasing.
turns.speaker: The Buddha

turns.text: And seeing this, what does one abandon?
turns.speaker: Kaccanagotta

turns.text: One abandons the thought ‘I am’ in regard to these processes.
turns.speaker: The Buddha

turns.text: So the sense of self depends on misunderstanding the process?
turns.speaker: Kaccanagotta

turns.text: Just so. Where there is arising and ceasing, no self is found.
turns.speaker: The Buddha

turns.text: Venerable sir, should one say ‘there is a self’?
turns.speaker: Kaccanagotta

turns.text: Kaccana, saying ‘there is a self’ is one extreme.
turns.speaker: The Buddha

turns.text: Then should one say ‘there is no self’?
turns.speaker: Kaccanagotta

turns.text: Saying ‘there is no self’ is the other extreme.
turns.speaker: The Buddha

turns.text: Then how should the matter be seen?
turns.speaker: Kaccanagotta

turns.text: With right wisdom seeing only arising and ceasing.
turns.speaker: The Buddha

turns.text: Lord, different teachers come to Kesaputta. Each declares his own doctrine true and condemns the others. We are confused and in doubt.
turns.speaker: KALAMAS

turns.text: It is fitting that you are in doubt, Kalamas. Doubt has arisen about matters that are doubtful.
turns.speaker: THE BUDDHA

turns.text: Do not go by reports, traditions, or legends. Do not go by the authority of texts.
turns.speaker: THE BUDDHA

turns.text: Do not go by reasoning, by logic, by inference, or by acceptance of a view.
turns.speaker: THE BUDDHA

turns.text: When you yourselves know: 'These qualities are unwholesome; these qualities are blameworthy; these qualities lead to harm,' then you should abandon them.
turns.speaker: THE BUDDHA

turns.text: And when you yourselves know: 'These qualities are wholesome; these qualities are blameless; these qualities lead to welfare,' then you should practice them.
turns.speaker: THE BUDDHA

turns.text: Yes, lord. This is clear.
turns.speaker: KALAMAS

turns.text: The Kalamas were uplifted by this teaching.
turns.speaker: NARRATION

turns.text: Lord, these unanswered questions trouble me: Is the world eternal? Not eternal? Finite? Infinite? What is the fate of the Tathagata after death?
turns.speaker: Malunkyaputta

turns.text: If the Lord does not answer, I will renounce the training and return to the world.
turns.speaker: Malunkyaputta

turns.text: Malunkyaputta, did I ever say: ‘Come, be my disciple, and I will explain these things to you’?
turns.speaker: The Buddha

turns.text: No, Lord.
turns.speaker: Malunkyaputta

turns.text: Then why do you claim a demand I never made?
turns.speaker: The Buddha

turns.text: Then what is the purpose of the training, Lord?
turns.speaker: Malunkyaputta

turns.text: Malunkyaputta, suppose a man were struck by a poisoned arrow.
turns.speaker: The Buddha

turns.text: His friends and family would bring a surgeon, but he would say: ‘I will not have this arrow removed until I know who shot me… his caste… his height… what bow he used.’
turns.speaker: The Buddha

turns.text: That man would die before he ever learned these things.
turns.speaker: The Buddha

turns.text: The man would perish, Lord.
turns.speaker: Malunkyaputta

turns.text: So too, Malunkyaputta, if anyone should say: ‘I will not lead the holy life until the Buddha explains the world as eternal or not eternal,’ he will die with those questions unanswered.
turns.speaker: The Buddha

turns.text: Then the unanswered questions are irrelevant to liberation?
turns.speaker: Malunkyaputta

turns.text: Lord, then what *is* declared by the Tathagata?
turns.speaker: Malunkyaputta

turns.text: Malunkyaputta, what I have declared is: ‘This is suffering.’
turns.speaker: The Buddha

turns.text: ‘This is the arising of suffering.’ ‘This is the cessation of suffering.’ ‘This is the path leading to the cessation of suffering.’
turns.speaker: The Buddha

turns.text: Just these four?
turns.speaker: Malunkyaputta

turns.text: These lead to liberation. They are worth knowing. They are sufficient.
turns.speaker: The Buddha

turns.text: Lord, how does one practice these teachings?
turns.speaker: Malunkyaputta

turns.text: By directly knowing: ‘Such is suffering.’
turns.speaker: The Buddha

turns.text: Knowing: ‘Such is its arising.’
turns.speaker: The Buddha

turns.text: Knowing: ‘Such is its cessation.’
turns.speaker: The Buddha

turns.text: Knowing: ‘Such is the path.’
turns.speaker: The Buddha

turns.text: Then the training is immediate and practical.
turns.speaker: Malunkyaputta

turns.text: Don’t answer, just listen. Do you feel incapable of becoming somebody?
turns.speaker: Visitor

turns.text: Probably you have a religious ideal; and do you feel you have not the capacity to live up to or achieve it? Do you feel a sense of hopelessness about it, a sense of guilt or frustration?
turns.speaker: Krishnamurti

turns.text: You are perfectly right. Ever since I heard you some years ago as a boy, it has been my ideal, if I may say so, to be like you. It’s in our blood to be religious, and I have felt I could be like that; but there has always been a deep fear of never coming near it.
turns.speaker: Visitor

turns.text: Let us go slowly. Though you are not frightened of being outwardly insecure, you are frightened of being insecure inwardly.
turns.speaker: Krishnamurti

turns.text: Why do you want to become or achieve an ideal? Isn’t it only to be secure, to feel safe?
turns.speaker: Krishnamurti

turns.text: This refuge you call an ideal; but actually you want to be safe, protected. Is that it?
turns.speaker: Krishnamurti

turns.text: Now that you point it out, that is exactly it.
turns.speaker: Visitor

turns.text: You have discovered this now, have you not? But let us proceed further.
turns.speaker: Krishnamurti

turns.text: You see the obvious shallowness of outward security; but do you also see the falseness of seeking inward security through becoming the ideal?
turns.speaker: Krishnamurti

turns.text: The ideal is your refuge, instead of money. Do you really see this?
turns.speaker: Krishnamurti

turns.text: Yes, I really do.
turns.speaker: Visitor

turns.text: Both pleasure and conflict are disturbing, are they not?
turns.speaker: Visitor

turns.text: Or do you think pleasure does not disturb?
turns.speaker: Visitor

turns.text: Is that true? Have you never noticed the pain of pleasure?
turns.speaker: Krishnamurti

turns.text: Is not the craving for pleasure ever on the increase, ever demanding more and more?
turns.speaker: Krishnamurti

turns.text: Is not the craving for more as disturbing as the urgency of avoidance?
turns.speaker: Krishnamurti

turns.text: If we have no desire we will die; if we have no conflict we will go to sleep.
turns.speaker: Visitor

turns.text: Are you speaking from experience, or have you merely an idea about it?
turns.speaker: Krishnamurti

turns.text: We are imagining what it would be like to have no conflict and so are preventing the experiencing of whatever that state is in which all conflict has ceased.
turns.speaker: Krishnamurti

turns.text: Our problem is, what causes conflict?
turns.speaker: Krishnamurti

turns.text: In this process, what is it that gives rise to conflict? Can we be free from conflict? And what is beyond conflict?
turns.speaker: Visitor

turns.text: It is naming that gives rise to conflict, is it not?
turns.speaker: Krishnamurti

turns.text: The interval between response and naming is experiencing. Experiencing, in which there is neither the experiencer nor the experienced, is beyond conflict.
turns.speaker: Krishnamurti

turns.text: I have been through all that yet I am completely dissatisfied.
turns.speaker: Doctor

turns.text: You may be dissatisfied with outward relationships, but perhaps you are seeking some psychological attachment that will give full satisfaction.
turns.speaker: Krishnamurti

turns.text: I have been through that too, but I am still dissatisfied.
turns.speaker: Doctor

turns.text: I wonder if you really are?
turns.speaker: Krishnamurti

turns.text: If you were wholly discontented, there would be no movement in any particular direction, would there?
turns.speaker: Krishnamurti

turns.text: If you are thoroughly dissatisfied with being in a room, you do not seek a bigger room with nicer furniture; yet this desire to find a better room is what you call dissatisfaction.
turns.speaker: Krishnamurti

turns.text: Your dissatisfaction arises from not having found complete satisfaction.
turns.speaker: Krishnamurti

turns.text: It looks that way, doesn’t it?
turns.speaker: Doctor

turns.text: So you are really not dissatisfied; it is simply that you have not so far been able to find complete and lasting satisfaction in anything.
turns.speaker: Krishnamurti

turns.text: What you really want is lasting self-gratification.
turns.speaker: Krishnamurti

turns.text: Why shouldn’t I be exploited? I don’t mind being used for the cause, which has great significance, and I want to be completely identified with it.
turns.speaker: Man

turns.text: But I have a problem of personal attachment which distracts me from the work. It is this attachment I want to understand.
turns.speaker: Man

turns.text: But why should you be exploited? Are you not as important as the individual or the group that is exploiting you?
turns.speaker: Krishnamurti

turns.text: I don’t mind being exploited for the cause, which I consider has great beauty and worth in the world.
turns.speaker: Man

turns.text: Those with whom I work are spiritual people with high ideals, and they know better than I do what should be done.
turns.speaker: Man

turns.text: Why do you think they are more capable of doing good than you are?
turns.speaker: Krishnamurti

turns.text: How do you know they are ‘spiritual,’ to use your own word, and have wider vision?
turns.speaker: Krishnamurti

turns.text: It is a beautiful cause, and I offered my services because I felt that I must help it.
turns.speaker: Man

turns.text: You are like those men who join the army to kill or to be killed for a noble cause. Do they know what they are doing?
turns.speaker: Krishnamurti

turns.text: Do you know what you are doing?
turns.speaker: Krishnamurti

turns.text: Of course you are right. I was in the army for four years during the last war.
turns.speaker: Man

turns.text: But the people I am helping now are spiritual.
turns.speaker: Man

turns.text: Is it beautiful to be ambitious and cover it up with a lot of high-sounding words about Masters, humanity, art, brotherhood?
turns.speaker: Krishnamurti

turns.text: I see that all right, and it is true; but what am I to do about it?
turns.speaker: Visitor

turns.text: You cannot do anything about it. Whatever you do is an activity of escape.
turns.speaker: Krishnamurti

turns.text: Then you will see that you are not different or separate from that hollowness.
turns.speaker: Krishnamurti

turns.text: You are that insufficiency. The observer is the observed emptiness.
turns.speaker: Krishnamurti

turns.text: Then if you proceed further, there is no longer calling it loneliness; the terming of it has ceased.
turns.speaker: Krishnamurti

turns.text: If you proceed still further, which is rather arduous, the thing known as loneliness is not.
turns.speaker: Krishnamurti

turns.text: There is a complete cessation of loneliness, emptiness, of the thinker as the thought.
turns.speaker: Krishnamurti

turns.text: Then what is love?
turns.speaker: Visitor

turns.text: Love is not identification; it is not thought about the loved.
turns.speaker: Krishnamurti

turns.text: You do not think about love when it is there; you think about it only when it is absent.
turns.speaker: Krishnamurti

turns.text: When the smoke is not, the flame is. The two cannot exist together.
turns.speaker: Krishnamurti

turns.text: I am constantly afraid of death. It is a shadow that follows me everywhere.
turns.speaker: Visitor

turns.text: Are you afraid of death itself, or of the ending of continuity?
turns.speaker: Krishnamurti

turns.text: What do you mean by continuity?
turns.speaker: Visitor

turns.text: The continuity of thought, of experience, of the things you have gathered as ‘you’.
turns.speaker: Krishnamurti

turns.text: You are frightened not of death, but of losing the things thought has put together.
turns.speaker: Krishnamurti

turns.text: But without continuity there is nothing left.
turns.speaker: Visitor

turns.text: Is that so? Or is it merely an assertion born of fear?
turns.speaker: Krishnamurti

turns.text: When the mind sees the falseness of continuity, there is a different state altogether.
turns.speaker: Krishnamurti

turns.text: You are saying that I don’t fear death but fear losing myself.
turns.speaker: Visitor

turns.text: The ‘self’ is continuity: memory, time, accumulation.
turns.speaker: Krishnamurti

turns.text: Death is the ending of that process, and you cling to the process.
turns.speaker: Krishnamurti

turns.text: Then my fear is of losing my past.
turns.speaker: Visitor

turns.text: I am jealous, and it tortures me.
turns.speaker: Man

turns.text: Jealousy is comparison, is it not? Comparing what you are with another.
turns.speaker: Krishnamurti

turns.text: Yes, but I cannot stop comparing.
turns.speaker: Man

turns.text: Who is the ‘I’ that compares?
turns.speaker: Krishnamurti

turns.text: I suppose the one who wants to be loved exclusively.
turns.speaker: Man

turns.text: So jealousy is the desire to possess?
turns.speaker: Krishnamurti

turns.text: Yes, it is that.
turns.speaker: Man

turns.text: Possession is the self wanting continuity through another.
turns.speaker: Krishnamurti

turns.text: And when that continuity is threatened, fear arises.
turns.speaker: Krishnamurti

turns.text: But how can I end jealousy?
turns.speaker: Man

turns.text: By seeing that the ‘I’ that wants continuity is the creator of pain.
turns.speaker: Krishnamurti

turns.text: See the process without condemning it, and the whole movement changes.
turns.speaker: Krishnamurti

turns.text: It’s strange—I feel some of the torment dropping away.
turns.speaker: Man

turns.text: I get bored with everything—my job, my friends, meditation, even my pleasures.
turns.speaker: Student

turns.text: Boredom is the desire for stimulation, is it not?
turns.speaker: Krishnamurti

turns.text: I suppose so, but I feel dead when there is no excitement.
turns.speaker: Student

turns.text: The mind that depends on stimulation becomes dull when it is absent.
turns.speaker: Krishnamurti

turns.text: Why does the mind demand stimulation?
turns.speaker: Krishnamurti

turns.text: Perhaps because I feel empty.
turns.speaker: Student

turns.text: Then the problem is not boredom but the fear of facing that emptiness.
turns.speaker: Krishnamurti

turns.text: That might be true.
turns.speaker: Student

turns.text: Can you look at the emptiness without running away from it?
turns.speaker: Krishnamurti

turns.text: If you do, the emptiness loses its terror.
turns.speaker: Krishnamurti

turns.text: It feels almost peaceful for a moment.
turns.speaker: Student

turns.text: In that moment, boredom disappears.
turns.speaker: Krishnamurti

turns.text: My fears repeat themselves endlessly.
turns.speaker: Man

turns.text: Fear repeats because thought repeats its memories.
turns.speaker: Krishnamurti

turns.text: How can I break the cycle?
turns.speaker: Man

turns.text: By understanding the cycle, not by resisting it.
turns.speaker: Krishnamurti

turns.text: Fear arises from memory meeting the present.
turns.speaker: Krishnamurti

turns.text: So fear is memory?
turns.speaker: Man

turns.text: Fear is the movement of memory in the form of thought.
turns.speaker: Krishnamurti

turns.text: See this movement clearly and it ends.
turns.speaker: Krishnamurti

turns.text: It sounds simple but feels impossible.
turns.speaker: Man

turns.text: It is impossible only when you try to change it, not when you observe it.
turns.speaker: Krishnamurti

turns.text: I feel deeply insecure, no matter what I do. Even when things are going well there is anxiety.
turns.speaker: Visitor

turns.text: Is the insecurity in the outer world, or does it lie within?
turns.speaker: Krishnamurti

turns.text: It must be within, because I can arrange the outer things but still feel unsafe.
turns.speaker: Visitor

turns.text: What is the ‘within’ that feels unsafe?
turns.speaker: Krishnamurti

turns.text: Myself, I suppose.
turns.speaker: Visitor

turns.text: Is the ‘self’ anything more than the images you have built about yourself?
turns.speaker: Krishnamurti

turns.text: Images of success, failure, being loved, being alone?
turns.speaker: Krishnamurti

turns.text: Those things matter a lot to me.
turns.speaker: Visitor

turns.text: But they are images created by thought, are they not?
turns.speaker: Krishnamurti

turns.text: Thought creates an image, then fears that the image may be hurt.
turns.speaker: Krishnamurti

turns.text: You mean I fear for my image, not myself.
turns.speaker: Visitor

turns.text: When the image is seen for what it is, insecurity dissolves.
turns.speaker: Krishnamurti

turns.text: I want to achieve something great, but I find myself in constant conflict.
turns.speaker: Student

turns.text: Conflict arises when there is division between ‘what is’ and ‘what should be.’
turns.speaker: Krishnamurti

turns.text: But without a goal, there is no meaning.
turns.speaker: Student

turns.text: Is meaning something you pursue, or does it exist only in the present?
turns.speaker: Krishnamurti

turns.text: I don’t know. I feel empty without a goal.
turns.speaker: Student

turns.text: Then the goal is an escape from that emptiness.
turns.speaker: Krishnamurti

turns.text: An escape… yes, perhaps that’s true.
turns.speaker: Student

turns.text: If the emptiness were understood directly, ambition might not be needed.
turns.speaker: Krishnamurti

turns.text: But the emptiness feels frightening.
turns.speaker: Student

turns.text: Fear of emptiness gives birth to ambition.
turns.speaker: Krishnamurti

turns.text: And ambition sustains conflict, does it not?
turns.speaker: Krishnamurti

turns.text: So the whole cycle begins with running away from what I feel.
turns.speaker: Student

turns.text: To see the cycle is already the beginning of freedom from it.
turns.speaker: Krishnamurti

turns.text: I am confused. I don’t know which direction to take in life.
turns.speaker: Visitor

turns.text: Confusion exists only when you choose.
turns.speaker: Krishnamurti

turns.text: How can there be no choice?
turns.speaker: Visitor

turns.text: Choice arises when the mind is uncertain; clarity has no choice.
turns.speaker: Krishnamurti

turns.text: But I do not have clarity.
turns.speaker: Visitor

turns.text: Clarity comes when confusion is observed without wanting to escape from it.
turns.speaker: Krishnamurti

turns.text: So I must not try to choose at all?
turns.speaker: Visitor

turns.text: See the confusion—do not act from it.
turns.speaker: Krishnamurti

turns.text: That feels difficult, but somehow right.
turns.speaker: Visitor

turns.text: The seeing itself ends the confusion.
turns.speaker: Krishnamurti

turns.text: I have lived with guilt for years. It never leaves me.
turns.speaker: Woman

turns.text: Guilt is the shadow of memory, is it not?
turns.speaker: Krishnamurti

turns.text: It feels like punishment.
turns.speaker: Woman

turns.text: Who is punishing whom?
turns.speaker: Krishnamurti

turns.text: I punish myself.
turns.speaker: Woman

turns.text: The ‘self’ punishes the ‘self’—a division created by thought.
turns.speaker: Krishnamurti

turns.text: Is the act itself alive now, or only the memory of it?
turns.speaker: Krishnamurti

turns.text: Only the memory.
turns.speaker: Woman

turns.text: When memory takes shape as punishment, guilt is born.
turns.speaker: Krishnamurti

turns.text: Then guilt is not moral but psychological?
turns.speaker: Woman

turns.text: Seeing this frees the mind from guilt’s weight.
turns.speaker: Krishnamurti

turns.text: I keep myself busy all day because if I stop even for a moment, a terrible loneliness comes over me.
turns.speaker: Man

turns.text: So activity is a means of escaping loneliness?
turns.speaker: Krishnamurti

turns.text: Yes, that is true.
turns.speaker: Man

turns.text: You have never looked at loneliness directly, have you?
turns.speaker: Krishnamurti

turns.text: I can’t bear it. It feels like death.
turns.speaker: Man

turns.text: Loneliness is the fear of not being anything.
turns.speaker: Krishnamurti

turns.text: When activity stops, the mind is faced with its own emptiness.
turns.speaker: Krishnamurti

turns.text: Then I must keep moving, otherwise I collapse.
turns.speaker: Man

turns.text: Movement away from something strengthens the very thing you escape from.
turns.speaker: Krishnamurti

turns.text: Do you see that escaping increases loneliness?
turns.speaker: Krishnamurti

turns.text: It seems so—but I still want to run.
turns.speaker: Man

turns.text: Wanting to run is part of loneliness itself.
turns.speaker: Krishnamurti

turns.text: Look at the loneliness without escape, and it changes entirely.
turns.speaker: Krishnamurti

turns.text: There is a strangely quiet feeling now.
turns.speaker: Man

turns.text: How is it, that you the philosopher who sailed to Sicily for the sake of these dishes, now when they are before you do not enjoy them?
turns.speaker: Diogenes

turns.text: Nay, by the gods, Diogenes, there also for the most part I lived upon olives and such like.
turns.speaker: Plato

turns.text: Why then, did you need to go to Syracuse? Was it that Attica at that time did not grow olives?
turns.speaker: Diogenes

turns.text: I trample upon Plato's vainglory.
turns.speaker: Diogenes

turns.text: How much pride you expose to view, Diogenes, by seeming not to be proud.
turns.speaker: Plato

turns.text: There are 3000 drachmas to your credit,
turns.speaker: Meidias

turns.text: There are 3000 blows to your credit.
turns.speaker: Diogenes

turns.text: Table and cup I see; but your tablehood and cuphood, Plato, I can nowise see.
turns.speaker: Diogenes

turns.text: That's readily accounted for, for you have the eyes to see the visible table and cup; but not the understanding by which ideal tablehood and cuphood are discerned.
turns.speaker: Plato

turns.text: Are you not afraid of me?
turns.speaker: Alexander

turns.text: Why, what are you? a good thing or a bad?
turns.speaker: Diogenes

turns.text: A good thing,
turns.speaker: Alexander

turns.text: Who then is afraid of the good?
turns.speaker: Diogenes

turns.text: Master, why does the sutra say the cow has no nostrils?
turns.speaker: Student

turns.text: If you say it has nostrils, I hit you thirty times. If you say it has none, I hit you thirty times.
turns.speaker: Teacher

turns.text: Then how should I answer?
turns.speaker: Student

turns.text: Moo!
turns.speaker: Teacher

turns.text: Master, what is true emptiness?
turns.speaker: Student

turns.text: If you open your mouth, wrong.
turns.speaker: Teacher

turns.text: Then I will stay silent.
turns.speaker: Student

turns.text: If you close your mouth, also wrong.
turns.speaker: Teacher

turns.text: Then what should I do?
turns.speaker: Student

turns.text: KATZ!
turns.speaker: Teacher

turns.text: Is Buddha inside my mind or outside it?
turns.speaker: Student

turns.text: If Buddha is outside, how do you see him?
turns.speaker: Teacher

turns.text: Inside, then.
turns.speaker: Student

turns.text: Show me where inside is.
turns.speaker: Teacher

turns.text: …I cannot.
turns.speaker: Student

turns.text: Then drop inside and outside.
turns.speaker: Teacher

turns.text: Master, where did you go when you fell asleep?
turns.speaker: Student

turns.text: I hit you thirty times.
turns.speaker: Teacher

turns.text: Thank you. But I still don't understand.
turns.speaker: Student

turns.text: Are you awake now?
turns.speaker: Teacher

turns.text: I think so.
turns.speaker: Student

turns.text: Then say one awake sentence.
turns.speaker: Teacher

turns.text: The curtain behind you is yellow.
turns.speaker: Student

turns.text: It is dark.
turns.speaker: Teacher

turns.text: Master, the mouse ate the cat’s food and the bowl broke. What does it mean?
turns.speaker: Student

turns.text: If you answer, wrong.
turns.speaker: Teacher

turns.text: Then I won’t answer.
turns.speaker: Student

turns.text: If you don’t answer, wrong.
turns.speaker: Teacher

turns.text: Then what should I do?
turns.speaker: Student

turns.text: See before thinking.
turns.speaker: Teacher

turns.text: Does a dog have Buddha-nature?
turns.speaker: Student

turns.text: No!
turns.speaker: Teacher

turns.text: But all beings have Buddha-nature.
turns.speaker: Student

turns.text: If you say ‘yes’, wrong. If you say ‘no’, wrong.
turns.speaker: Teacher

turns.text: Then what is correct?
turns.speaker: Student

turns.text: MU.
turns.speaker: Teacher

turns.text: Master, what are you?
turns.speaker: Student

turns.text: What did you say?
turns.speaker: Teacher

turns.text: I said—what are you?
turns.speaker: Student

turns.text: Thank you very much.
turns.speaker: Teacher

turns.text: …I don’t know.
turns.speaker: Student

turns.text: Exactly.
turns.speaker: Teacher

turns.text: Master, what is Buddha?
turns.speaker: Student

turns.text: A pebble hits bamboo—*tok!*
turns.speaker: Teacher

turns.text: Is that the teaching?
turns.speaker: Student

turns.text: Do you hear it or think it?
turns.speaker: Teacher

turns.text: Master, what is love?
turns.speaker: Student

turns.text: Attachment.
turns.speaker: Teacher

turns.text: Then what is true love?
turns.speaker: Student

turns.text: When there is no you and no other—only this.
turns.speaker: Teacher

turns.text: Is this cup real or empty?
turns.speaker: Student

turns.text: If you say ‘real’, attached.
turns.speaker: Teacher

turns.text: Then it is empty.
turns.speaker: Student

turns.text: If you say ‘empty’, also attached.
turns.speaker: Teacher

turns.text: What should I say?
turns.speaker: Student

turns.text: Put it down.
turns.speaker: Teacher

turns.text: If everything is empty, may I drink wine?
turns.speaker: Student

turns.text: Is your cheek empty?
turns.speaker: Teacher

turns.text: Yes—
turns.speaker: Student

turns.text: *slaps him hard*
turns.speaker: Teacher

turns.text: OW!
turns.speaker: Student

turns.text: If emptiness still works, drink all you want.
turns.speaker: Teacher

turns.text: Is the Bodhisattva attached to compassion?
turns.speaker: Student

turns.text: The universe is infinite; all people are infinite. So the Bodhisattva's attachment is infinite. A Bodhisattva attachment is no attachment. No attachment is a Bodhisattva attachment.
turns.speaker: Soen-sa

turns.text: Does he have it in mind to save all people or does this just happen wherever he is?
turns.speaker: Student

turns.text: Do you understand what the Bodhisattva is?
turns.speaker: Soen-sa

turns.text: No.
turns.speaker: Student

turns.text: First, understand what the Bodhisattva is. Then you will understand the Bodhisattva's attachment. The Bodhisattva is your true self… He always acts together with all people.
turns.speaker: Soen-sa

turns.text: Thank you.
turns.speaker: Student

turns.text: "Your mind is a pail of stinking garbage."
turns.speaker: Soen-sa

turns.text: "What do you mean?"
turns.speaker: Student

turns.text: "Everything you see, hear, smell, taste, and touch is covered with your opinions, your likes and dislikes. It all stinks. Put it all down!"
turns.speaker: Soen-sa

turns.text: "What does this 'No' mean?"
turns.speaker: Ko Bong

turns.text: Ko Bong was stunned. As he struggled to come up with an answer, the Master took his staff, hit him viciously on the shoulder, and chased him out.
turns.speaker: Student

turns.text: So, in great pain, and weeping with humiliation, he returned to his monastery.
turns.speaker: Student

turns.text: "Good morning. How is your search coming along?"
turns.speaker: Master (Seorl Am)

turns.text: "If a man kills his desire to search, he will surely find what he is searching for."
turns.speaker: Ko Bong

turns.text: Suddenly the Master grabbed him by the collar and shouted, "Who is dragging this corpse?"
turns.speaker: Master (Seorl Am)

turns.text: "Are you awake?"
turns.speaker: Student

turns.text: "You are breathing in a dream."
turns.speaker: Soen-sa

turns.text: "No."
turns.speaker: Student

turns.text: "No?! Then give me one awake sentence."
turns.speaker: Soen-sa

turns.text: "The bamboo curtain behind you is yellow."
turns.speaker: Student

turns.text: "No, it is dark."
turns.speaker: Soen-sa

turns.text: "That's because it's behind you; if you turn around you'll see it's yellow."
turns.speaker: Student

turns.text: "Your head is a dragon, your tail is a snake."
turns.speaker: Soen-sa

turns.text: "What does the dialogue mean?"
turns.speaker: Student

turns.text: "I hit you thirty times."
turns.speaker: Soen-sa

turns.text: "But I don't understand the story."
turns.speaker: Student

turns.text: "I already explained: I hit you thirty times."
turns.speaker: Soen-sa

turns.text: "Oh, now I understand."
turns.speaker: Student

turns.text: "What do you understand?"
turns.speaker: Soen-sa

turns.text: "Ouch!"
turns.speaker: Student

turns.text: "If you are hungry, take a meal and have a good rest."
turns.speaker: Student

turns.text: "Your leg is itching, but you are scratching my leg."
turns.speaker: Soen-sa

turns.text: "What do you think of these answers?"
turns.speaker: Soen-sa

turns.text: "Not bad, not good. But the dog runs after the bone."
turns.speaker: Student

turns.text: (*hits the floor*)
turns.speaker: Student

turns.text: "I don't believe you."
turns.speaker: Soen-sa

turns.text: (silent)
turns.speaker: Student

turns.text: "You understand One; but you don't understand Two."
turns.speaker: Soen-sa

turns.text: The mouse eats cat-food, but the cat-bowl is broken. What does this mean?
turns.speaker: Soen-sa

turns.text: If you are hungry, take a meal and have a good rest.
turns.speaker: Student

turns.text: Your leg is itching, but you are scratching my leg. You are trying to hit the moon with a stick. Your answer is 18,000 miles away from the correct one.
turns.speaker: Soen-sa

turns.text: Birds fly in the sky, fish swim in the water.
turns.speaker: Student

turns.text: This is scratching your left foot when your right foot itches.
turns.speaker: Soen-sa

turns.text: (hits the floor)
turns.speaker: Student

turns.text: I don’t believe you.
turns.speaker: Soen-sa

turns.text: Your first answer was good. But then you began to think. No good.
turns.speaker: Soen-sa

turns.text: What are you?
turns.speaker: Student

turns.text: What did you say?
turns.speaker: Soen-sa

turns.text: What are you?
turns.speaker: Student

turns.text: Thank you very much.
turns.speaker: Soen-sa

turns.text: I don’t know.
turns.speaker: Student

turns.text: I hit you. Now do you understand?
turns.speaker: Soen-sa

turns.text: No.
turns.speaker: Student

turns.text: Which of these three answers is the best?
turns.speaker: Student

turns.text: They are all bad.
turns.speaker: Soen-sa

turns.text: Why?
turns.speaker: Student

turns.text: The bee goes to the flower.
turns.speaker: Soen-sa

turns.text: That’s a terrible answer.
turns.speaker: Student

turns.text: Why?
turns.speaker: Soen-sa

turns.text: Outside the window, the tree is green.
turns.speaker: Student

turns.text: This infinite and eternal self of mine, how am I to know it?
turns.speaker: Questioner

turns.text: The self you want to know, is it some second self? Are you made of several selves? Surely, there is only one self and you are that self. The self you are is the only self there is. Remove and abandon your wrong ideas about yourself and there it is, in all its glory. It is only your mind that prevents self-knowledge.
turns.speaker: Maharaj

turns.text: How am I to be rid of the mind? And is life without mind at all possible on the human level?
turns.speaker: Questioner

turns.text: There is no such thing as mind. There are ideas and some of them are wrong. Abandon the wrong ideas, for they are false and obstruct your vision of yourself.
turns.speaker: Maharaj

turns.text: Which ideas are wrong and which are true?
turns.speaker: Questioner

turns.text: Assertions are usually wrong and denials -- right.
turns.speaker: Maharaj

turns.text: One cannot live by denying everything!
turns.speaker: Questioner

turns.text: Only by denying can one live. Assertion is bondage. To question and deny is necessary. It is the essence of revolt and without revolt there can be no freedom. There is no second, or higher self to search for. You are the highest self, only give up the false ideas you have about your self. Both faith and reason tell you that you are neither the body, nor its desires and fears, nor are you the mind with its fanciful ideas, nor the role society compels you to play, the person you are supposed to be. Give up the false and the true will come into its own. You say you want to know your self. You are your self -- you cannot be anything but what you are. Is knowing separate from being? Whatever you can know with your mind is of the mind, not you; about yourself you can only say: 'I am, I am aware, I like It'.
turns.speaker: Maharaj

turns.text: I find being alive a painful state.
turns.speaker: Questioner

turns.text: You cannot be alive for you are life itself. It is the person you imagine yourself to be that suffers, not you. Dissolve it in awareness. It is merely a bundle of memories and habits. From the awareness of the unreal to the awareness of your real nature there is a chasm which you will easily cross, once you have mastered the art of pure awareness.
turns.speaker: Maharaj

turns.text: All I know is that I do not know myself.
turns.speaker: Questioner

turns.text: How do you know, that you do not know your self? Your direct insight tells you that yourself you know first, for nothing exists to you without your being there to experience its existence. You imagine you do not know your self, because you cannot describe your self. You can always say: 'I know that I am' and you will refuse as untrue the statement: 'I am not'. But whatever can be described cannot be your self, and what you are cannot be described. You can only know your self by being yourself without any attempt at self-definition and self-description. Once you have understood that you are nothing perceivable or conceivable, that whatever appears in the field of consciousness cannot be your self, you will apply yourself to the eradication of all self-identification, as the only way that can take you to a deeper realisation of your self. You literally progress by rejection -- a veritable rocket. To know that you are neither in the body nor in the mind, though aware of both, is already self-knowledge.
turns.speaker: Maharaj

turns.text: If I am neither the body nor mind, how am I aware of them? How can I perceive something quite foreign to myself?
turns.speaker: Questioner

turns.text: 'Nothing is me,' is the first step. 'Everything is me' is the next. Both hang on the idea: 'there is a world'. When this too is given up, you remain what you are -- the non-dual Self. You are it here and now, but your vision is obstructed by your false ideas about your self.
turns.speaker: Maharaj

turns.text: You were telling us that there are many self-styled Gurus, but a real Guru is very rare. There are many jnani who imagine themselves realised, but all they have is book knowledge and a high opinion of themselves. Sometimes they impress, even fascinate, attract disciples and make them waste their time in useless practices. After some years, when the disciple takes stock of himself, he finds no change. When he complains to his teacher, he gets the usual rebuke that he did not try hard enough. The blame is on the lack of faith and love in the heart of the disciple, while in reality the blame is on the Guru, who had no business in accepting disciples and raising their hopes. How to protect oneself from such Gurus?
turns.speaker: Questioner

turns.text: Why be so concerned with others? Whoever may be the Guru, if he is pure of heart and acts in good faith, he will do his disciples no harm. If there is no progress, the fault lies with the disciples, their laziness and lack of self-control. On the other hand, if the disciple is earnest and applies himself intelligently and with zest to his sadhana, he is bound to meet a more qualified teacher, who will take him further. Your question flows from three false assumptions: that one needs concern oneself with others; that one can evaluate another and that the progress of the disciple is the task and responsibility of his Guru. In reality, the Guru's role is only to instruct and encourage; the disciple is totally responsible for himself.
turns.speaker: Maharaj
