turns.text: We are told that total surrender to the Guru is enough, that the Guru will do the rest.
turns.speaker: Questioner

turns.text: Of course, when there is total surrender, complete relinquishment of all concern with one's past, presents and future, with one's physical and spiritual security and standing, a new life dawns, full of love and beauty; then the Guru is not important, for the disciple has broken the shell of self-defence. Complete self-surrender by itself is liberation.
turns.speaker: Maharaj

turns.text: When both the disciple and his teacher are inadequate, what will happen?
turns.speaker: Questioner

turns.text: In the long run all will be well. After all, the real Self of both is not affected by the comedy they play for a time. They will sober up and ripen and shift to a higher level of relationship.
turns.speaker: Maharaj

turns.text: Or, they may separate.
turns.speaker: Questioner

turns.text: Yes, they may separate. After all, no relationship is forever. Duality is a temporary state.
turns.speaker: Maharaj

turns.text: Is it by accident that I met you and by another accident shall we separate never to meet again? Or is my meeting you a part of some cosmic pattern, a fragment in the great drama of our lives?
turns.speaker: Questioner

turns.text: The real is meaningful and the meaningful relates to reality. If our relationship is meaningful to you and me, it cannot be accidental. The future affects the present as much, as the past.
turns.speaker: Maharaj

turns.text: How can I make out who is a real saint and who is not?
turns.speaker: Questioner

turns.text: You cannot, unless you have a clear insight into the heart of man. Appearances are deceptive. To see clearly, your mind must be pure and unattached. Unless you know yourself well, how can you know another? And when you know yourself -- you are the other. Leave others alone for some time and examine yourself. There are so many things you do not know about yourself -- what are you, who are you, how did you come to be born, what are you doing now and why, where are you going, what is the meaning and purpose of your life, your death, your future? Have you a past, have you a future? How did you come to live in turmoil and sorrow, while your entire being strives for happiness and peace? These are weighty matters and have to be attended to first. You have no need, nor time for finding who is a jnani and who is not?
turns.speaker: Maharaj

turns.text: I must select my Guru rightly.
turns.speaker: Questioner

turns.text: Be the right man and the right Guru will surely find you.
turns.speaker: Maharaj

turns.text: You are not answering my question: how to find the right Guru?
turns.speaker: Questioner

turns.text: But I did answer your question. Do not look for a Guru, do not even think of one. Make your goal your Guru. After all, the Guru is but a means to an end, not the end in itself. He is not important, it is what you expect of him that matters to you. Now, what do you expect?
turns.speaker: Maharaj

turns.text: By his grace I shall be made happy, powerful and peaceful.
turns.speaker: Questioner

turns.text: What ambitions! How can a person limited in time and space, a mere body-mind, a gasp of pain between birth and death, be happy? The very conditions of its arising make happiness impossible. Peace, power, happiness, these are never personal states, nobody can say 'my peace', 'my power' -- because 'mine' implies exclusivity, which is fragile and insecure.
turns.speaker: Maharaj

turns.text: I know only my conditioned existence; there is nothing else.
turns.speaker: Questioner

turns.text: Surely, you cannot say so. In deep sleep you are not conditioned. How ready and willing you are to go to sleep, how peaceful, free and happy you are when asleep!
turns.speaker: Maharaj

turns.text: I know nothing of it.
turns.speaker: Questioner

turns.text: Put it negatively. When you sleep, you are not in pain, nor bound, nor restless.
turns.speaker: Maharaj

turns.text: I see your point. While awake, I know that I am, but am not happy; in sleep I am, I am happy, but I do not know it. All I need is to know that I am free and happy.
turns.speaker: Questioner

turns.text: Quite so. Now, go within, into a state which you may compare to a state of waking sleep, in which you are aware of yourself, but not of the world. In that state you will know, without the least trace of doubt, that at the root of your being you are free and happy. The only trouble is that you are addicted to experience and you cherish your memories. In reality it is the other way round; what is remembered is never real; the real is now.
turns.speaker: Maharaj

turns.text: All this I grasp verbally, but it does not become a part of myself. It remains as a picture in my mind to be looked at. Is it not the task of the Guru to give life to the picture?
turns.speaker: Questioner

turns.text: Again, it is the other way round. The picture is alive; dead is the mind. As the mind is made of words and images, so is every reflection in the mind. It covers up reality with verbalisation and then complains. You say a Guru is needed, to do miracles with you. You are playing with words only. The Guru and the disciple are one single thing, like the candle and its flame. Unless the disciple is earnest, he cannot be called a disciple. Unless a Guru is all love and self-giving, he cannot be called a Guru. Only reality begets reality, not the false.
turns.speaker: Maharaj

turns.text: I can see that I am false. Who will make me true?
turns.speaker: Questioner

turns.text: The very words you said will do it. The sentence: 'I can see that I am false' contains all you need for liberation. Ponder over it, go into it deeply, go to the root of it; it will operate. The power is in the word, not in the person.
turns.speaker: Maharaj

turns.text: I do not grasp you fully. On one hand you say a Guru is needed; on the other -- the Guru can only give advice, but the effort is mine. Please state clearly -- can one realise the Self without a Guru, or is the finding of a true Guru essential?
turns.speaker: Questioner

turns.text: More essential is the finding of a true disciple. Believe me, a true disciple is very rare, for in no time he goes beyond the need for a Guru, by finding his own self. Do not waste your time on trying to make out whether the advice you get flows from knowledge only, or from valid experience! Just follow it faithfully. Life will bring you another Guru, if another one is needed. Or deprive you of all outer guidance and leave you to your own lights. It is very important to understand that it is the teaching that matters, not the person or the Guru. You get a letter that makes you laugh or cry. It is not the postman who does it. The Guru only tells you the good news about your real Self and shows you the way back to it. In a way the Guru is its messenger. There will be many messengers, but the message is one: be what you are. Or, you can put it differently: Until you realise yourself, you cannot know who is your real Guru. When you realise, you find that all the Gurus you had have contributed to your awakening. Your realisation is the proof that your Guru was real. Therefore, take him as he is, do what he tells you, with earnestness and zeal and trust your heart to warn you if anything goes wrong. If doubt sets in, do not fight it. Cling to what is doubtless and leave the doubtful alone.
turns.speaker: Maharaj

turns.text: I have a Guru and I love him very much. But whether he is my true Guru I do not know.
turns.speaker: Questioner

turns.text: Watch yourself. If you see yourself changing, growing, it means you have found the right man. He may be beautiful or ugly, pleasant or unpleasant, flattering you or scolding; nothing matters except the one crucial fact of inward growth. If you do not, well, he may be your friend, but not your Guru.
turns.speaker: Maharaj

turns.text: When I meet a European with some education and talk to him about a Guru and his teachings, his reaction is: 'the man must be mad to teach such nonsense'. What am I to tell him?
turns.speaker: Questioner

turns.text: Take him to himself. Show him, how little he knows himself, how he takes the most absurd statements about himself for holy truth. He is told that he is the body, was born, will die, has parents, duties, learns to like what others like and fear what others fear. Totally a creature of heredity and society, he lives by memory and acts by habits. Ignorant of himself and his true interests, he pursues false aims and is always frustrated. His life and death are meaningless and painful, and there seems to be no way out. Then tell him, there is a way out within his easy reach, not a conversion to another set of ideas, but a liberation from all ideas and patterns of living. Do not tell him about Gurus and disciples -- this way of thinking is not for him. His is an inner path, he is moved by an inner urge and guided by an inner light. Invite him to rebel and he will respond. Do not try to impress on him that so-and-so is a realised man and can be accepted as a Guru. As long as he does not trust himself, he cannot trust another. And confidence will come with experience.
turns.speaker: Maharaj

turns.text: How strange! I cannot imagine life without a Guru.
turns.speaker: Questioner

turns.text: It is a matter of temperament. You too are right. For you, singing the praises of God is enough. You need not desire realisation or take up a sadhana. God's name is all the food you need. Live on it.
turns.speaker: Maharaj

turns.text: This constant repetition of a few words, is it not a kind of madness?
turns.speaker: Questioner

turns.text: It is madness, but it is a deliberate madness. All repetitiveness is tamas, but repeating the name of God is sattva-tamas due to its high purpose. Because of the presence of sattva, the tamas will wear out and will take the shape of complete dispassion, detachment, relinquishment, aloofness, immutability. Tamas becomes the firm foundation on which an integrated life can be lived. The immutable neither lives nor dies; it is the timeless witness of life and death.
turns.speaker: Maharaj

turns.text: My case is hopeless.
turns.speaker: Questioner

turns.text: In a way yours is a most hopeful case. There is an alternative to sadhana, which is trust. If you cannot have the conviction born from fruitful search, then take advantage of my discovery, which I am so eager to share with you. I can see with the utmost clarity that you have never been, nor are, nor will be estranged from reality, that you are the fullness of perfection here and now and that nothing can deprive you of your heritage, of what you are. You are in no way different from me, only you do not know it. You do not know what you are and therefore you imagine your self to be what you are not. Hence desires and fear and overwhelming despair. And meaningless activity in order to escape. Just trust me and live by trusting me. I shall not mislead you. You are the Supreme Reality beyond the world and its creator, beyond consciousness and its witness, beyond all assertions and denials. Remember it, think of it, act on it. Abandon all sense of separation, see yourself in all and act accordingly. With action bliss will come and, with bliss, conviction. After all, you doubt yourself because you are in sorrow. Happiness, natural, spontaneous and lasting cannot be imagined. Either it is there, or it is not. Once you begin to experience the peace, love and happiness which need no outer causes, all your doubts will dissolve. Just catch hold of what I told you and live by it.
turns.speaker: Maharaj

turns.text: You are telling me to live by memory?
turns.speaker: Questioner

turns.text: You are living by memory anyhow. I am merely asking you to replace the old memories by the memory of what I told you. As you were acting on your old memories, act on the new one. Do not be afraid. For some time there is bound to be a conflict between the old and the new, but if you put yourself resolutely on the side of the new, the strife will soon come to an end and you will realise the effortless state of being oneself, of not being deceived by desires and fears born of illusion.
turns.speaker: Maharaj

turns.text: Many Gurus have the habit of giving tokens of their grace -- their head cloth, or their sticks, or begging bowl, or robe, thus transmitting or confirming the self-realisation of their disciples. I can see no value in such practices. It is not self-realisation that is transmitted, but self-importance. Of what earthly use is being told something very flattering, but not true? On one hand you are warning me against the many self-styled Gurus, on the other you want me to trust you. Why do you claim to be an exception?
turns.speaker: Questioner

turns.text: I do not ask you to trust me. Trust my words and remember them, I want your happiness, not mine. Distrust those who put a distance between you and your true being and offer themselves as a go-between. I do nothing of the kind. I do not even make any promises. I merely say: if you trust my words and put them to test, you will for yourself discover how absolutely true they are. If you ask for a proof before you venture, I can only say: I am the proof. I did trust my teacher's words and kept them in my mind and I did find that he was right, that I was, am and shall be the Infinite Reality, embracing all, transcending all. As you say, you have neither the time nor the energy for lengthy practices. I offer you an alternative. Accept my words on trust and live anew, or live and die in sorrow.
turns.speaker: Maharaj

turns.text: It seems too good to be true.
turns.speaker: Questioner

turns.text: Do not be misled by the simplicity of the advice. Very few are those who have the courage to trust the innocent and the simple. To know that you are a prisoner of your mind, that you live in an imaginary world of your own creation is the dawn of wisdom. To want nothing of it, to be ready to abandon it entirely, is earnestness. Only such earnestness, born of true despair, will make you trust me.
turns.speaker: Maharaj

turns.text: Have I not suffered enough?
turns.speaker: Questioner

turns.text: Suffering has made you dull, unable to see its enormity. Your first task is to see the sorrow in you and around you; your next to long intensely for liberation. The very intensity of longing will guide you; you need no other guide.
turns.speaker: Maharaj

turns.text: Whatever may be the cause; I am dull. I have neither the will nor the energy.
turns.speaker: Questioner

turns.text: Oh, no. You have enough for the first step. And each step will generate enough energy for the next. Energy comes with confidence and confidence comes with experience.
turns.speaker: Maharaj

turns.text: Is it right to change Gurus?
turns.speaker: Questioner

turns.text: Why not change? Gurus are like milestones? It is natural to move on from one to another. Each tells you the direction and the distance, while the sadguru, the eternal Guru, is the road itself. Once you realise that the road is the goal and that you are always on the road, not to reach a goal, but to enjoy its beauty and its wisdom, life ceases to be a task and becomes natural and simple, in itself an ecstasy.
turns.speaker: Maharaj

turns.text: Does this knowledge come to you from within or from outside?
turns.speaker: Questioner

turns.text: It does not apply. My inner is outside and my outer is inside. I may get from you the knowledge needed at the moment, but you are not apart from me.
turns.speaker: Maharaj

turns.text: I cannot grasp how inner can be outer.
turns.speaker: Questioner

turns.text: You take space and distance as real. In truth there is no distance. Things are as you see them; when you see rightly, you find the separation was imagined.
turns.speaker: Maharaj

turns.text: Still, I feel knowledge must come from somewhere.
turns.speaker: Questioner

turns.text: Knowledge appears where understanding is ripe. What is called 'from within' and 'from without' is only the mind drawing divisions.
turns.speaker: Maharaj

turns.text: So knowledge is not really transmitted?
turns.speaker: Questioner

turns.text: It appears as needed, like a reflection in a mirror. The mirror does not send or receive. It merely shows.
turns.speaker: Maharaj

turns.text: What is "turiya"?
turns.speaker: Questioner

turns.text: To be the point of light tracing the world is turiya. To be the light itself is turiyatita.
turns.speaker: Maharaj

turns.text: Then these names describe distinct states?
turns.speaker: Questioner

turns.text: They describe the mind’s attempt to mark what cannot be marked. Names arise from the need to communicate, not from the reality they try to point to.
turns.speaker: Maharaj

turns.text: Then why use them at all?
turns.speaker: Questioner

turns.text: Because you ask. But having answered, I show you the limitation: reality is so near that naming it pushes it away.
turns.speaker: Maharaj

turns.text: Is naming always misleading?
turns.speaker: Questioner

turns.text: It is useful until it becomes a cage. Use the name to turn inward, then drop even the turning.
turns.speaker: Maharaj

turns.text: A grain of sand is a thing. A planet is a thing. How are these related to consciousness?
turns.speaker: Questioner

turns.text: Where consciousness does not reach, matter begins.
turns.speaker: Maharaj

turns.text: Do you mean things are outside consciousness?
turns.speaker: Questioner

turns.text: A 'thing' is only a form of being you have not understood. When you understand, you will see no things — only consciousness taking shapes.
turns.speaker: Maharaj

turns.text: Then what is the foundation of the physical world?
turns.speaker: Questioner

turns.text: Memory. The world persists because memory repeats patterns. When memory ceases, the world dissolves like a dream upon waking.
turns.speaker: Maharaj

turns.text: This is difficult to accept.
turns.speaker: Questioner

turns.text: It is difficult because you take your concepts as facts. See concepts as concepts, and the world becomes transparent.
turns.speaker: Maharaj

turns.text: Is there no escape from all this?
turns.speaker: Questioner

turns.text: I am doing nothing else but showing the escape.
turns.speaker: Maharaj

turns.text: Where is it? I do not see it.
turns.speaker: Questioner

turns.text: Understand that the One includes the Three — creation, preservation, destruction. You are the One, not the movement.
turns.speaker: Maharaj

turns.text: If I am the One, why do I feel trapped?
turns.speaker: Questioner

turns.text: Because you identify with the movement. A wave cannot escape the ocean until it ceases to be only a wave.
turns.speaker: Maharaj

turns.text: How does one cease?
turns.speaker: Questioner

turns.text: By giving up identification. When self-identification is abandoned, what you are remains by itself — free.
turns.speaker: Maharaj

turns.text: It is a matter of daily experience that on waking up the world suddenly appears. Where does it come from?
turns.speaker: Questioner

turns.text: Before anything can come into being there must be somebody to whom it comes. All appearance and disappearance presupposes a change against some changeless background.
turns.speaker: Maharaj

turns.text: Before waking up I was unconscious.
turns.speaker: Questioner

turns.text: In what sense? Having forgotten, or not having experienced? Don’t you experience even when unconscious? Can you exist without knowing?
turns.speaker: Maharaj

turns.text: A lapse in memory: is it a proof of non-existence? And can you validly talk about your own non-existence as an actual experience?
turns.speaker: Maharaj

turns.text: Did you not wake up on being called? And on waking up, was it not the sense ‘I am’ that came first?
turns.speaker: Maharaj

turns.text: On waking up the experience runs: ‘I am -- the body -- in the world.’ It may appear to arise in succession but in fact it is all simultaneous, a single idea of having a body in a world.
turns.speaker: Maharaj

turns.text: Can there be the sense of ‘I am’ without being somebody or other?
turns.speaker: Maharaj

turns.text: What benefit is there in knowing that I am not the body?
turns.speaker: Questioner

turns.text: Even to say that you are not the body is not quite true. In a way you are all the bodies, hearts and minds and much more.
turns.speaker: Maharaj

turns.text: Go deep into the sense of ‘I am’ and you will find.
turns.speaker: Maharaj

turns.text: The sense of being, of 'I am' is the first to emerge. Ask yourself whence it comes, or just watch it quietly.
turns.speaker: Maharaj

turns.text: When the mind stays in the 'I am' without moving, you enter a state which cannot be verbalised but can be experienced.
turns.speaker: Maharaj

turns.text: Then what am I?
turns.speaker: Questioner

turns.text: It is enough to know what you are not. You need not know what you are.
turns.speaker: Maharaj

turns.text: All you can say is: ‘I am not this, I am not that’. You cannot meaningfully say ‘this is what I am’.
turns.speaker: Maharaj

turns.text: The sense of being an experiencer, the sense of ‘I am’, is it not also an experience?
turns.speaker: Questioner

turns.text: Obviously, every thing experienced is an experience. And in every experience there arises the experiencer of it.
turns.speaker: Maharaj

turns.text: Memory creates the illusion of continuity.
turns.speaker: Maharaj

turns.text: In reality each experience has its own experiencer and the sense of identity is due to the common factor at the root of all experiencer–experience relations.
turns.speaker: Maharaj

turns.text: How do I get at it?
turns.speaker: Questioner

turns.text: You need not get at it, for you are it. It will get at you, if you give it a chance.
turns.speaker: Maharaj

turns.text: Let go your attachment to the unreal and the real will swiftly and smoothly step into its own.
turns.speaker: Maharaj

turns.text: Still, you are different. Your mind seems to be always quiet and happy. And miracles happen round you.
turns.speaker: Questioner

turns.text: I know nothing about miracles… As to my mind, there is no such thing. There is consciousness in which everything happens.
turns.speaker: Maharaj

turns.text: What do you see?
turns.speaker: Questioner

turns.text: You give no attention to your self. Bring your self into focus, become aware of your own existence.
turns.speaker: Maharaj

turns.text: See how you function, watch the motives and the results of your actions. Study the prison you have built around yourself by inadvertence.
turns.speaker: Maharaj

turns.text: By knowing what you are not, you come to know your self.
turns.speaker: Maharaj

turns.text: What has gone wrong is the ‘inner body’, call it mind, consciousness, antahkarana, whatever the name.
turns.speaker: Questioner

turns.text: What do you consider to be wrong with your mind?
turns.speaker: Maharaj

turns.text: It is restless, greedy of the pleasant and afraid of the unpleasant.
turns.speaker: Questioner

turns.text: Between the banks of pain and pleasure the river of life flows. It is only when the mind refuses to flow with life… that it becomes a problem. Desire not, fear not, observe the actual, as and when it happens, for you are not what happens, you are to whom it happens. Ultimately even the observer you are not. You are the ultimate potentiality of which the all-embracing consciousness is the manifestation
turns.speaker: Maharaj

turns.text: Even when a man is killed?
turns.speaker: Questioner

turns.text: The calamity is of the killer.
turns.speaker: Maharaj

turns.text: Still, it seems there are two worlds, mine and yours.
turns.speaker: Questioner

turns.text: Mine is real, yours is of the mind.
turns.speaker: Maharaj

turns.text: You give no attention to your self. Your mind is all with things, people and ideas, never with your self.
turns.speaker: Maharaj

turns.text: See how you function, watch the motives and the results of your actions.
turns.speaker: Maharaj

turns.text: Study the prison you have built around yourself by inadvertence.
turns.speaker: Maharaj

turns.text: If I create the world, why have I made it bad?
turns.speaker: Questioner

turns.text: Everyone lives in his own world. Not all the worlds are equally good or bad.
turns.speaker: Maharaj

turns.text: What determines the difference?
turns.speaker: Questioner

turns.text: The mind that projects the world, colours it its own way. When you meet a man, he is a stranger.
turns.speaker: Maharaj

turns.text: That's what you say! Did God come and tell you that the world is His creation and concern and not yours?
turns.speaker: Questioner

turns.text: Consider. The world in which you live, who else knows about it?
turns.speaker: Maharaj

turns.text: You know. Everybody knows.
turns.speaker: Questioner

turns.text: Did anybody come from outside of your world to tell you? Myself and everybody else appear and disappear in your world. We are all at your mercy.
turns.speaker: Maharaj

turns.text: It cannot be so bad! I exist in your world as you exist in mine.
turns.speaker: Questioner

turns.text: You have no evidence of my world. You are completely wrapped up in the world of your own making.
turns.speaker: Maharaj

turns.text: So all my questions, my search and study are of no use?
turns.speaker: Questioner

turns.text: These are but the stirrings of a man who is tired of sleeping. They are not the causes of awakening, but its early signs. But, you must not ask idle questions, to which you already know the answers.
turns.speaker: Maharaj

turns.text: How am I to get a true answer?
turns.speaker: Questioner

turns.text: By asking a true question -- non-verbally, but by daring to live according to your lights. A man willing to die for truth will get it.
turns.speaker: Maharaj

turns.text: Who is the jnani? The witness or the supreme?
turns.speaker: Questioner

turns.text: The jnani is the supreme and also the witness. He is both being and awareness. In relation to consciousness he is awareness. In relation to the universe he is pure being.
turns.speaker: Maharaj

turns.text: And what about the person? What comes first, the person or the knower?
turns.speaker: Questioner

turns.text: The person is a very small thing. Actually it is a composite, it cannot be said to exist by itself. Unperceived, it is just not there. It is but the shadow of the mind, the sum total of memories. Pure being is reflected in the mirror of the mind, as knowing. What is known takes the shape of a person, based on memory and habit.
turns.speaker: Maharaj

turns.text: All desires are painful, the holy as well as the unholy.
turns.speaker: Questioner

turns.text: They are not the same and pain is not the same. Passion is painful, compassion -- never. The entire universe strives to fulfil a desire born of compassion.
turns.speaker: Maharaj

turns.text: Are you living in the Supreme Unknown?
turns.speaker: Questioner

turns.text: Where else?
turns.speaker: Maharaj

turns.text: What makes you say so?
turns.speaker: Questioner

turns.text: No desire ever arises in my mind.
turns.speaker: Maharaj

turns.text: And if I desire nothing, not even the Supreme?
turns.speaker: Questioner

turns.text: Then you are as good as dead, or you are the Supreme.
turns.speaker: Maharaj

turns.text: What is your work?
turns.speaker: Questioner

turns.text: I am a probation officer.
turns.speaker: Questioner

turns.text: Must you work?
turns.speaker: Maharaj

turns.text: Who works? Work happens to take place.
turns.speaker: Questioner

turns.text: Do you need to work?
turns.speaker: Maharaj

turns.text: I need it for the sake of money. I like it, because it puts me in touch with living beings.
turns.speaker: Questioner

turns.text: What do you need them for?
turns.speaker: Maharaj

turns.text: They may need me and it is their destinies that made me take up this work. It is one life, after all.
turns.speaker: Questioner

turns.text: You say that nothing happens to you. Are you not affected at all by the suffering in the world?
turns.speaker: Questioner

turns.text: Suffering happens in consciousness, like clouds passing in the sky. I am not the cloud, I am the space in which it appears.
turns.speaker: Maharaj

turns.text: But you see it. Does seeing not make you responsible?
turns.speaker: Questioner

turns.text: Seeing clearly is compassion. To suffer because others suffer is still ignorance. In clear seeing, right action happens by itself.
turns.speaker: Maharaj

turns.text: So you feel nothing when people suffer?
turns.speaker: Questioner

turns.text: There is feeling, but no owner of feeling. Pain is there, but not the story 'this should not be'. The story is your personal addition.
turns.speaker: Maharaj

turns.text: Is it not cruel to stand apart like that?
turns.speaker: Questioner

turns.text: Cruelty is to remain confused and add your fear and anger to the world. Wake up from the dream of being a separate sufferer; only then can your presence be truly helpful.
turns.speaker: Maharaj

turns.text: However much I listen to you, the fear of death does not leave me.
turns.speaker: Questioner

turns.text: Who is afraid? The body, which is going to end anyway, or the witness, which never began?
turns.speaker: Maharaj

turns.text: It feels like I, as this person, will vanish and that terrifies me.
turns.speaker: Questioner

turns.text: Every night in deep sleep this person vanishes, yet you are not terrified then. You enjoy the rest. Only waking imagination calls it death and trembles.
turns.speaker: Maharaj

turns.text: But deep sleep comes and goes. Death seems final.
turns.speaker: Questioner

turns.text: Final for whom? The forms change, the movie ends, but the screen remains unstained. Find yourself as the screen, not the story.
turns.speaker: Maharaj

turns.text: How can I be sure I am this screen and not the story?
turns.speaker: Questioner

turns.text: Right now, notice that all that appears — body, thoughts, fear of death — is known. The knower is not in danger. Attend to the knower, not to what it knows.
turns.speaker: Maharaj

turns.text: Sometimes you say effort is needed, sometimes you say all is grace. Which is true?
turns.speaker: Questioner

turns.text: Effort belongs to the person, grace to reality. Your effort prepares the ground; grace is the rain. Both are needed for the crop.
turns.speaker: Maharaj

turns.text: If all is grace, why bother to make any effort at all?
turns.speaker: Questioner

turns.text: The impulse to 'bother' or not is itself grace. Even your laziness is seen. That which sees is not lazy. Stay with that.
turns.speaker: Maharaj

turns.text: I still feel I must do something to deserve realisation.
turns.speaker: Questioner

turns.text: Deserving is a childish idea. Your only 'doing' is to stop pretending you are what you are not. Grace is already there as your very being.
turns.speaker: Maharaj

turns.text: So should I strive or surrender?
turns.speaker: Questioner

turns.text: Strive until striving exhausts itself and surrender happens by itself. Both are movements in the same one consciousness that you are.
turns.speaker: Maharaj

turns.text: My Guru gave me a mantra. You tell me to stay with 'I am'. Should I drop the mantra?
turns.speaker: Questioner

turns.text: If a boat has brought you to the other shore, you do not carry it on your head. Use what helps you to be still and present; discard what keeps you busy and dull.
turns.speaker: Maharaj

turns.text: The mantra calms me, but sometimes I just repeat it mechanically.
turns.speaker: Questioner

turns.text: Mechanical repetition puts the body to sleep and leaves the mind dreaming. Let the words point you back to the sense of being, then stay with that nakedly.
turns.speaker: Maharaj

turns.text: So is 'I am' also a mantra?
turns.speaker: Questioner

turns.text: 'I am' is not a sound to worship but a fact to see. The mantra is a finger; 'I am' is the moon it points to. Look where it points, not at the finger.
turns.speaker: Maharaj

turns.text: If I let go of all words, I feel lost.
turns.speaker: Questioner

turns.text: You are not lost; your usual distractions are missing. Stay with that bare discomfort; it is the threshold of reality, not a mistake.
turns.speaker: Maharaj

turns.text: I have a family and many responsibilities. Is it not selfish to turn inward and think of freedom?
turns.speaker: Questioner

turns.text: You are selfish now, because you take yourself to be this one body-mind and seek its security. To discover your real nature is the end of selfishness, not its peak.
turns.speaker: Maharaj

turns.text: But my family expects attention and care. Won't they suffer if I withdraw into myself?
turns.speaker: Questioner

turns.text: You do not have to withdraw from them, only from your fantasies about them. Be fully present, free of anxiety and claims; then your actions will be simple and kind.
turns.speaker: Maharaj

turns.text: Sometimes I feel torn between spiritual practice and practical life.
turns.speaker: Questioner

turns.text: Life is your practice. Let every demand, every irritation, every joy throw you back on the question: 'To whom does this come?' Use your family as a mirror, not as a chain.
turns.speaker: Maharaj

turns.text: So I do not need to leave anything?
turns.speaker: Questioner

turns.text: Leave only your ignorance of yourself. What needs to fall away will fall away by itself, when you stop holding it with fear and habit.
turns.speaker: Maharaj

turns.text: In dream, things seem real, but they vanish on waking. How do I know this waking state is not just a longer dream?
turns.speaker: Questioner

turns.text: You do not know. You assume. In both states, there is one constant: the sense 'I am' which witnesses their coming and going.
turns.speaker: Maharaj

turns.text: So what should I trust, if not the world I see?
turns.speaker: Questioner

turns.text: Trust the fact that you are, not what you appear to be. Appearances contradict each other; the being that knows them does not change.
turns.speaker: Maharaj

turns.text: But even 'I am' disappears in deep sleep.
turns.speaker: Questioner

turns.text: The memory of 'I am' disappears. The potential to know does not. From that potential, both dream and waking spring. Be interested in the source, not its waves.
turns.speaker: Maharaj

turns.text: Can this source be experienced?
turns.speaker: Questioner

turns.text: Experience needs subject and object. The source is before both. You cannot experience it, but you can cease to pretend you are anything else.
turns.speaker: Maharaj

turns.text: Is there free will, or is everything predetermined?
turns.speaker: Questioner

turns.text: For the person you take yourself to be, there is neither freedom nor bondage. It is a bundle of tendencies acting itself out. For the reality that you are, the question does not arise.
turns.speaker: Maharaj

turns.text: Then why do I feel I am choosing all the time?
turns.speaker: Questioner

turns.text: A leaf moved by the wind may feel it is deciding where to fall. Your feeling of choice is just the mind commenting on movements it does not understand.
turns.speaker: Maharaj

turns.text: If there is no real choice, what is the point of effort or practice?
turns.speaker: Questioner

turns.text: Effort appears as part of the play. It refines the mind, makes it transparent. Then it becomes clear that what you really are was never bound by any destiny.
turns.speaker: Maharaj

turns.text: So should I act as if I have free will or not?
turns.speaker: Questioner

turns.text: Act as you must, but do not conclude anything from it. Let actions happen, and stay with the silent fact of being in which they rise and set.
turns.speaker: Maharaj

turns.text: You always tell us to rely on the inner Guru. Then why do you sit here and allow us to worship your form?
turns.speaker: Questioner

turns.text: If you only worship this form, you are wasting your time. If this form reminds you of your own true nature, then it has done its work, and you can forget it.
turns.speaker: Maharaj

turns.text: Yet when I come here and sit near you, I feel quiet and full. Away from you I lose it.
turns.speaker: Questioner

turns.text: Here you forget your usual stories about yourself, so peace appears. Away from here you remember them again and call it 'losing peace'. The peace is not mine; it is what remains when you stop disturbing yourself.
turns.speaker: Maharaj

turns.text: So the Guru does nothing for the disciple?
turns.speaker: Questioner

turns.text: The Guru is a function: to reveal your own Guru. When you see that the same presence shines in you, this old man in front of you is no longer needed.
turns.speaker: Maharaj

turns.text: How do I know that inner presence is not just my imagination?
turns.speaker: Questioner

turns.text: Imagination comes and goes and needs effort to be maintained. This presence is there before imagination and after it, quietly knowing. Trust what does not need to be produced.
turns.speaker: Maharaj

turns.text: Sometimes everything feels meaningless. Even spiritual talk becomes just more words. Is there any point to all this?
turns.speaker: Questioner

turns.text: Good. When your toys bore you, you begin to look at the child. When all meanings feel empty, you are close to what does not need meaning.
turns.speaker: Maharaj

turns.text: So my boredom is useful?
turns.speaker: Questioner

turns.text: If you use it. Instead of running to new entertainments, stay with the naked sense 'I am' that remains when everything else is tasteless. That is the doorway.
turns.speaker: Maharaj

turns.text: But when I do that, it feels flat and dull.
turns.speaker: Questioner

turns.text: It feels dull because you are comparing it with the excitement of becoming. Drop the comparison. The 'dullness' is only the mind complaining that it has nothing to play with.
turns.speaker: Maharaj

turns.text: Will this 'I am' ever become blissful like the scriptures promise?
turns.speaker: Questioner

turns.text: It does not become anything. When you stop demanding experiences from it, its quiet joy becomes obvious. You do not find it by decoration, but by subtraction.
turns.speaker: Maharaj

turns.text: Did you, then, since you had an affectionate disposition to your child, do right when you ran off and left her; and has the mother no affection for the child?
turns.speaker: Epictetus

turns.text: Certainly, she has.
turns.speaker: Magistrate

turns.text: Ought, then, the mother also to have left her, or ought she not?
turns.speaker: Epictetus

turns.text: She ought not.
turns.speaker: Magistrate

turns.text: And the nurse, does she love her?
turns.speaker: Epictetus

turns.text: She does.
turns.speaker: Magistrate

turns.text: Ought, then, she also to have left her?
turns.speaker: Epictetus

turns.text: By no means.
turns.speaker: Magistrate

turns.text: And the pedagogue, does he not love her?
turns.speaker: Epictetus

turns.text: He does love her.
turns.speaker: Magistrate

turns.text: Ought, then, he also to have deserted her? and so should the child have been left alone and without help on account of the great affection of you, the parents, and of those about her, or should she have died in the hands of those who neither loved her nor cared for her?
turns.speaker: Epictetus

turns.text: Certainly not.
turns.speaker: Magistrate

turns.text: Now this is unfair and unreasonable, not to allow those who have equal affection with yourself to do what you think to be proper for yourself to do because you have affection.
turns.speaker: Epictetus

turns.text: Since reason is the faculty which analyses and perfects the rest, and it ought itself not to be unanalysed, by what should it be analysed? for it is plain that this should be done either by itself or by another thing.
turns.speaker: Epictetus

turns.text: Yes.
turns.speaker: Interlocutor

turns.text: Either, then, this other thing also is reason, or something else superior to reason; which is impossible. But if it is reason, again who shall analyse that reason? For if that reason does this for itself, our reason also can do it. But we shall require something else, the thing, will go on to infinity and have no end.
turns.speaker: Epictetus

turns.text: It is more urgent to cure our opinions.
turns.speaker: Interlocutor

turns.text: Reason therefore is analysed by itself.
turns.speaker: Epictetus

turns.text: Tell me the secret which you possess.
turns.speaker: Tyrant

turns.text: I will not, for this is in my power.
turns.speaker: Epictetus

turns.text: But I will put you in chains.
turns.speaker: Tyrant

turns.text: Man, what are you talking about? Me in chains? You may fetter my leg, but my will not even Zeus himself can overpower.
turns.speaker: Epictetus

turns.text: I will throw you into prison.
turns.speaker: Tyrant

turns.text: My poor body, you mean.
turns.speaker: Epictetus

turns.text: I will cut your head off.
turns.speaker: Tyrant

turns.text: When, then, have I told you that my head alone cannot be cut off?
turns.speaker: Epictetus

turns.text: Suppose it to be night.
turns.speaker: Epictetus

turns.text: I suppose that it is night.
turns.speaker: Student

turns.text: Well then; is it day?
turns.speaker: Epictetus

turns.text: No, for I admitted the hypothesis that it was night.
turns.speaker: Student

turns.text: Suppose that you think that it is night?
turns.speaker: Epictetus

turns.text: Suppose that I do.
turns.speaker: Student

turns.text: But also think that it is night.
turns.speaker: Epictetus

turns.text: That is not consistent with the hypothesis.
turns.speaker: Student

turns.text: So in this case also: "Suppose that you are unfortunate." Well, suppose so. "Are you then unhappy?" Yes. "Well, then, are you troubled with an unfavourable demon?" Yes. "But think also that you are in misery."
turns.speaker: Epictetus

turns.text: This is not consistent with the hypothesis; and Another forbids me to think so.
turns.speaker: Student

turns.text: Frequently I desired to hear you and came to you, and you never gave me any answer: and now, if it is possible, I entreat you to say something to me.
turns.speaker: Person

turns.text: Do you think that as there is an art in anything else, so there is also an art in speaking, and that he who has the art, will speak skillfully, and he who has not, will speak unskillfully?
turns.speaker: Epictetus

turns.text: I do think so.
turns.speaker: Person

turns.text: He, then, who by speaking receives benefit himself and is able to benefit others, will speak skillfully: but he who is rather damaged by speaking and does damage to others, will he be unskilled in this art of speaking?
turns.speaker: Epictetus

turns.text: He will be unskilled.
turns.speaker: Person

turns.text: Is there then a skill in hearing also, as there is in speaking?
turns.speaker: Epictetus

turns.text: It seems so.
turns.speaker: Person

turns.text: If you choose, consider the matter in this way also. The practice of music, to whom does it belong?
turns.speaker: Epictetus

turns.text: To a musician.
turns.speaker: Person

turns.text: And the proper making of a statue, to whom do you think that it belongs?
turns.speaker: Epictetus

turns.text: To a statuary.
turns.speaker: Person

turns.text: Then if speaking properly is the business of the skillful man, do you see that to hear also with benefit is the business of the skillful man?
turns.speaker: Epictetus

turns.text: Why do not you go down?
turns.speaker: Florus

turns.text: Because I do not even deliberate about the matter.
turns.speaker: Agrippinus

turns.text: For he who has once brought himself to deliberate about such matters, and to calculate the value of external things, comes very near to those who have forgotten their own character. For why do you ask me the question, whether death is preferable or life? I say "life." "Pain or pleasure?" I say "pleasure." But if I do not take a part in the tragic acting, I shall have my head struck off. Go then and take a part, but I will not.
turns.speaker: Epictetus

turns.text: Why?
turns.speaker: Florus

turns.text: Because you consider yourself to be only one thread of those which are in the tunic.
turns.speaker: Epictetus

turns.text: It is in your power not to allow me to be a member of the senate, but so long as I am, I must go in.
turns.speaker: Priscus Helvidius

turns.text: Well, go in then, but say nothing.
turns.speaker: Vespasian

turns.text: Do not ask my opinion, and I will be silent.
turns.speaker: Priscus Helvidius

turns.text: But I must ask your opinion.
turns.speaker: Vespasian

turns.text: And I must say what I think right.
turns.speaker: Priscus Helvidius

turns.text: But if you do, I shall put you to death.
turns.speaker: Vespasian

turns.text: When then did I tell you that I am immortal? You will do your part, and I will do mine: it is your part to kill; it is mine to die, but not in fear: yours to banish me; mine to depart without sorrow.
turns.speaker: Priscus Helvidius

turns.text: How then shall my brother cease to be angry with me?
turns.speaker: Man

turns.text: Bring him to me and I will tell him. But I have nothing to say to you about his anger.
turns.speaker: Epictetus

turns.text: I seek to know this- how, even if my brother is not reconciled to me, shall I maintain myself in a state conformable to nature?
turns.speaker: Man

turns.text: Nothing great is produced suddenly, since not even the grape or the fig is. If you say to me now that you want a fig, I will answer to you that it requires time: let it flower first, then put forth fruit, and then ripen. Is, then, the fruit of a fig-tree not perfected suddenly and in one hour, and would you possess the fruit of a man's mind in so short a time and so easily? Do not expect it, even if I tell you.
turns.speaker: Epictetus

turns.text: But if we lay aside this fidelity for which we are formed and make designs against our neighbor's wife, what are we are we doing? What else but destroying and overthrowing? Whom? The man of fidelity, the man of modesty, the man of sanctity. Is this all? And are we not overthrowing neighbourhood, and friendship, and the community; and in what place are we putting ourselves? How shall I consider you, man? As a neighbour, as a friend? What kind of one? As a citizen? Wherein shall I trust you?
turns.speaker: Epictetus

turns.text: Then will you say, "No man, cares for me, a man of letters"?
turns.speaker: Adulterer

turns.text: They do not, because you are bad and useless. It is just as if the wasps complained because no man cares for them, but all fly from them, and if a man can, he strikes them and knocks them down. You have such a sting that you throw into trouble and pain any man that you wound with it. What would you have us do with you? You have no place where you can be put.
turns.speaker: Epictetus

turns.text: What then, are not women common by nature?
turns.speaker: Adulterer

turns.text: So I say also; for a little pig is common to all the invited guests, but when the portions have been distributed, go, if you think it right, and snatch up the portion of him who reclines next to you, or slyly steal it, or place your hand down by it and lay hold of it, and if you cannot tear away a bit of the meat, grease your fingers and lick them. A fine companion over cups, and Socratic guest indeed!
turns.speaker: Epictetus

turns.text: Can you tell me, Sir, to whose care you have entrusted your horses?
turns.speaker: Epictetus

turns.text: I can tell you.
turns.speaker: Consular

turns.text: Here you entrusted them to a person indifferently and to one who has no experience of horses?
turns.speaker: Epictetus

turns.text: By no means.
turns.speaker: Consular

turns.text: Well then; can you tell me to whom you entrust your gold or silver things or your vestments?
turns.speaker: Epictetus

turns.text: I don't entrust even these to anyone indifferently.
turns.speaker: Consular

turns.text: Well; your own body, have you already considered about entrusting the care of it to any person?
turns.speaker: Epictetus

turns.text: Certainly.
turns.speaker: Consular

turns.text: To a man of experience, I suppose, and one acquainted with the aliptic, or with the healing art?
turns.speaker: Epictetus

turns.text: Without a doubt.
turns.speaker: Consular

turns.text: Are these the best things that you have, or do you also possess something else which is better than all these?
turns.speaker: Epictetus

turns.text: What kind of thing do you mean?
turns.speaker: Consular

turns.text: That I mean which makes use of these things, and tests each of these things and deliberates.
turns.speaker: Epictetus

turns.text: Is it the soul that you mean? In truth I do think the soul is a much better thing than all the others which I possess.
turns.speaker: Consular

turns.text: Does the envious man rejoice?
turns.speaker: Socrates

turns.text: By no means, but he is rather pained.
turns.speaker: Adversary

turns.text: Do you think that envy is pain over evils? and what envy is there of evils?
turns.speaker: Socrates

turns.text: (Implied negation/agreement that envy concerns goods)
turns.speaker: Adversary

turns.text: Well then, would any man envy those who are nothing to him?
turns.speaker: Socrates

turns.text: By no means.
turns.speaker: Adversary

turns.text: I have resolved.
turns.speaker: Companion

turns.text: But still tell me what it was which induced you to resolve; for if you have resolved rightly, we shall sit with you and assist you to depart; but if you have made an unreasonable resolution, change your mind.
turns.speaker: Epictetus

turns.text: We ought to keep to our determinations.
turns.speaker: Companion

turns.text: What are you doing, man? We ought to keep not to all our determinations, but to those which are right; for if you are now persuaded that it is right, do not change your mind, if you think fit, but persist and say, "We ought to abide by our determinations." Will you not make the beginning and lay the foundation in an inquiry whether the determination is sound or not sound, and so then build on it firmness and security? But if you lay a rotten and ruinous foundation, will not your miserable little building fall down the sooner, the more and the stronger are the materials which you shall lay on it?
turns.speaker: Epictetus

turns.text: I am determined.
turns.speaker: Companion

turns.text: Will you not act like a sick man and call in the physician?
turns.speaker: Epictetus

turns.text: I know not what I ought to do, but I am come to learn.
turns.speaker: Companion

turns.text: Not so; but, "Speak to me about other things: upon this I have determined." What other things? for what is greater and more useful than for you to be persuaded that it is not sufficient to have made your determination and not to change it. This is the tone of madness, not of health.
turns.speaker: Epictetus

turns.text: Show me a Stoic, if you can. Where or how? But you can show me an endless number who utter small arguments of the Stoics. For do the same persons repeat the Epicurean opinions any worse? And the Peripatetic, do they not handle them also with equal accuracy? who then is a Stoic? As we call a statue Phidiac which is fashioned according to the art of Phidias; so show me a man who is fashioned according to the doctrines which he utters. Show me a man who is sick and happy, in danger and happy, dying and happy, in exile and happy, in disgrace and happy. Show him: I desire, by the gods, to see a Stoic.
turns.speaker: Epictetus

turns.text: (Silence/Inability to produce one)
turns.speaker: Students (implied)

turns.text: You cannot show me one fashioned so; but show me at least one who is forming, who has shown a tendency to be a Stoic. Do me this favor: do not grudge an old man seeing a sight which I have not seen yet. Do you think that you must show me the Zeus of Phidias or the Athena, a work of ivory and gold? Let any of you show me a human soul ready to think as God does, and not to blame either God or man, ready not to be disappointed about anything, not to consider himself damaged by anything, not to be angry, not to be envious, not to be jealous.
turns.speaker: Epictetus

turns.text: I wish I could learn everything before I return: but much labour is necessary, and no one sends me anything, and the baths at Nicopolis are dirty; everything is bad at home, and bad here.
turns.speaker: Student

turns.text: Then they say, "No one gains any profit from the school." Why, who comes to the school, who comes for the purpose of being improved? who comes to present his opinions to he purified? who comes to learn what he is in want of? Why do you wonder then if you carry back from the school the very things which you bring into it?
turns.speaker: Epictetus

turns.text: But I wish to prattle about theorems.
turns.speaker: Student

turns.text: Do not your little theorems give you some opportunity of display? You solve sophistical syllogisms. Do you not examine the assumptions of the syllogism named "The Liar"? Do you not examine hypothetical syllogisms? Why, then, are you still vexed if you receive the things for which you come to the school?
turns.speaker: Epictetus

turns.text: Yes; but if my child die or my brother, or if I must die or be racked, what good will these things do me?
turns.speaker: Student

turns.text: Well, did you come for this? for this do you sit by my side?
turns.speaker: Epictetus

turns.text: But I also am rich.
turns.speaker: Student

turns.text: Are you then richer than Agamemnon?
turns.speaker: Epictetus

turns.text: But I am also handsome.
turns.speaker: Student

turns.text: Are you then more handsome than Achilles?
turns.speaker: Epictetus

turns.text: But I have also beautiful hair.
turns.speaker: Student

turns.text: But had not Achilles more beautiful hair and gold-colored? and he did not comb it elegantly nor dress it.
turns.speaker: Epictetus

turns.text: But I am also strong.
turns.speaker: Student

turns.text: Can you then lift so great a stone as Hector or Ajax?
turns.speaker: Epictetus

turns.text: But I am also of noble birth.
turns.speaker: Student

turns.text: Are you the son of a goddess mother? are you the son of a father sprung from Zeus? What good then do these things do to him, when he sits and weeps for a girl?
turns.speaker: Epictetus

turns.text: Can, then, a man think that a thing is useful to him and not choose it?
turns.speaker: Epictetus

turns.text: He cannot.
turns.speaker: Interlocutor

turns.text: How says Medea? 'Tis true I know what evil I shall do, But passion overpowers the better council.' She thought that to indulge her passion and take vengeance on her husband was more profitable than to spare her children.
turns.speaker: Epictetus

turns.text: It was so; but she was deceived.
turns.speaker: Interlocutor

turns.text: Show her plainly that she is deceived, and she will not do it; but so long as you do not show it, what can she follow except that which appears to herself? Nothing else. Why, then, are you angry with the unhappy woman that she has been bewildered about the most important things, and is become a viper instead of a human creature?
turns.speaker: Epictetus

turns.text: But I cannot comprehend all these things at once.
turns.speaker: Interlocutor

turns.text: But who tells you that you have equal power with Zeus? Nevertheless he has placed by every man a guardian, every man's Demon, to whom he has committed the care of the man, a guardian who never sleeps, is never deceived. For to what better and more careful guardian could He have entrusted each of us? When, then, you have shut the doors and made darkness within, remember never to say that you are alone, for you are not; but God is within, and your Demon is within, and what need have they of light to see what you are doing?
turns.speaker: Epictetus

turns.text: When death appears an evil, we ought to have this rule in readiness, that it is fit to avoid evil things, and that death is a necessary thing. For what shall I do, and where shall I escape it?
turns.speaker: Epictetus

turns.text: I cannot escape from death.
turns.speaker: Student

turns.text: Shall I not escape from the fear of death, but shall I die lamenting and trembling? For the origin of perturbation is this, to wish for something, and that this should not happen.
turns.speaker: Epictetus

turns.text: Then, at last, when I am neither able to change circumstances nor to tear out the eyes of him who hinders me, I sit down and groan, and abuse whom I can, Zeus and the rest of the gods.
turns.speaker: Student

turns.text: For if they do not care for me, what are they to me?
turns.speaker: Epictetus

turns.text: Yes, but you will be an impious man.
turns.speaker: Student

turns.text: In what respect then will it be worse for me than it is now? To sum up, remember this that unless piety and your interest be in the same thing, piety cannot be maintained in any man.
turns.speaker: Epictetus

turns.text: Does any one among us think of these lessons out of the schools? Does any one meditate by himself to give an answer to things as in the case of questions? Is it day?
turns.speaker: Epictetus

turns.text: Yes.
turns.speaker: Student

turns.text: Is it night?
turns.speaker: Epictetus

turns.text: No.
turns.speaker: Student

turns.text: Well, is the number of stars even?
turns.speaker: Epictetus

turns.text: I cannot say.
turns.speaker: Student

turns.text: When money is shown to you, have you studied to make the proper answer, that money is not a good thing? Have you practiced yourself in these answers, or only against sophisms? Why do you wonder then if in the cases which you have studied, in those you have improved; but in those which you have not studied, in those you remain the same?
turns.speaker: Epictetus

turns.text: I have not been vexed to-day, nor the day after, nor yet on any succeeding day during two or three months; but I took care when some exciting things happened.
turns.speaker: Student

turns.text: Be assured that you are in a good way. To-day when I saw a handsome person, I did not say to myself, "I wish I could lie with her," and "Happy is her husband"; for he who says this says, "Happy is her adulterer also." Nor do I picture the rest to my mind; the woman present, and stripping herself and lying down by my side. I stroke my head and say, "Well done, Epictetus, you have solved a fine little sophism, much finer than that which is called the master sophism."
turns.speaker: Epictetus

turns.text: Yes, but my nose runs.
turns.speaker: Student

turns.text: For what purpose then, slave, have you hands? Is it not that you may wipe your nose?
turns.speaker: Epictetus

turns.text: Is it, then, consistent with reason that there should be running of noses in the world?
turns.speaker: Student

turns.text: Nay, how much better it is to wipe your nose than to find fault. What do you think that Hercules would have been if there had not been such a lion, and hydra, and stag, and boar, and certain unjust and bestial men, whom Hercules used to drive away and clear out? And what would he have been doing if there had been nothing of the kind? Is it not plain that he would have wrapped himself up and have slept?
turns.speaker: Epictetus

turns.text: Socrates, then, knew how to play at ball.
turns.speaker: Epictetus

turns.text: How?
turns.speaker: Student

turns.text: By using pleasantry in the court where he was tried. "Tell me," he says, "Anytus, how do you say that I do not believe in God. The Demons, who are they, think you? Are they not sons of Gods, or compounded of gods and men?" When Anytus admitted this, Socrates said, "Who then, think you, can believe that there are mules, but not asses"; and this he said as if he were playing at ball.
turns.speaker: Epictetus

turns.text: And what was the ball in that case?
turns.speaker: Student

turns.text: Life, chains, banishment, a draught of poison, separation from wife and leaving children orphans. These were the things with which he was playing; but still he did play and threw the ball skillfully.
turns.speaker: Epictetus

turns.text: Whence shall I get bread to eat when I have nothing?
turns.speaker: Student

turns.text: And how do slaves, and runaways, on what do they rely when they leave their masters? Do they rely on their lands or slaves, or their vessels of silver? They rely on nothing but themselves, and food does not fail them. And shall it be necessary for one among us who is a philosopher to travel into foreign parts, and trust to and rely on others, and not to take care of himself, and shall he be inferior to irrational animals and more cowardly?
turns.speaker: Epictetus

turns.text: But we are fettered by these bonds, the body.
turns.speaker: Student

turns.text: Wait for God; when He shall give the signal and release you from this service, then go to Him; but for the present endure to dwell in this place where He has put you.
turns.speaker: Epictetus

turns.text: When will the west wind blow?
turns.speaker: Student

turns.text: When it shall choose, my good man, or when it shall please AEolus; for God has not made you the manager of the winds, but AEolus.
turns.speaker: Epictetus

turns.text: What then?
turns.speaker: Student

turns.text: We must make the best use that we can of the things which are in our power, and use the rest according to their nature.
turns.speaker: Epictetus

turns.text: What is their nature then?
turns.speaker: Student

turns.text: As God may please.
turns.speaker: Epictetus

turns.text: Suggest something to me [for my trial].
turns.speaker: Student

turns.text: What should I suggest to you?
turns.speaker: Epictetus

turns.text: Form my mind so as to accommodate itself to any event.
turns.speaker: Student

turns.text: Why that is just the same as if a man who is ignorant of letters should say, "Tell me what to write when any name is proposed to me." For if I should tell him to write Dion, and then another should come and propose to him not the name of Dion but that of Theon, what will be done? what will he write? But if you have practiced writing, you are also prepared to write anything that is required. If you are not, what can I now suggest? For if circumstances require something else, what will you say or what will you do?
turns.speaker: Epictetus

turns.text:
Q. What are the kind of things to look for in trying to separate false
personality from the rest of oneself?
turns.speaker: Q.

turns.text:
A. It is necessary to understand the features of false personality—what
makes it up. You may be able to see it in the glimpses you remember of
the age to which you can attribute the beginning of false personality.
There are two things that are permanent in us—buffers and weaknesses or features
of false personality. Everyone has one, two or three particular weaknesses, and
everybody has certain buffers that are especially important, for they enter into all his
decisions and his understanding of things. This is all that is permanent in us, and it is
lucky for us that there is nothing more permanent, because these things can be
changed. Buffers are artificial, they are not organic, they are chiefly acquired by
imitation. Children begin to imitate grown-ups and create buffers, and some others are
unwittingly created by education. Features or weaknesses can sometimes be found out,
and if one knows a feature and keeps it in mind, one may find certain moments when
one can act not from this feature. Everybody has many features but two or three are
particularly important because they enter into every subjectively important situation in
one's life; everything passes through them, all perceptions and all reactions. It is very
difficult to realize what this means because we are so accustomed to it that we do not
notice it; we are too much in those features, we have not got enough perspective.
turns.speaker: A.

turns.text: Q. Must the chief feature necessarily be bad?
turns.speaker: Q.

turns.text:
A. It is chief weakness; unfortunately we cannot think that our chief feature is
strength, because we have no strength.
turns.speaker: A.

turns.text: Q. How can it be weakness if there is no not-weakness?
turns.speaker: Q.

turns.text:
A. It means mechanicalness. We are mechanical in all things, but in one
or two things we are particularly mechanical and particularly blind; that is why they
are chief weaknesses, for we cannot see them. Other things, that are not weaknesses,
we can see.
turns.speaker: A.

turns.text: Q. What would you call a weakness? Do you judge by ethical standards?
turns.speaker: Q.

turns.text:
A. No. As I said, a weakness is a thing in which you are most mechanical. Naturally,
things concerning which you are absolutely helpless, where you are most asleep, most
blind are bound to be your chief weaknesses, because there are degrees in everything.
turns.speaker: A.

turns.text:
Q. You say we have nothing but weaknesses. Surely desire to be free is not a
weakness?
turns.speaker: Q.

turns.text:
A. There can be one or another kind of desire. Suppose one realizes one's weakness
and wishes to get rid of it, and at the same time one does not wish to learn the
methods of getting rid of this weakness. This would be a second weakness, helping
and protecting the first weakness.
turns.speaker: A.

turns.text: Q. But if one makes constant efforts?
turns.speaker: Q.

turns.text:
A. Again, that will belong to the other side of you, to what I call 'you'. This 'you' is
not a power or a force, it is merely a combination of certain desires, desires to get rid
of something. If you realize that something is wrong, and you formulate a desire to
get rid of it, then if you can keep your mind on it sufficiently long, it becomes a
certain plan of action; and if this line of action is sufficiently prolonged it can attain
results.
turns.speaker: A.

turns.text:
Only, it is necessary to add again that several different lines of action are
needed to attain results, not just one line. We have to work at the same time on one
thing and another thing and a third thing. One line of action won't do because there
are many liabilities and the balance of things has to change in many points at the
same time.
turns.speaker: A.

turns.text:
Q. I did not understand it when you said once that we cannot change anything but we
must act differently.
turns.speaker: Q.

turns.text:
A. Try to think: while we still remain as we are, we have to act differently. You
cannot change at once, change is slow. But you have many things to do, and if you do
them in a wrong way you will never change.
turns.speaker: A.

turns.text:
Q. How can I make better use of moments when I feel the miraculousness of the
system?
turns.speaker: Q.

turns.text:
A. Make more regular efforts, not occasional efforts. You know why I always speak
about this? Because it is self-deception to think that one can awake without special and
long work. We must realize how difficult it is. Thinking, not thinking, talking, not
talking, feeling, not feeling, everything keeps us asleep. Now we speak theoretically
about it, but work cannot be theoretical. The fact that one is asleep must become a
permanent realization, one must feel it emotionally. But by itself this realization will
not make one awake: special efforts are necessary to wake oneself up for a moment.
turns.speaker: A.

turns.text: Q. Is it not necessary to be fairly awake to formulate one's aim?
turns.speaker: Q.

turns.text:
A. This is another thing. Realizing and understanding are possible in a kind of half-
sleep; just as one can find one's way home, so we can find the way to our aim.
Awakening is a long process.
turns.speaker: A.

turns.text: Q. Is hesitation between two different aims a sign of sleep?
turns.speaker: Q.

turns.text:
A. Partly of sleep and partly of incomplete understanding. When one knows what is
most important, one has no hesitation.
turns.speaker: A.

turns.text:
Q. I find that when I discover a method to make me remember myself, this works for a
few times and then wears off.
turns.speaker: Q.

turns.text:
A. You must always change those methods; they do not work for long— it is part of
our state. Take it as a fact; there is no need to analyse it. The more new and
unexpected things are, the better they will work. This is connected with the
fundamental principle of all mental and physical life. We observe, in the ordinary
sense, only changes in our associations. We do not feel permanent associations; we
notice only changes. So when you are accustomed to them, you have to make some
kind of alarm; then you get accustomed to this alarm and it does not work any more. If
you make your alarm-clock ring permanently, you will notice it only when it stops
ringing.
turns.speaker: A.

turns.text: Q. Does the realization of being asleep create its own force for awakening?
turns.speaker: Q.

turns.text:
A. If one realizes one is asleep, one must study means and methods to awake, but it
must cease to be a word; it must become a fact based on observation. Only then is it
possible to speak with more precision and more practically about it. When one realizes
one is asleep, at that moment one is already half-awake, but it is not long enough; the
next moment something begins to turn in one's head and one gets carried away into
sleep again. This is why one cannot awake by oneself, why elaborate methods are
necessary—one must be shaken and shaken.
turns.speaker: A.

turns.text: Q. Is an effort to self-remember practical?
turns.speaker: Q.

turns.text: A. It may be practical, it may be theoretical and it may be philosophical.
turns.speaker: A.

turns.text: Q. Objective consciousness seems to belong to the philosophical scale?
turns.speaker: Q.

turns.text:
A. Quite the reverse: it is very practical. But if you mean for us, then,
certainly, objective consciousness is a philosophical idea. At the same
time the study of descriptions of glimpses of this state is possible. If one
studies these descriptions and tries to find similarities, it can become
theoretical.
turns.speaker: A.

turns.text:
Q. I should like to understand more about this division. I do not know
what is practical.
turns.speaker: Q.

turns.text:
A. It means what you can do—in all senses. Only, 'doing' can be on one
scale or another scale. Doing is always more important than thinking or
talking. So if we take it that philosophical is thinking, theoretical talking
and practical doing, the practical is more important.
turns.speaker: A.

turns.text: Q. Isn't it in a way a school of thought too, since doing must come from thinking?
turns.speaker: Q.

turns.text:
A. I think it is better to say all three. It has three sides. Also, some people take the
system practically, others only philosophically and theoretically. There are things to
which we have no practical approach and for which we must find analogies. So
sometimes it is quite right. But there are things which you can take only practically,
for only then can you value them.
turns.speaker: A.

turns.text:
Q. You said that another of our chief difficulties is formatory thinking. I do not in the
least know how to think not formatorily.
turns.speaker: Q.

turns.text:
A. Think to the best of your ability and compare results—when your thinking gives
results and when it does not. In that way you will come to a better understanding, at
any rate better than just wondering about it. Definitions will not help you: desire for
definitions is only an excuse. If you find yourself in a very difficult position, you will
think to the best of your ability how to get out of it. Think in the same way.
turns.speaker: A.

turns.text: Q. Before we can think differently, is it necessary to perceive things differently?
turns.speaker: Q.

turns.text:
A. We cannot perceive differently until we think differently. We have control only of
our thoughts; we have no control over perception. Perception depends particularly on
the state of consciousness. If one awakes for sufficiently long, one can perceive many
things one does not perceive now. It does not depend on desire or decision.
turns.speaker: A.

turns.text: Q. Is all thinking formatory, except when we are trying to self-remember?
turns.speaker: Q.

turns.text:
A. No, not all, but a great deal of our thinking is formatory. But when we think about
serious things, such as the ideas of this system, we either cannot think at all or our
thinking is not formatory. Formatory thinking is always poor, but for some problems it
is ridiculous.
turns.speaker: A.

turns.text:
Q. You said once that thinking about the big ideas of the system can be a way of
stopping identification. I cannot see why this is so and why identification should
necessarily spoil thinking?
turns.speaker: Q.

turns.text:
A. Because identification makes thought narrow and defective, it binds you, you
cannot think, you cannot make deductions. It lowers the standard of man's normal
intellectual capacity. As to why thinking about the big ideas of the system stops
identification, it is because you cannot think about them if you identify with them.
Your thinking will produce no effect. When we are studying, trying to understand,
this means a new way of thinking. The moment we go back to the old way of
thinking, we identify.
turns.speaker: A.

turns.text:
Q. You said formatory thinking always concerns itself with opposites;
but how can we know anything other than by opposites?
turns.speaker: Q.

turns.text:
A. Not always—I said it is one of the characteristics of formatory thinking. And when
we think, we must think about the subject itself, not about its opposite.
turns.speaker: A.

turns.text: Q. But if I am to know about some particular thing, I must know what it is not.
turns.speaker: Q.

turns.text:
A. Not at all. You can know what one or another thing is without making a catalogue
of what it is not. It is quite a wrong self-accusation to say that you have to use such a
clumsy method of thinking, because in that way you would have to think for two
years about every small thing. You can think about things without opposites—just
about what they are. Formatory thinking is not thinking. Never forget that formatory
thinking can serve many useful purposes, but it is not for thinking.
turns.speaker: A.

turns.text:
Q. I feel my chief obstacle is imagination, chiefly about myself. Is there
any special work against this?
turns.speaker: Q.

turns.text:
A. Imagination may be very different. If there are special ways, it is only
possible to arrive at them through a detailed study. If you ask me in
general, I can only answer—self-remembering.
If you mean day-dreams, they are only half of our imaginings, and the most innocent
half. Certainly they mean loss of time, but we waste time in so many ways that a little
more or less does not make much difference. It is much more dangerous if you imagine
certain qualities in yourself in other people, in humanity or in nature, and then come to
believe in these imaginary ideas and put your faith in them. We are surrounded by these
imaginary qualities, and it is with these that we must struggle.
turns.speaker: A.

turns.text: Q. In trying to resist imagination, should one find the cause of it?
turns.speaker: Q.

turns.text:
A. No, stop it at once. There are always causes. Replace it by something else—some
intentional thinking.
turns.speaker: A.

turns.text: Q. Why is it of no value to observe and study imagination as a means to selfknowledge?
turns.speaker: Q.

turns.text:
A. You will very soon see that it does not give anything. Imagination always turns in the
same circle. It is an uncontrolled mind activity, and by imagination we create many false
values, keep to them and use them in our thinking. This is why imagination is
dangerous. We do not verify things. We imagine things either because we like them, or
sometimes because we dislike them and are afraid of them. We live in an imaginary
world.
turns.speaker: A.

turns.text: Q. By escaping from reality?
turns.speaker: Q.

turns.text:
A. Not consciously escaping, but it happens like that. It is partly due to mental laziness:
for instance, it is easier to imagine a thing than to study it.
turns.speaker: A.

turns.text: Q. Wouldn't knowing that be an easy way of stopping it?
turns.speaker: Q.

turns.text:
A. No, you can know it and it will still go on.
A special effort is necessary to stop it. We are so mechanical that we can know and still
do the same thing.
turns.speaker: A.

turns.text:
Q. I feel I cannot wait any longer to try and find a path out of the morass
in which I now find myself. The more I see my mechanicalness, the more I see the
urgency of so doing.
turns.speaker: Q.

turns.text:
A. You must realize that a long time is necessary. Years and years have passed in
ordinary life. When you hear about mechanicalness and are just beginning to struggle
with it, you want results at once. It is necessary first to get accustomed to these ideas.
There are no secrets or special methods to make it quicker.
turns.speaker: A.

turns.text: Q. I find it difficult to realize that imagination enters into all our emotions.
turns.speaker: Q.

turns.text:
A. Every emotion based on identification is imagination. Identification is a sign of
imagination. When you find an emotion without identification, you will find an
emotion without imagination.
turns.speaker: A.

turns.text: Q. Is thought the only way to test imagination?
turns.speaker: Q.

turns.text:
A. No, not thought but attention, because imagination is one of the manifestations that
go without attention. The moment you turn your attention to it, imagination stops.
turns.speaker: A.

turns.text: Q. Do you mean that one cannot observe imagination without stopping it?
turns.speaker: Q.

turns.text:
A. You cannot observe it for long. If you just notice it and turn away, it can go on, but
if you keep attention on it, it stops. Attention acts like a light, and imagination is like a
chemical process that can only go on in the dark and stops with light,
turns.speaker: A.

turns.text: Q. Does it not mean that when you notice it thought comes up?
turns.speaker: Q.

turns.text:
A. Thought brings attention. Attention is a different faculty, because even thought can
go on without attention. But thought can work with attention, while imagination
cannot. Some faculties can work only with attention and some others can work without
attention.
turns.speaker: A.

turns.text:
Q. I cannot say whether something is imagination or not and I do not know how to
begin to recognize it.
turns.speaker: Q.

turns.text:
A. Nobody can help you to begin, you must begin yourself. You must catch yourself in
some kind of imagination—I do not mean exactly daydreaming. You must have some
standard of imagination: then, when in doubt, you can compare. Imagination can take
three forms; passive imagination, imagination expressing itself in talk, and
imagination expressing itself in activity. There are lines and lines of our activity, each
quite different from another. Some start with effort and go on with effort. Others may
be imagination. One may think it is effort when in reality it is imagination expressing
itself in activity which cannot stop and needs no effort. Talking is the same: some
people must talk, others must do something, but both are manifestations of the same
thing.
turns.speaker: A.

turns.text:
Q. I notice that imagining seems to take place in memory, going from one association
to another. Is this a correct observation?
turns.speaker: Q.

turns.text:
A. No. Memory by itself is not responsible for anything. Memory is impartial; it
supplies material for whatever you want. You may want it for serious thinking,
imagination, expression of negative emotions and so on.
turns.speaker: A.

turns.text: Q. Is memory mechanical?
turns.speaker: Q.

turns.text:
