A. Memory itself is mechanical, but the use of memory, the application of memory, the
functioning of memory can be more mechanical or less mechanical. Memory is
inscriptions on the rolls of our centres. How to use them, how to find them, how to
verify them—that is another thing.
turns.speaker: A.

turns.text:
Q. Should it matter much whether one knows the cause of any negative moods one
observes: is it enough just to recognize that it is negative?
turns.speaker: Q.

turns.text:
A. No. Sometimes it is very useful to know the cause, because when you want to fight
with it, you cannot fight unless you know the cause, and the cause is generally in your
own imagination. All the causes are in you, so it is necessary to know them.
turns.speaker: A.

turns.text:
Q. Sometimes when one is unhappy or perhaps feeling negative one is brought back to
real issues. Since we have been told to guard against negative emotion, I cannot quite
fit that in with the system.
turns.speaker: Q.

turns.text:
A. You mix the idea of suffering and the idea of negative emotion. It is not the same.
Suffering is very useful; you can get many things only through suffering. But when
suffering is connected with identification and imagination, it becomes negative
emotion.
turns.speaker: A.

turns.text:
Q. You say that man must give up suffering and also that he must suffer in order to
develop. How can both things be true?
turns.speaker: Q.

turns.text:
A. Different cases, different days, different moments. These are not two contradictory
principles. There is much unnecessary suffering which one does not want to give up.
Then there is some inevitable and necessary suffering which one must accept if one
wants to get something.
turns.speaker: A.

turns.text: Q. Do you mean that one is not guided by the external similarity of facts?
turns.speaker: Q.

turns.text:
A. This is one aspect. If you meet with it, you will know what is psychological method
and what is not.
turns.speaker: A.

turns.text: Q. Is the psychological method the use of the intellectual part of the intellectual centre?
turns.speaker: Q.

turns.text:
A. No, not quite. The more centres and the more parts of centres you use, the better the
psychological method. It means using all the powers you have. Logical method means
the use of only the mechanical part of intellectual centre.
turns.speaker: A.

turns.text: Q. And is the esoteric method the use of higher centres?
turns.speaker: Q.

turns.text:
A. No, it is the use of the system. You cannot use higher centres, but you can use the
system.
turns.speaker: A.

turns.text: Q. Is psychological thinking only possible when all our functions are working rightly?
turns.speaker: Q.

turns.text:
A. We must start as we are. We cannot wait till we change, because if we do we will
never change; and if we change mechanically, we change only for the worse.
turns.speaker: A.

turns.text:
Q. What are the first things to learn in trying to think psychologically? I feel it is more
than I can accomplish.
turns.speaker: Q.

turns.text:
A. When you say it is more than you can accomplish you think about the completed
process. And I speak about the process itself, about beginning to work. If you say this
is beyond you, you can do nothing and so, naturally, nothing happens. It is again this
habit of thinking in absolutes.
turns.speaker: A.

turns.text: Q. What are the essential features of esotericism?
turns.speaker: Q.

turns.text:
A. It is difficult to speak about essential features, because it depends on how you take
this word. The word 'esoteric' means inner. Esotericism includes in itself the idea of the
existence of an inner circle of humanity. You remember how humanity was described
as consisting of four circles —esoteric, mesoteric and exoteric, which constitute the
inner circle, and the outer circle in which we live. The idea of esotericism implies
transmission of knowledge; it presumes the existence of a group of people to whom a
certain knowledge belongs. This must not be understood in some mystical way, but
more definitely, concretely. There are a great many differences between the inner and
the outer circles. For instance, many things we want to find or create can exist only in
the inner circle, such things as positive emotions, understanding between people,
certain kinds of knowledge; all this belongs to the inner circle. I think this is sufficient
for understanding the idea of the inner or esoteric circle.
turns.speaker: A.

turns.text:
Q. I understand that the primary feature of esoteric knowledge is that it is hidden and
one would not be likely to find it. So how can we recognize esoteric knowledge or an
esoteric school?
turns.speaker: Q.

turns.text:
A. We are studying a system which is supposed to be esoteric, so with its help we will
be able to recognize it. And although esoteric knowledge is hidden from ordinary life,
it can be found. It is not hidden absolutely,
so that nobody can find it, otherwise it would have no meaning. This would be
contrary to its aims and would spoil the results of its existence. The only meaning of
hidden knowledge is that it can be found; the important thing is how to recognize it.
With the help of these ideas, comparing what can be found in the ordinary intellectual
way and what cannot and then comparing it with the system, we shall be able to
establish with a certain degree of probability the level of the knowledge we meet with.
turns.speaker: A.

turns.text: Is an effort to self-remember practical?
turns.speaker: Q.

turns.text: A. It may be practical, it may be theoretical and it may be philosophical.
turns.speaker: A.

turns.text: Q. Objective consciousness seems to belong to the philosophical scale?
turns.speaker: Q.

turns.text:
A. Quite the reverse: it is very practical. But if you mean for us, then,
certainly, objective consciousness is a philosophical idea. At the same
time the study of descriptions of glimpses of this state is possible. If one
studies these descriptions and tries to find similarities, it can become
theoretical
turns.speaker: A.

turns.text:
Q When I first came to lectures I thought the word 'school' meant a school of thought,
but now it seems to be just like the school I was in when I was a boy.
turns.speaker: Q.

turns.text: A. Exactly. It is not a question of thought, it is a question of doing
turns.speaker: A.

turns.text: Q. Isn't it in a way a school of thought too, since doing must come from thinking?
turns.speaker: Q.

turns.text:
A Certainly there must be a certain amount of thinking, for without thinking we can do
nothing, but thinking is only an auxiliary process, it is not the aim In a school of
thought it is sufficient to think about freedom, whereas we want to be free, we are not
satisfied with merely thinking about it.
turns.speaker: A.

turns.text: Q Would this school be of all three kinds or only one?
turns.speaker: Q.

turns.text:
A. I think it is better to say all three It has three sides Also, some people take the
system philosophically, others theoretically and yet others practically You must not
forget that the same thing can be taken in different ways
turns.speaker: A.

turns.text: Q Is, then, this system connected with philosophy?
turns.speaker: Q.

turns.text:
A. It cannot be quite free from it In some ways it is a legitimate form of thinking. But
in thinking of man's development, of man's progress, it is better to look for
psychological landmarks and not for philosophical ones.
turns.speaker: A.

turns.text: Q. Who assesses psychological values?
turns.speaker: Q.

turns.text:
A. There are definite objective signs by which one can judge—definite inner standards.
At a certain point they may become objective. As I said, we do not look for
philosophical landmarks, we want psychological landmarks. It is very important to
understand this. Philosophical conclusions may be just words, rhetoric, but about
psychological landmarks there can be no mistake—for oneself.
turns.speaker: A.

turns.text: Q. Is it lazy to use philosophical thinking?
turns.speaker: Q.

turns.text:
A. Not necessarily. Sometimes there are things you can take only philosophically,
others only philosophically and theoretically. There are things to which we have no
practical approach and for which we must find analogies. So sometimes it is quite
right. But there are things which you can take only practically, for only then can you
value them.
turns.speaker: A.

turns.text:
Q. You spoke of 'thinking in new categories'. This seems to me as impossible as being
able to 'do'.
turns.speaker: Q.

turns.text:
A. Quite right. At the same time, when you begin to understand different categories,
you will be able to think, at least sometimes, in a different way. But this is not the
whole description of right thinking. Very often you do not think in right categories
because you do
turns.speaker: A.

turns.text: Q. Can you give an example of what it means that it is taught in fragments?
turns.speaker: Q.

turns.text:
A. Many things are taught like that: all about building up energies, the psychological
side, the explanation of how the machine works, the side concerning the world and so
on. It is very important to understand this. Only when you begin to understand how the
scale changes will you be able to understand the system. As I said, it is taught in
fragments each of which is on a different scale. You have to put them together and at
the same time correct the scale. It is like several geographical maps, each on a different
scale, cut into pieces. You have to see which piece fits which, where the scale is very
different and where it is less different. This is the only way to study this system.
turns.speaker: A.

turns.text: Q. Do you mean we cannot talk about the worlds unless we reduce them to our scale?
turns.speaker: Q.

turns.text:
A. No, what I meant is quite different. Of course, we reduce everything, but what I
meant is that we have to study things on different scales and we must remember this
and realize the relationship of different scales and the fact that things change with
change of scale. Also we must bear in mind that, about many things, we believe that
they mean something, when actually they mean nothing at all. The system teaches us to
find the difference between realities and imaginary quantities (and even worse than
imaginary).
turns.speaker: A.

turns.text: Q. I feel we have only half the knowledge of the system we could have.
turns.speaker: Q.

turns.text:
A. Much less than half. Such as we are, we can only get fragments but sufficiently big
to build something out of them. We must try to understand the structure. When you
have all the fragments before you, you may see certain connections, and when you find
these connections you may see many other things.
turns.speaker: A.

turns.text: Q. Have you altered the teaching much?
turns.speaker: Q.

turns.text:
A. I have not altered it. But I prefer sometimes to start from a different point. In this
system, as in any organic system, one can start from any point—this is not an
alteration. Everything else remains the same, but I prefer to start with the
psychological side.
turns.speaker: A.

turns.text: Q. Have the people in the inner circle any control over people in the outer circle?
turns.speaker: Q.

turns.text:
A. Yes, but with many reservations. The conscious circle cannot act directly, but only
through B influences. Influences C can appear only if influences B are accepted and if
people look for them. Men in the inner circle cannot have control over people who do
not wish to know them. They cannot use violence, because it would mean a wrong
triad, a wrong activity. For every kind of result there is a special triad. For instance, if
people wish to acquire control, they can achieve it only in one way. If they act in
another way they will get the opposite result. Wars, revolutions and so on never give
the desired results, but always the opposite results, because wrong triads are used. If
people of the inner circles wish to influence other people, they can produce good
results only if there is understanding, and only with people who wish it. This is a
useful question. Try to think about it.
turns.speaker: A.

turns.text:
Q. You spoke of the insecure times we live in. Will the school take precautions to
protect itself? I understood you to say that a school is not under the law of accident.
turns.speaker: Q.

turns.text:
A. I meant that a school cannot be formed by accident, but it can be destroyed by
accident. It cannot be formed mechanically, but it can be destroyed mechanically.
Take some work of art—it will not be created purely mechanically, it will be made by
some special triad—but it can be burnt like anything else.
turns.speaker: A.

turns.text: Q. If schools are real living things, why do they die?
turns.speaker: Q.

turns.text:
A. What do you mean by saying that schools are living things? It is vague and
indefinite. But if we take it literally it will make it quite clear why schools die. All
living beings die sooner or later. If people die, schools must also
turns.speaker: A.

turns.text:
Q. Should not the present state of the world make more people look for schools?
People are frightened, they feel uncomfortable.
turns.speaker: Q.

turns.text:
A. Why should one discomfort lead to another discomfort? Do you think that will
make them come? You expect too much of them. You can say to a man that if he
studies the system he will be more awake, but you cannot say he will be better off.
turns.speaker: A.

turns.text: Q. They will get rid of identification.
turns.speaker: Q.

turns.text:
A. And they will say that they cannot work without identification, and if they are not
identified, they will lose all their money. There is no connection between interest in the
system and the discomfort of the present situation.
turns.speaker: A.

turns.text:
Q. I have been very puzzled by my observation of young people. If they are happy and
thoroughly normal, the idea of esotericism does not seem to appeal to them.
turns.speaker: Q.

turns.text:
A. The idea of esotericism is very difficult. Sometimes one can catch its meaning at an
early age, but often one fails to see it from the right angle. We have so many wrong
attitudes and wrong ideas that nothing can be expected. I think a person who becomes
seriously interested in these ideas is an exception, because people's minds are in such a
confusion with absurd and contradictory ideas.
turns.speaker: A.

turns.text: Q. I am only interested in the psychological side of the system, but not in esotericism.
turns.speaker: Q.

turns.text:
A. But the psychological side is also esoteric. The system gives you nothing that is not
esoteric, for the whole of it comes from minds that are not ordinary minds; it comes
from people who understood things. Ordinary systems cannot bring about any change.
The psychological side of the system is even more esoteric than the other side, or it
would have no value. It has value only because it comes from higher minds, from their
understanding and their ideas. This must be understood. We got this system somehow.
If we suppose it has been created by men on the same level as we are, or that it is a
theory, it has no value at all. But it is not a theory; it
turns.speaker: A.

turns.text:
Q. I should like to understand more about this division. I do not know
what is practical.
turns.speaker: Q.

turns.text:
A. It means what you can do—in all senses. Only, 'doing' can be on one
scale or another scale Doing is always more important than thinking or
talking. So if we take it that philosophical is thinking, theoretical talking
and practical doing, the practical is more important
turns.speaker: A.

turns.text: Q What is philosophical thinking?
turns.speaker: Q.

turns.text:
A. Thinking on a very large scale.
A thing may look very beautiful on
the philosophical scale, the same thing taken on the theoretical scale may
be a very narrow and stupid theory and, taken practically, it may be a
crime
turns.speaker: A.

turns.text:
I cannot separate the idea of not being able to 'do' from fatalism
When and how have we the power of choice and how do we differ from
animals?
turns.speaker: Questioner

turns.text:
In the present state we differ very little. Our power of choice begins
only when we begin to realize our situation, our mechanicalness, and
when we begin to struggle for something else There are possibilities for
that But this is a formatory way of thinking—either determinism or
freedom Some things are determined, some less determined, some are in
our power, if we know how to change them or how to turn them Only,
we must know.
turns.speaker: Teacher

turns.text: I thought perhaps we ought not to take this idea that we cannot 'do’ too literally?
turns.speaker: Questioner

turns.text:
No, quite literally. Only this refers to people who are not connected with any
teaching. When one begins to study certain teachings or systems which give school
methods, one has to try to do certain things. In the work we have to 'do', for if we do
not try to 'do', nothing will happen. We have to 'do' from the very beginning—not
much, but very definite things. If you can not identify it is already the beginning of
'doing'.
turns.speaker: Teacher

turns.text:
If I wish to obtain a particular result and fail, and if I then do the thing differently,
will the result be still the same in spite of my effort?
turns.speaker: Questioner

turns.text:
You must not deceive yourself. If you do something and the result corresponds to
your expectations, it is simply luck, chance—that is all. And in some cases you may
do something entirely different and still have the same result.
turns.speaker: Teacher

turns.text: It seems that one is caught up in a vicious circle!
turns.speaker: Questioner

turns.text:
Certainly one is caught, and the system is the way out of this vicious circle, for in
ordinary conditions of life one cannot get out.
turns.speaker: Teacher

turns.text:
We are told to keep rules. This presupposes we can keep them,
which
would be 'doing’. It seems to me incompatible with the idea that we cannot
'do'.
turns.speaker: Questioner

turns.text:
Everything is relative. We can 'do' some inner actions, for we have
a certain control. For instance, we have a certain control of our thoughts:
we can think about one thing or another. This is the beginning of the possibility. If we
continue to keep our interests directed in a certain line, our thinking process acquires a
certain power and, after some time, it can create at least moments of self-awareness
which, when it comes more often and stays longer, can begin to change other things.
turns.speaker: Teacher

turns.text:
Are the distinctions between men 1, 2, 3 and 4 definite, or, like tramps, lunatics,
householders, are we a bit of each?
turns.speaker: Questioner

turns.text:
You know, you absolutely spoil ideas for yourself when you take them like this and
mix them up. These ideas are very important. First you must take one, quite separately,
and try to understand it. Then take another and try to understand that one. The division
of men Nos. 1, 2, 3 and so on is one thing and it was not given parallel to anything
else. You must study it as it is—what is meant by man No. 1, by man No. 2, by man
No. 3, what are the various combinations of these, how they are mixed and so on.
Then take this second idea... You cannot take them all together and talk about them in one breath.
turns.speaker: Teacher

turns.text: Is such a state realisable?
turns.speaker: Questioner

turns.text: I would not talk about it, if it were not. Why should I engage in fancies?
turns.speaker: Maharaj

turns.text: Everybody quotes scriptures.
turns.speaker: Questioner

turns.text: Those who know only scriptures know nothing. To know is to be. I know what I am talking about; it is not from reading, or hearsay.
turns.speaker: Maharaj

turns.text: I am studying Sanskrit under a professor, but really I am only reading scriptures. I am in search of self-realisation and I came to get the needed guidance. Kindly tell me what am I to do?
turns.speaker: Questioner

turns.text: Since you have read the scriptures, why do you ask me?
turns.speaker: Maharaj

turns.text: The scriptures show the general directions but the individual needs personal instructions.
turns.speaker: Questioner

turns.text: Your own self is your ultimate teacher (sadguru). The outer teacher (Guru) is merely a milestone. It is only your inner teacher that will walk with you to the goal, for he is the goal.
turns.speaker: Maharaj

turns.text: The inner teacher is not easily reached.
turns.speaker: Questioner

turns.text: Since he is in you and with you, the difficulty cannot be serious. Look within, and you will find him.
turns.speaker: Maharaj

turns.text: When I look within, I find sensations and perceptions, thoughts and feelings, desires and fears, memories and expectations. I am immersed in this cloud and see nothing else.
turns.speaker: Questioner

turns.text: That which sees all this, and the nothing too, is the inner teacher. He alone is, all else only appears to be. He is your own self (swarupa), your hope and assurance of freedom; find him and cling to him and you will be saved and safe.
turns.speaker: Maharaj

turns.text: I do believe you, but when it comes to the actual finding of this inner self, I find it escapes me.
turns.speaker: Questioner

turns.text: The idea 'it escapes me', where does it arise?
turns.speaker: Maharaj

turns.text: In the mind.
turns.speaker: Questioner

turns.text: And who knows the mind?
turns.speaker: Maharaj

turns.text: The witness of the mind knows the mind.
turns.speaker: Questioner

turns.text: Did anybody come to you and say: 'I am the witness of your mind'?
turns.speaker: Maharaj

turns.text: Of course not. He would have been just another idea in the mind.
turns.speaker: Questioner

turns.text: Then who is the witness?
turns.speaker: Maharaj

turns.text: I am.
turns.speaker: Questioner

turns.text: So, you know the witness because you are the witness. You need not see the witness in front of you. Here again, to be is to know.
turns.speaker: Maharaj

turns.text: Yes, I see that I am the witness, the awareness itself. But in which way does it profit me?
turns.speaker: Questioner

turns.text: What a question! What kind of profit do you expect? To know what you are, is it not good enough?
turns.speaker: Maharaj

turns.text: What are the uses of self-knowledge?
turns.speaker: Questioner

turns.text: It helps you to understand what you are not and keeps you free from false ideas, desires and actions.
turns.speaker: Maharaj

turns.text: If I am the witness only, what do right and wrong matter?
turns.speaker: Questioner

turns.text: What helps you to know yourself is right. What prevents, is wrong. To know one's real self is bliss, to forget is sorrow.
turns.speaker: Maharaj

turns.text: Is the witness-consciousness the real Self?
turns.speaker: Questioner

turns.text: It is the reflection of the real in the mind (buddhi). The real is beyond. The witness is the door through which you pass beyond.
turns.speaker: Maharaj

turns.text: What is the purpose of meditation?
turns.speaker: Questioner

turns.text: Seeing the false as the false, is meditation. This must go on all the time.
turns.speaker: Maharaj

turns.text: We are told to meditate regularly.
turns.speaker: Questioner

turns.text: Deliberate daily exercise in discrimination between the true and the false and renunciation of the false is meditation. There are many kinds of meditation to begin with, but they all merge finally into one.
turns.speaker: Maharaj

turns.text: Please tell me which road to self-realisation is the shortest.
turns.speaker: Questioner

turns.text: No way is short or long, but some people are more in earnest and some are less. I can tell you about myself. I was a simple man, but I trusted my Guru. What he told me to do, I did. He told me to concentrate on 'I am' — I did. He told me that I am beyond all perceivables and conceivables — I believed. I gave him my heart and soul, my entire attention and the whole of my spare time. As a result of faith and earnest application, I realised my self (swarupa) within three years.
turns.speaker: Maharaj

turns.text: Life is so intelligent. How can it be unconscious?
turns.speaker: Questioner

turns.text: You talk of the unconscious when there is a lapse in memory. In reality there is only consciousness. All life is conscious, all consciousness — alive.
turns.speaker: Maharaj

turns.text: Even stones?
turns.speaker: Questioner

turns.text: Even stones are conscious and alive.
turns.speaker: Maharaj

turns.text: The worry with me is that I am prone to denying existence to what I cannot imagine.
turns.speaker: Questioner

turns.text: You would be wiser to deny the existence of what you imagine. It is the imagined that is unreal.
turns.speaker: Maharaj

turns.text: Is all imaginable unreal?
turns.speaker: Questioner

turns.text: Imagination based on memories is unreal. The future is not entirely unreal.
turns.speaker: Maharaj

turns.text: Which part of the future is real and which is not?
turns.speaker: Questioner

turns.text: The unexpected and unpredictable is real.
turns.speaker: Maharaj

turns.text: Are there not good desires and bad, high desires and low?
turns.speaker: Questioner

turns.text: All desires are bad, but some are worse than others. Pursue any desire, it will always give you trouble.
turns.speaker: Maharaj

turns.text: Even the desire to be free of desire?
turns.speaker: Questioner

turns.text: Why desire at all? Desiring a state of freedom from desire will not set you free. Nothing can set you free, because you are free. See yourself with desireless clarity, that is all.
turns.speaker: Maharaj

turns.text: It takes time to know oneself.
turns.speaker: Questioner

turns.text: How can time help you? Time is a succession of moments; each moment appears out of nothing and disappears into nothing, never to reappear. How can you build on something so fleeting?
turns.speaker: Maharaj

turns.text: What is permanent?
turns.speaker: Questioner

turns.text: Look to yourself for the permanent. Dive deep within and find what is real in you.
turns.speaker: Maharaj

turns.text: How to look for myself?
turns.speaker: Questioner

turns.text: Whatever happens, it happens to you. What you do, the doer is in you. Find the subject of all that you are as a person.
turns.speaker: Maharaj

turns.text: What else can I be?
turns.speaker: Questioner

turns.text: Find out. Even if I tell you that you are the witness, the silent watcher, it will mean nothing to you, unless you find the way to your own being.
turns.speaker: Maharaj

turns.text: My question is: How to find the way to one's own being?
turns.speaker: Questioner

turns.text: Give up all questions except one: 'Who am I?' After all, the only fact you are sure of is that you are. The 'I am' is certain. The 'I am this' is not. Struggle to find out what you are in reality.
turns.speaker: Maharaj

turns.text: I am doing nothing else for the last 60 years.
turns.speaker: Questioner

turns.text: What is wrong with striving? Why look for results? Striving itself is your real nature.
turns.speaker: Maharaj

turns.text: Striving is painful.
turns.speaker: Questioner

turns.text: You make it so by seeking results. Strive without seeking, struggle without greed.
turns.speaker: Maharaj

turns.text: Why has God made me as I am?
turns.speaker: Questioner

turns.text: Which God are you talking about? What is God? Is he not the very light by which you ask the question?
turns.speaker: Maharaj

turns.text: What is God then?
turns.speaker: Questioner

turns.text: 'I am' itself is God. The seeking itself is God. In seeking you discover that you are neither the body nor mind, and the love of the self in you is for the self in all. The two are one.
turns.speaker: Maharaj

turns.text: How am I to find that love?
turns.speaker: Questioner

turns.text: What do you love now? The 'I am'. Give your heart and mind to it, think of nothing else. This, when effortless and natural, is the highest state. In it love itself is the lover and the beloved.
turns.speaker: Maharaj

turns.text: Everybody wants to live, to exist. Is it not self-love?
turns.speaker: Questioner

turns.text: All desire has its source in the self. It is all a matter of choosing the right desire.
turns.speaker: Maharaj

turns.text: What is right and what is wrong varies with habit and custom. Standards vary with societies.
turns.speaker: Questioner

turns.text: Discard all traditional standards. Leave them to the hypocrites. Only what liberates you from desire and fear and wrong ideas is good.
turns.speaker: Maharaj

turns.text: Then how am I to judge my desires?
turns.speaker: Questioner

turns.text: See whether they bind you or free you. What turns you to yourself is right; what turns you away from yourself is wrong.
turns.speaker: Maharaj

turns.text: You said no will was possible for us?
turns.speaker: Questioner

turns.text:
Will is a relative term: there are different wills on different levels. A mechanical man who never thinks of development has only a multitude of small
wills that are quite mechanical. He has a certain desire: one side of him wants to do
something and another side is afraid he will be punished if he does it. A struggle ensues between the different tendencies and the result of this struggle we
call 'will'.
turns.speaker: Teacher

turns.text: Then in order to develop will one must go against desires?
turns.speaker: Questioner

turns.text:
First of all you must become one. You are many and you have hundreds of 'I's and
hundreds of wills. If you want to develop an independent will you must become one
and conscious. Will depends on unity and consciousness.
turns.speaker: Teacher

turns.text:
If we are determined to do something we do not like, and manage to do it, are we
not using will?
turns.speaker: Questioner

turns.text:
It may be fear; perhaps you are afraid not to do it, or you may expect some reward
either in this life or the next—many things are possible. Generally we are either afraid
of something, or expect some kind of benefit from it. As a rule the term 'will' is used in
a relative sense, but when we speak of will, we speak of a certain level. Before we can
speak of the possibility of will we must at least have a central point which can control
the rest.
turns.speaker: Teacher

turns.text: What is a super-effort?
turns.speaker: Questioner

turns.text:
A super-effort can have many characteristics, but generally it is doing not what you
think best, but what you are advised to do. From our own intentions we are ready to do
many things, but we are not ready to do or not to do what we are told.
turns.speaker: Teacher

turns.text: In what way does super-effort differ from an ordinary effort?
turns.speaker: Questioner

turns.text:
It differs in degree, but not only in degree. Super-effort is effort made consciously,
as much as we can, for a definite purpose which is not
required by any external circumstances. We never really make serious efforts; it is all
pretence, for we do not know what it means to make efforts. In exceptional conditions,
when we are obliged to make efforts, we make them, but not super-efforts. Besides,
ordinary efforts one makes in life are necessary, useful.
A super-effort may look useless for its purpose.
turns.speaker: Teacher

turns.text:
I feel I am getting into a vicious circle. The more efforts I make, the more I see I
cannot 'do'.
turns.speaker: Questioner

turns.text:
Then make more efforts and realize it constantly;
make it more permanent. You will
see that you are not always in the same state. People in ordinary life cannot 'do', but for
you it is different—all the time you must try to do. You are always identified and you
must not identify, you must watch your talk, you are constantly negative and you must
struggle against negative emotions, you must remember yourself. All this is doing. You
must observe these things and try to change them.
turns.speaker: Teacher

turns.text:
I find it almost impossible not to utilize the knowledge so far gained to assist one's
friends.
turns.speaker: Questioner

turns.text:
It cannot be utilized yet, because if you try to do something with the amount of
knowledge you have, you will distort it. It is necessary to have more, because only
then will you be able to judge whether you can do something with it in a given case or
not... For us many things are facts, or at least should
be facts. If you tell them to people who have not gone slowly through this study, for
them it will be something like faith. They will either believe or not believe... So why should we produce more disbelievers?
turns.speaker: Teacher

turns.text:
It is difficult to discuss something with anyone without it being coloured by what
we have heard here.
turns.speaker: Questioner

turns.text:
Until it becomes easy you cannot begin to do anything; everything will be
transformed into talk and will remain talk. Only when you are able to keep silent, keep
something to yourself, only then can you accumulate more knowledge or material. If
you make a hole in a balloon, the contents of the balloon will escape. If you make a
hole in yourself, something will also escape. Rules are difficult to keep, because by
remembering rules and obeying rules you accumulate conscious energy.
turns.speaker: Teacher

turns.text:
I am puzzled by the question of expressing emotions: if it is beyond ordinary
human experience to feel positive emotion, and we are told not to express negative
emotions, is it meant that we are not to express any emotion whatsoever?
turns.speaker: Questioner

turns.text:
No, it is necessary to navigate between the two. We must be as emotional as
possible, for we miss many perceptions... because at the moment
we are not emotional. We have no positive
emotions, but we can say that we have negative emotions and pleasant and unpleasant
emotions that are not negative.
turns.speaker: Teacher

turns.text: Positive means not negative?
turns.speaker: Questioner

turns.text:
Yes, and much more besides... To have positive emotions is advised and
recommended in religions, but they do not say how to get them. They say, 'Have faith,
have love'. How? Christ says, 'Love your enemies'. It is not for us;
we cannot even
love our friends. It is the same as saying to a blind man, 'You must see!' A blind man cannot see, otherwise he would not be a blind man. That is what positive
emotion means.
turns.speaker: Teacher

turns.text: How can we learn to love our enemies?
turns.speaker: Questioner

turns.text:
Learn to love yourself first—you do not love yourself enough; you love your false
personality, not yourself.
turns.speaker: Teacher

turns.text:
You said once that it is necessary to be serious in relation to the work. What does
being serious mean?
turns.speaker: Questioner

turns.text:
First it is necessary to divide two things: being serious and taking things seriously.
In thinking about this, people usually think about how to take things seriously, and
which things, but never about what it means to be serious. I will tell you what it
means. To be serious means to take nothing seriously—with the exception of things
about which you know for certain that they are important in relation to what you want. This looks too small, but when you apply it in practice you will see that it is the only
solution and the most necessary thing.
turns.speaker: Teacher

turns.text:
You said that certain negative emotions make serious work impossible. Does that
mean they must be absolutely exterminated before one begins, and what do you mean
by serious work?
turns.speaker: Questioner

turns.text:
By serious work I mean not only study but change. First you must study certain
things, then you work to change them... With certain negative emotions serious work is practically impossible, because they
will spoil all results: one side of you will work and another will spoil it. So if you start
this work without conquering certain negative emotions, after some time you may find
yourself in a worse state than before.
turns.speaker: Teacher

turns.text: What is the purpose of struggling against self-will?
turns.speaker: Questioner

turns.text:
You remember how we started. The aim was to create a centre of gravity, create
moon in ourselves. We cannot do it through self-will. Creating moon in ourselves is connected with the idea of sacrificing suffering.
turns.speaker: Teacher

turns.text: When we begin to sacrifice suffering we begin to create moon in ourselves.
turns.speaker: Questioner

turns.text:
We
always want to keep our suffering, yet moon can only be created from our suffering. Only we must remember that giving up suffering is one action and creating moon is
the result of a continuous series of actions.
turns.speaker: Teacher

turns.text: You said that the second line is work with people. I find it easier to work alone.
turns.speaker: Questioner

turns.text:
Everybody finds that. Certainly it would be much better if you could sit here alone
and talk to me, without any other people, and particularly 'these' people, because these
people are especially unpleasant. We all think that. I thought that when I began to
study. It is one of the most mechanical things in the world.
turns.speaker: Teacher

turns.text: But is there a tie between me and other people here?
turns.speaker: Questioner

turns.text:
There must be a tie, but the tie is produced by work... The whole work, the whole
system is arranged in such a way that you cannot get anything from the first line if you
do not work on the second and third lines. In the first line you can get certain ideas,
certain information, but after a while you come to a stop if you do not work on the
other two lines.
turns.speaker: Teacher

turns.text: And one has to pay in advance—there is no credit.
turns.speaker: Teacher

turns.text:
There is no check on the price? You cannot find out whether it is
too high?
turns.speaker: Questioner

turns.text: Some people think it is too high, refuse to pay and get nothing.
turns.speaker: Teacher

turns.text: I do not understand about paying in advance. How is it done?
turns.speaker: Questioner

turns.text:
The only way is to pay in advance, but how to do it is another thing—
all that we study here is how to pay in advance... Payment is a most important principle in the work, and it must be understood.
Without payment you cannot get anything. But as a rule we want to get something for
nothing, and that is why we have nothing. If we really decided to go for this kind of
knowledge—or even for quite a small thing—and we went for it regardless of
everything else, we would get it... We will pay for anything else, but for this we are not
prepared to pay anything, and so, as a result, we get nothing.
turns.speaker: Teacher

turns.text:
Is one of the features of a lunatic that he wants certain things out of proportion to
other things, in such a way that it will be bad for him as A whole?
turns.speaker: Questioner

turns.text:
'Lunatic' means a man who always runs after false values, who has no right
discrimination. He is always formatory... lunatics are particularly devoted to formatory thinking: that is their chief affection in
one way or another.
turns.speaker: Teacher

turns.text:
Is the tramp side in oneself a sort of irresponsibility that is prepared to throw
everything overboard?
turns.speaker: Questioner

turns.text:
Quite right. Sometimes it can take very poetical forms: 'There are no values in the
world'—'Nothing is worth anything'—'Everything is relative'—those are favourite
phrases. But actually the tramp is not so dangerous. The lunatic is more dangerous,
since it means false values and formatory thinking.
turns.speaker: Teacher

turns.text:
It seems paradoxical that we are trying to get free from laws and are putting
ourselves under more.
turns.speaker: Questioner

turns.text:
In order to get free it is necessary to submit to many more laws for a certain time,
for one can learn to be free only by obeying more laws. There are many reasons for
this. One reason is that we are too lenient with ourselves; if we set ourselves a task,
after some time we begin to make excuses. And then we deceive ourselves too much. So, as I said, if people want to continue to study, they must accept certain
conditions.
turns.speaker: Teacher

turns.text:
You spoke about the possibility of a wrong separation. What did you
mean by that?
turns.speaker: Questioner

turns.text:
Suppose I call everything I like 'I' and everything I dislike
'Ouspensky', it would be a wrong separation. The 'I' from which I
observe is a point, it has no material existence yet, it is only the embryo
from which 'I' can grow It I give it material existence, it would be wrong.
turns.speaker: Teacher

turns.text: Should not some weight be given to it?
turns.speaker: Questioner

turns.text:
Yes, but only in relation to the work Who remembers the aim, who wants to work
is 'I', the rest is 'Ouspensky'.
turns.speaker: Teacher

turns.text: Then one cannot get much from books?
turns.speaker: Questioner

turns.text:
One can get some ideas, but a person will get one thing and miss ten other things. As a matter of fact, there are books in which very deep secrets are written, but people
can read them and never get these secrets. It is quite safe. Again, this is connected
with the fundamental idea that understanding depends not only on knowledge but also
on being.
turns.speaker: Teacher

turns.text:
That is why one needs a school. In school you cannot deceive yourself, and
in school it can be explained to you why you cannot understand. It means there is
something in you that you have to conquer in order to understand more.
turns.speaker: Teacher

turns.text:
For instance, you are talking to somebody, trying to persuade this person that you
are right about something and he is wrong. The more you argue, the more he is
convinced that he is right. Stop, and you may suddenly see that this person
understands you... Or you may even pretend to agree with him and in that way
make him understand what you want.
turns.speaker: Teacher

turns.text:
I suppose in a case like that we should be capable of knowing whether to argue or
agree?
turns.speaker: Questioner

turns.text:
If you do not identify you will see. Arguing is one way to persuade, agreeing is
another. Generally what prevents us from seeing what method to use is identifying.
turns.speaker: Teacher

turns.text: I have often tried to think what I want, but I only find a muddle of many things.
turns.speaker: Questioner

turns.text:
That's it. I want you to realize how difficult it is to define what one wants. Suppose
you are given full choice to have what you want: you will not know what to say. But it
is important that you should understand and know it; you must be able to formulate it.
turns.speaker: Teacher

turns.text: Is everything mechanical evil?
turns.speaker: Questioner

turns.text:
It does not necessarily mean that all that is mechanical is evil;
but evil cannot be
conscious, it can only be mechanical. You must ask yourself:
Can evil be conscious in we?
Everything else is philosophy... In exactly the same way you cannot be negative consciously, without
identification.
Negative emotions are the best conductors of evil, because they are one
of the most mechanical things we have.
turns.speaker: Teacher

turns.text:
You said that conscience is feeling all our emotions at the same time. I cannot
quite see how we can feel them all together.
turns.speaker: Questioner

turns.text:
No, I never said that. I said that in a moment of conscience, whether you wish it or
not, you will feel all your emotions on the same subject at once. But it is not a
definition of conscience. Conscience can be defined as an emotional feeling of truth
on a given subject.
turns.speaker: Teacher

turns.text: Is saying to oneself, 'I will do it to-morrow' a buffer?
turns.speaker: Questioner

turns.text: It is not a buffer, but a very good method of keeping the buffers going well.
turns.speaker: Teacher

turns.text:
In considering likes and dislikes, how can one separate what is real
and what is false personality?
turns.speaker: Questioner

turns.text:
Start by realizing that it is all false personality, and then try to find out
what is not. You cannot do the second before the first. First you must
understand that all is false personality, and when you become convinced
of that, you may find what is 'yourself'. Go on observing. Work begins
from the moment one realizes that one is not.
turns.speaker: Teacher

turns.text: Why does the soul at death go to the moon?
turns.speaker: Questioner

turns.text: The moon is hungry.
turns.speaker: Teacher

turns.text: Is not the earth hungry too?
turns.speaker: Questioner

turns.text:
The whole surface of the earth, its composition and structure, depend on organic
life. The earth receives the body, for that is what it wants... The moon wants one thing, the earth another... Certain matters pass to the moon in that way which otherwise would not
be able to reach it. And they come in an already digested form.
turns.speaker: Teacher

turns.text: Nature seems to be very unjust and very cruel to man.
turns.speaker: Questioner

turns.text:
What do you call nature? An earthquake is also nature... Evidently it was created like it is because there
was no other means. If we do not like it, we can study methods of how to run away... All life from beginning to end is an injustice.
For instance, we have to die—it is most unjust. We divide things into just and unjust,
and what right have we? All organic life is based on injustice;
it is a self-supporting
farm to breed cats and rats. Cats eat rats and rats eat cats. What is justice among cats
and rats? This is life. It is nothing very beautiful. Our aim is to get out;
it is not our
business to feel indignation, that is simply loss of energy.
turns.speaker: Teacher

turns.text: Cannot drugs put us in touch with higher centres?
turns.speaker: Questioner

turns.text:
The idea of drugs is not new... It was found that interesting states result from a
clever use of drugs. But the system objects to drugs. The use of drugs does not give
good results because drugs cannot affect consciousness, they cannot add
consciousness. By stupefying lower centres they can put us into contact with higher
centres;
but it would be of no use to us, because we can remember only as much as we
have consciousness. Since we have no consciousness, connection with higher centres
will only result in dreams or in unconsciousness.
turns.speaker: Teacher

turns.text:
To me diagrams are only knowledge—I do not get any understanding out of them
that helps me to struggle.
turns.speaker: Questioner

turns.text:
They cannot help with struggling, but they can help your thinking. Even now, in
this initial form, diagrams can help you to solve many of your troubles and problems... They may not
give an answer, but they will give you knowledge about where and how you can look
for an answer. This is the real meaning of diagrams. They speak in a language that
you learn a little ahead.
turns.speaker: Teacher

turns.text:
I want to ask about the big accumulator. I do not understand that
practically.
turns.speaker: Questioner

turns.text:
Efforts! Efforts! The more efforts you make, the more energy you can
get. Without efforts you cannot get energy. Even if it is in you, it may be
in the wrong place. Do not think about it theoretically;
think simply that
you have much energy in you that you never use, and you must make
more efforts to use it.
turns.speaker: Teacher

turns.text: In what way are we under the influence of the moon?
turns.speaker: Questioner

turns.text:
The moon controls all our movements. If I move my arm, it is the moon that
does it, because without the influence of the moon it cannot happen. The moon is like
the weight on an old-fashioned clock and organic life is like the clock mechanism
which is kept going by this weight.
turns.speaker: Teacher

turns.text:
All our mechanicalness depends on the moon. We are like marionettes moved by
wires, but we can be more free of the moon or less free.
turns.speaker: Teacher

turns.text:
At present we cannot move
a step without the energy of the moon;
the wires cannot be cut at once, for then the
marionettes would simply collapse. It is necessary to learn to move first. All sleeping
people are under the influence of the moon.
turns.speaker: Teacher

turns.text:
It is quite simple to establish that we have no permanent 'I'. Try to remember
yourself for fifteen minutes; this will show the degree of your being. If you had a
permanent 'I', you would be able to remember yourself
for fifteen hours I
turns.speaker: Teacher

turns.text:
It is all very simple, really, only we have no keys to our machine. If
we had the keys, it would be easy to open it and see what is inside, and then separate
the imaginary from the real. But even that we have to learn: we are too used to the
unreal.
turns.speaker: Teacher

turns.text: Could we hear more about what Carbon 12 is? Where does it come from?
turns.speaker: Questioner

turns.text:
Carbon 12 may have many different manifestations... It is probably some energy of the emotional centre. But the
important thing is not the source. What is important is how to bring it... Impressions come in as
Oxygen 48 and can be transformed into Nitrogen 24 only with the help of Carbon 12, 
but it happens that exactly at the place where impressions can be assimilated there is
no Carbon 12, or only a little. So we must bring it there by a special effort, and this
effort is self-remembering and self-observation.
turns.speaker: Teacher

turns.text:
I speak in this language because you asked your question in this language, but it can
be observed psychologically. Impressions come in and you do not feel them, which
means that they come and do not go on. But you can make an effort to remember
yourself, and then you begin to notice things... Absence of Carbon 12 at the necessary place means that we are not
emotional enough.
turns.speaker: Teacher

turns.text:
Laughter, in the sense of humour, plays a very important part in connection
with impressions— again remember that I said in an ordinary man... It can be said that for a man on the ordinary level who does not try to understand
what self-remembering means... laughter fulfils a certain
definite function in the organism It replaces self-remembering in a very small,
insufficient way, since it helps quite dull, uninteresting impressions to pass further
and become vivid.
turns.speaker: Teacher

turns.text:
But in higher centres there is no need for it. In higher centres we see things not
as contradictions, not as opposed to one another, but we see them as they are.
turns.speaker: Teacher

turns.text: Laughter seems to have a physiological effect.
turns.speaker: Questioner

turns.text:
Yes, maybe a contradictory impression that cannot be harmonized
produces a tension, and laughter relaxes it.
turns.speaker: Teacher

turns.text:
If
one begins to work, one has a chance. But even in the work there are dangers... if they go on putting off these efforts until to-morrow, then this continual hesitation begins to produce an effect and, after some
time, there comes a dangerous moment.
turns.speaker: Teacher

turns.text:
Then, instead of one, one can become split into two, so that all
features and all personalities are divided into two groups— one part useful to the
work and helping personal work and another part indifferent or even unfriendly. These two groups can continue to exist side by side... one may come in the morning, the other in the afternoon.
turns.speaker: Teacher

turns.text:
This is a real danger, because... weakness and
strength cannot grow at the same time. So it is necessary to struggle very quickly and
ruthlessly against that, otherwise it may lead to double crystallization.
turns.speaker: Teacher

turns.text: I do not understand about the speed of emotions. How can it be measured?
turns.speaker: Questioner

turns.text:
By realizing how many different feelings can pass in you during one thought or
during one swing of the pendulum.
turns.speaker: Teacher

turns.text:
By speed of emotions do you mean the time between the cause and effect of an
emotion?
turns.speaker: Questioner
Teacher

turns.text: The rate varies according to the degree of consciousness?
turns.speaker: Questioner

turns.text:
But, as I said, the emotional centre in us does not work with its
proper speed, because mostly only the moving parts of it work;
and when a centre
works with the moving part its speed is much slower, whereas when it works with the
intellectual part it is much quicker.
turns.speaker: Teacher

turns.text:
There can be no justice in our present state, no justice in prison. The
only thing one can seriously think about when one realizes that one is in prison is how
to escape, not sit and cry about injustice in prison.
turns.speaker: Teacher

turns.text:
People are machines, they are
pushed in a certain way and roll, and when they hit a wall they stop and then begin to
roll back.
turns.speaker: Teacher

turns.text:
The energy in the accumulator gets lower and
lower, and when it is at its lowest he gets tired. Then he makes an effort, or has a short
rest, or yawns, and becomes connected with the second small accumulator.
turns.speaker: Teacher

turns.text:
It is very
interesting that yawning is a special help provided by nature for passing from one
accumulator to
another.
turns.speaker: Teacher

turns.text: When a man yawns, does he connect with the other accumulator?
turns.speaker: Questioner

turns.text:
Not every time... Besides, yawning
is pumping energy, it is not necessarily switching over, although a really
good yawn may produce a switch over when necessary.
turns.speaker: Teacher

turns.text:
Only sincerity and complete recognition of the fact that we are slaves to
mechanicalness and its inevitable results can help us... We can understand what mechanicalness is
and all the horror of mechanicalness only when we do something horrible and fully
realize that it was mechanicalness in us that made us do it.
turns.speaker: Teacher

turns.text:
It may hurt dreadfully, but we must bear it and
try to understand that only by fully confessing it to ourselves can we avoid repeating
it again and again... We can escape from the tentacles of mechanicalness and break its force by big
suffering. If we try to avoid suffering... not only shall we never escape, but
we shall become more and more mechanical.
turns.speaker: Teacher

turns.text: How can a man who realizes his position formulate his aim?
turns.speaker: Questioner

turns.text:
He will see that
the centre of gravity of his position is sleep;
then his aim will be to awake. Or if he sees his mechanicalness, his aim will be to get
rid of mechanicalness. Both come to the same thing.
turns.speaker: Teacher

turns.text:
I see more clearly that what hinders progress is not wanting to escape
mechanicalness sufficiently. How can one intensify the desire to escape?
turns.speaker: Questioner

turns.text:
This is one of the constantly recurring questions which it is almost impossible to
answer... More understanding is necessary, and if you want a complete explanation,
self-remembering, because it is the only real answer. If self-remembering increases,
all the rest increases.
turns.speaker: Teacher

turns.text: So one can never be happy?
turns.speaker: Questioner

turns.text:
Happiness means balance, and balance in our state is impossible, taking balance in
the sense of harmoniousness. We are always balanced in a certain way, but a wrong
way. If we were harmonious in our present state, there would be no reason for us to
change;
so nature arranged it
very well that we cannot be harmonious such as we are, in order that we should not be
happy in this state.
turns.speaker: Teacher

turns.text: Work seems to make one more unhappy.
turns.speaker: Questioner

turns.text:
Study of the system, acquiring more control, cannot make one more unhappy.
There is no abnegation in it. What one has to lose is imagination. Anything that is real
is not an obstacle to awakening. It is the imaginary things that keep us asleep, and
those we have to give up.
turns.speaker: Teacher

turns.text: But if you help a poor person to make his life tolerable?
turns.speaker: Questioner

turns.text:
If you help a poor person, it happens. If someone takes from this poor person what
little remains to him, this also happens. One person will give him a penny, another
will take away the last he has. It is first necessary to understand the principle that
nobody can 'do' anything. If you think of life, not personal life but the life of
humanity, wars, revolutions, you will see this clearly.
turns.speaker: Teacher

turns.text:
You must try to find a right case
for observation... The simplest thing is to try and remember
yourself. Can you do it or not? People think they can 'do' because sometimes they
make certain plans and really get what they wanted. But this only means that they
have got into a certain stream of events and things happened to coincide with their
plan... it is just accident.
turns.speaker: Teacher

turns.text:
When a buffer has gone down, and you see something that seems unbearable, what
is the next step?
turns.speaker: Questioner

turns.text:
All the work is preparation for that. If one does not work but only thinks that one
works and a buffer suddenly disappears by some accident, one finds oneself in a very
unpleasant situation, and one also sees that one only pretended to work. Buffers help
us to pretend instead of really working. This is why people in the ordinary state
cannot have conscience, because if conscience suddenly came, they would go mad.
turns.speaker: Teacher

turns.text:
Buffers are useful in this respect; they help to keep us asleep... So it is not even advisable to destroy buffers before one is
ready. One must be ready first. We can bear ourselves only because we do not know
ourselves. If we knew ourselves as we are, it would be unbearable.
turns.speaker: Teacher

turns.text:
Must we find ordinary standards of conduct, or find new ones in the
work?
turns.speaker: Questioner

turns.text:
Very often we excuse ourselves or find excuses for not remembering
ordinary standards, because we think that we must have new ones... you must understand that you have to follow ordinary standards
until you have new ones.
turns.speaker: Teacher

turns.text:
Should we not find out for ourselves what is right and wrong, and
not be told?
turns.speaker: Questioner

turns.text:
How can you find it out for yourself? People have looked for an
answer to this problem from the creation of the world and have not found
it yet.
turns.speaker: Teacher

turns.text:
There are many things one does deliberately, knowing that they are
wrong, but one is not strong enough to stop it.
turns.speaker: Questioner

turns.text:
Certainly, because if you are mechanical in everything, you cannot
become conscious in only one thing. Besides, deliberately does not mean
consciously; things just happen. If everything happens, one thing cannot
not happen; it has to happen also.
turns.speaker: Teacher

turns.text: If we find out our chief features, can we correct them?
turns.speaker: Questioner

turns.text:
In the ordinary way we cannot. But here it means using the result of experience and
knowledge that does not belong to ordinary life.
turns.speaker: Teacher

turns.text: But an ordinary man changes too.
turns.speaker: Questioner

turns.text:
Of course he changes, he becomes more mechanical, more narrow, more set. There
may be exceptions, but as a rule things do not progress in ordinary life.
turns.speaker: Teacher

turns.text: Having observed a certain tendency in oneself, one decides that it shall not happen.
turns.speaker: Questioner

turns.text:
Usually after one has decided it still goes on happening. Or if it docs not happen,
generally another tendency appears in its place. As a rule only one thing stops things—
fear.
turns.speaker: Teacher

turns.text: Can one see false personality without help?
turns.speaker: Questioner

turns.text:
There is nothing against it theoretically, only I never saw such a case Even with
help, people will not see it. You can show a man a mirror, and he will say, 'This is not
me, it is an artificial mirror, not a real mirror. It is not a reflection of me.'
turns.speaker: Teacher

turns.text: How can one eliminate false personality?
turns.speaker: Questioner

turns.text:
You cannot eliminate it. It is just the same as trying to cut your head off. But you
can make it less insistent, less permanent... If, at a certain moment, you feel the
danger of a manifestation of false personality and you find a way to stop it, this is what
you have to begin with. The question of elimination does not enter at all... You must have control.
turns.speaker: Teacher

turns.text: Could one stop having impressions if one wanted to?
turns.speaker: Questioner

turns.text:
No, certainly not. You cannot stop impressions altogether, but... you can
keep off undesirable impressions and attract to yourself another kind of impressions... For instance, people stand in the street looking at a street accident, and then talk about
it until the next accident. These people collect wrong impressions.
turns.speaker: Teacher

turns.text:
You have to think not so much about choosing the right
impressions as about isolating yourself from wrong impressions. Only by doing this
will you have a certain control. If you try to choose right impressions, you will only
deceive yourself. So, although you cannot bring desirable impressions to yourself, you
can... learn to control them by isolating yourself from
certain kinds of wrong impressions.
turns.speaker: Teacher

turns.text: Do you think there is anything in telepathy?
turns.speaker: Questioner

turns.text:
For men 1, 2 and 3 it does not exist at all;
it is imagination. But men of a much
higher development control forces which can produce so-called telepathy... But ordinary mind and ordinary
emotions cannot do it.
turns.speaker: Teacher

turns.text:
I wonder by what process Jesus was able to expel devils and whether anything in
the system could be used for similar purpose? Has it anything to do with higher
centres?
turns.speaker: Questioner

turns.text:
Jesus probably dealt with big devils. We have to begin with small devils—a kind of
vivisection—until we are able to deal with big devils.
turns.speaker: Teacher

turns.text: I do not understand about the speed of emotions. How can it be measured?
turns.speaker: Questioner

turns.text:
By realizing how many different feelings can pass in you during one thought or
during one swing of the pendulum.
turns.speaker: Teacher

turns.text:
By speed of emotions do you mean the time between the cause and effect of an
emotion?
turns.speaker: Questioner
Teacher

turns.text: The rate varies according to the degree of consciousness?
turns.speaker: Questioner

turns.text:
Your observation will vary... But, as I said, the emotional centre in us does not work with its
proper speed, because mostly only the moving parts of it work;
and when a centre
works with the moving part its speed is much slower, whereas when it works with the
intellectual part it is much quicker.
turns.speaker: Teacher

turns.text: I find that I work for immediate results. Is it a wrong aim?
turns.speaker: Questioner

turns.text:
There is no question of right and wrong: there is only the question of knowing your
aim. Aim must always be in the present and refer to the future.
turns.speaker: Teacher

turns.text: How can one see how to make big efforts?
turns.speaker: Questioner

turns.text:
By making small efforts. You
cannot begin with big efforts. You must begin with small efforts, like, for instance,
trying to remember yourself, or trying to stop thoughts three times a day. It is quite a
small effort, but if you do it regularly, the need or the possibility of a big effort may
come.
turns.speaker: Teacher

turns.text:
When I first came to lectures, I had a very large aim, but now it has got much
smaller.
turns.speaker: Questioner

turns.text:
Yes, aims shrink very much when you begin to work. They start enormous—like
balloons—and then they become quite small, so that you can put them in your pocket.
turns.speaker: Teacher

turns.text: If the substance of the auspicious things was not produced in dependence on anything, there would be no religious practice. There would be neither right nor wrong nor worldly conventions.
turns.speaker: Realist

turns.text: They would be permanent and substantial; because they are permanent they are acausal. [cite_start]While there is no cause there is no arising, remaining, and decay. [cite: 2552, 2563]
turns.speaker: Nagarjuna

turns.text: In this context, the non-existence of religious practice would follow exactly. And there is a contradiction with your own position. Why? [cite_start]Because the Blessed One said that all compounded things are impermanent. [cite: 2557-2558]
turns.speaker: Nagarjuna

turns.text: And if there was no substance, there would also not even be the name "insubstantiality of things," for there is no name without a referent.
turns.speaker: Realist

turns.text: The name "non-existent"—what is this, something existent or again something non-existent? [cite_start]For if it is existent or if it is nonexistent, either way your position is deficient. [cite: 2572-2573]
turns.speaker: Nagarjuna

turns.text: If in this context the name "non-existent" is the name of an existent, to that extent the thesis is abandoned. [cite_start]Moreover, if the name "non-existent" is the name of a non-existent—there is no name of something which does not exist. [cite: 2575-2577]
turns.speaker: Nagarjuna

turns.text: If that statement [of yours] exists substantially, your earlier thesis is refuted. There is an inequality to be explained, and the specific reason for this should be given.
turns.speaker: Realist

turns.text: Moreover, you could think that there should not be this mistake by arguing, "This statement exists substantially and because it is a substance it is not empty. [cite_start]Therefore it negates the substance of all things." We say in reply: If it is like this, your earlier thesis that all things are empty is refuted. [cite: 19-22]
turns.speaker: Realist

turns.text: This speech does not exist substantially, therefore there is no destruction of my position. [cite_start]There is no inequality, and no particular reason to be mentioned. [cite: 161-162]
turns.speaker: Nagarjuna

turns.text: As far as my speech is empty and all the other things are also empty, there is no inequality. If we say "this speech is not empty, yet all the other things are empty," there would be an inequality. [cite_start]But it is not like this. [cite: 165-167]
turns.speaker: Nagarjuna

turns.text: To the extent to which the negation "there is no pot in the house" is precisely a negation of an existent, your negation is a negation of an existing substance.
turns.speaker: Realist

turns.text: Thus the statement "there is no pot in the house" brings about the negation of an existent, not of a non-existent pot. [cite_start]Just in this way, the statement "there is no substance of things" achieves the negation of an existent substance. [cite: 95-98]
turns.speaker: Realist

turns.text: If negation is of an existent thing, is it not that emptiness is established? Because you negate the insubstantiality of things.
turns.speaker: Nagarjuna

turns.text: If negation is of an existent thing and not of a non-existent one, and if you negate the insubstantiality of all things, is it not that the insubstantiality of all things is established? [cite_start]Your speech, which is a negation, establishes emptiness because it is the negation of the insubstantiality of all things. [cite: 351-353]
turns.speaker: Nagarjuna

turns.text: If, sire, you walk at noon-time on the hot scorching ground, trampling on sharp grit, pebbles and sand, your feet will hurt you, your body will be tired, your mind will be disturbed and you will suffer bodily pain. Now, did you come on foot or in a vehicle?
turns.speaker: Nāgasena

turns.text: I, revered sir, did not come on foot. I came in a chariot.
turns.speaker: King Milinda

turns.text: If, sire, you came in a chariot, show me the chariot. Is the pole the chariot, sire?
turns.speaker: Nāgasena

turns.text: No, revered sir.
turns.speaker: King Milinda

turns.text: Is the axle the chariot?
turns.speaker: Nāgasena

turns.text: No, revered sir.
turns.speaker: King Milinda

turns.text: Are the wheels the chariot?
turns.speaker: Nāgasena

turns.text: No, revered sir.
turns.speaker: King Milinda

turns.text: Then, sire, are the pole, the axle, the wheels, the body, the flag-staff, the yoke, the reins, the goad all together the chariot?
turns.speaker: Nāgasena

turns.text: No, revered sir.
turns.speaker: King Milinda

turns.text: Well then, sire, is the chariot apart from the pole, the axle, the wheels, the body, the flag-staff, the yoke, the reins and the goad?
turns.speaker: Nāgasena

turns.text: No, sire.
turns.speaker: King Milinda

turns.text: Sire, though I have been asking you repeatedly, I do not see this chariot. Chariot is only a sound. What then is the chariot you say you came in? You, sire, have spoken a falsehood, an untruth. There is no chariot.
turns.speaker: Nāgasena

turns.text: I am not, revered sir, speaking a lie. It is because of the pole, because of the axle, the wheels, the body, the flag-staff, the yoke, the reins and because of the goad that ‘chariot’ exists as a mere designation.
turns.speaker: King Milinda

turns.text: It is good, sire, that you understand a chariot. Even so is it for me, sire, because of the hairs of the head … because of the urine, because of material form … because of consciousness, that ‘Nāgasena’ exists as a mere designation. However, in the ultimate sense there is no person as such that is found.
turns.speaker: Nāgasena

turns.text: Revered Nāgasena, will you converse with me?
turns.speaker: King Milinda

turns.text: I will converse if you, sire, will converse in the speech of the learned, but if you converse in the speech of kings I will not converse.
turns.speaker: Nāgasena

turns.text: How, revered Nāgasena, do the learned converse?
turns.speaker: King Milinda

turns.text: When the learned are conversing, sire, there is a turning over and an unravelling of the subject; then there is a refutation and an acknowledgement of a mistake; distinctions and contradistinctions are drawn; yet, thereby, they are not angered. It is thus, sire, that the learned converse.
turns.speaker: Nāgasena

turns.text: And how, revered sir, do kings converse?
turns.speaker: King Milinda

turns.text: When kings are conversing, sire, they approve of some matter and order punishment for anyone who disagrees with that matter, saying: ‘Inflict a punishment on him.’ It is thus, sire, that kings converse.
turns.speaker: Nāgasena

turns.text: I, revered sir, will converse in the speech of the learned, not in the speech of kings. Let the revered one converse unreservedly as he converses with a monk or a novice or a lay follower or with a monastery attendant. Let the revered one converse thus, let him not be afraid.
turns.speaker: King Milinda

turns.text: Revered Nāgasena, is he who uprises the same or is he another?
turns.speaker: King Milinda

turns.text: Neither the same nor another. What do you think about this, sire? Now that you are grown up are you the same as you were when you were a boy, young, tender, lying on your back?
turns.speaker: Nāgasena

turns.text: No, revered sir. That boy, young, tender, lying on his back was one thing. I, who am now full-grown, am another.
turns.speaker: King Milinda

turns.text: That being so, sire, you can have no mother, nor can you have a father, nor can you have a teacher... It is one ‘I’ that was the boy, young, tender, lying on his back and it is the same ‘I’ that am now full-grown, and all these are held together as a unity in dependence on this body itself.
turns.speaker: Nāgasena

turns.text: Make a simile.
turns.speaker: King Milinda

turns.text: It is as if, sire, some person might light a lamp. Would it burn all night long?
turns.speaker: Nāgasena

turns.text: Yes, revered sir, it might burn all night long.
turns.speaker: King Milinda

turns.text: Is the flame of the first watch of the night the same as the flame of the middle watch?
turns.speaker: Nāgasena

turns.text: No, revered sir.
turns.speaker: King Milinda

turns.text: Is the flame of the middle watch the same as the flame of the third watch?
turns.speaker: Nāgasena

turns.text: No, revered sir.
turns.speaker: King Milinda

turns.text: Is it then, sire, that the lamp in the first watch was one thing, the lamp in the middle watch another, and the lamp in the third watch still another?
turns.speaker: Nāgasena

turns.text: No, revered sir, it was burning all through the night in dependence on itself.
turns.speaker: King Milinda

turns.text: Even so, sire, a continuity of phenomena is linked together. It uprises as one and ceases as another, linked together as though there were no before and no after. Hence it is neither the same nor another, but the subsequent consciousness is reckoned (together with) the preceding consciousness.
turns.speaker: Nāgasena

turns.text: Revered Nāgasena, who takes rebirth?
turns.speaker: King Milinda

turns.text: Mind-and-matter, sire, takes rebirth.
turns.speaker: Nāgasena

turns.text: What, is it this same mind-and-matter itself that takes rebirth?
turns.speaker: King Milinda

turns.text: This same mind-and-matter does not itself take rebirth, sire; but, sire, by means of this mind-and-matter one does a good or bad deed and, because of this deed, another mind-and-matter takes rebirth.
turns.speaker: Nāgasena

turns.text: If, revered sir, this mind-and-matter itself does not take rebirth would one not be freed from evil deeds?
turns.speaker: King Milinda

turns.text: If, sire, it did not take rebirth one would be freed from evil deeds. But because, sire, it takes rebirth one is not freed from evil deeds. ... Suppose, sire, some man were to steal another man’s mangoes and the owner of the mangoes were to seize him and bring him before the king... and he were to say, ‘Your majesty, I did not steal his mangoes; the mangoes he planted were different from these that I stole; I do not deserve punishment.’ Would he, sire, not deserve punishment?
turns.speaker: Nāgasena

turns.text: Yes, revered sir, he would deserve punishment.
turns.speaker: King Milinda

turns.text: For what reason?
turns.speaker: Nāgasena

turns.text: Whatever he may say, the mangoes he stole resulted from the mangoes which, he admits, the other man planted.
turns.speaker: King Milinda

turns.text: Even so, sire, by means of this mind-and-matter one does a good or bad deed and, because of this deed, another mind-and-matter takes rebirth; therefore, one is not freed from evil deeds.
turns.speaker: Nāgasena

turns.text: Revered Nāgasena, is there such a thing as an experiencer?
turns.speaker: King Milinda

turns.text: What does this ‘experiencer’ mean, sire?
turns.speaker: Nāgasena

turns.text: A soul within that sees a visible form with the eye, hears a sound with the ear... Just as we who are sitting here in the palace can look out of any window we want to look out of, even so, revered sir, this soul within can look out of any door it wants to look out of.
turns.speaker: King Milinda

turns.text: I will talk to you, sire, about the five doors. Listen and attend carefully. If the soul within sees a visible form through the eye just as we who are sitting here in the palace can look out of any window we want to look out of... can it not hear a sound, smell a smell, taste a taste, feel a touch and discriminate mental states through each of the other five doors besides the one you have specified in each case?
turns.speaker: Nāgasena

turns.text: No, revered sir.
turns.speaker: King Milinda

turns.text: Again, sire, we who are sitting here in the palace will see visible forms out there before us more clearly in the great space if these network windows are removed. Thus too, would this soul within see visible forms more clearly when the doors of the eyes are removed? And if the ears were removed, the nose removed, the tongue removed, the body removed, would it hear a sound, smell a smell, taste a taste and feel a touch more clearly on account of the great space?
turns.speaker: Nāgasena

turns.text: No, revered sir.
turns.speaker: King Milinda

turns.text: Because, sire, of the eye and visible form eye-consciousness arises. ... Thus these things are produced from a condition and there is no experiencer found here.
turns.speaker: Nāgasena
